records.title: PREFACE
records.text:
PREFACE

This thesis began a long time ago. The tradition of Savoy College came to have a part in my knowledge of far-away things in my childhood as I garnered it bit by bit from reminiscent talks of my mother, Mrs. Pamela Paxton Boyd, who attended the College—music, primary, preparatory, and collegiate departments—for the fourteen years of its existence. With passing years its particular corner of my memory became a storehouse of pleasant but somewhat unrelated stories of the students, teachers, and customs of the time.

When, therefore, a more mature appreciation of the significance of this pioneer college to Texan education in the '80s suggested the appropriateness of a thesis on its history, the research was naturally motivated by a strong personal interest and sentiment. Through exchange of many letters and later through personal contacts, the unrelated incidents from my memory store began to take on reality; and the isolated facts began to take on meaning and order. The most helpful source of information throughout the year's work on this thesis has been my mother, who has recognized identified faces in pictures; verified and supplemented information as it came to me; aided in tracing through the degrees of kinship, marriage, and personal relationships, the causes, courses, and methods; and in reliving her college days as the work progressed, supplied the enthusiasm necessary for carrying it through. First place in the long list of those to whom I express gratefulness I therefore accord to my mother.

In the same vein of deep gratitude I acknowledge the enthusiastic and friendly help of my mother's schoolmates—ex-students of Savoy College—who have made possible or more possible the detail of this study by their letters and by entertaining me in their homes and libraries. Their help was so fundamental that their names are officially listed

records.title: Chapter I — Plan and Scope of the Work
records.text:
Chapter I

Plan and Scope of the Work

WHY THE STUDY WAS UNDERTAKEN

The idea of treating the history of Savoy College as a thesis arose after a scattering of ex-students of the College had requested some research work to be done from a file of Bonham newspapers, available then at The University of Texas Library. These ex-students had waited a history written; however, at that time it was desired to have it very brief. The idea grew; interest grew; preliminary research revealed that the College had been unique in several important points, and that in its brief span of fourteen years it had created a definite place in the growth of public education in Texas before the State had made adequate provision for that important branch of formal schooling. This research showed also that the College was not so far removed from reach that much material, enough valuable data were available to make the undertaking worthwhile.

Ever present has been the author's desire to gather and present facts that may aid ex-students to keep their college days in memory and to record for future historians the workings of an able and much-loved educator—Professor R. R. Halsell—and his noteworthy pioneering school.

SOURCES OF INFORMATION

The richest source of material for this history has been found in the ex-students themselves. Between twenty-five and forty-five letters, representing correspondence with about forty different students (together with more than forty-five personal interviews), have been most helpful in the endeavor to gather data of the College as it was more than fifty years ago.

Ex-students have frequently stated, fixing dates and certifying official data by relating incidents. Invaluable aids in this matter have been the college-printed copies of The Platonian Messenger, published by the Platonian Liter-

(1)

records.title: Page 17
records.text:
The Savoy Male and Female College

ary society of the College, preserved by Judge Lee A. Clark, Mrs. V. E. Conway, and Mr. W. I. Hunt. Other old newspaper files were of assistance, among the most helpful being The Bonham News, The Chriesman Star, The Roy Savoy Star, and The Dallas News.

Documentary data have been gleaned from the original charter, the Biennial Report of the Secretary of State, 1879-1883, The Official Register of State and County Officers, and other official documents. Maps have identified the early Fannin County deed records, the charter of the Platonian Literary Society has been preserved, photographs show the Arts diploma issued in 1887, and two diplomas of years 1889 and 1890.

Books, as source material for this study, have been of very little value except for a book of biographical notes, pictorial Souvenir of Texas, published in 1889, and Carter's History of Fannin County. The lack of Texas history books of value made necessary an extended use of newspaper files and social foundation upon which this institution was built, a brief sketch of its origin, the list of known trustees and faculty members of the College. Other books have served as comparative data only.

ORGANIZATION OF THE MATERIAL

The skeleton framework of an historical study, of course, is the chronological account; in this case the natural gain of interest in the study suggested that the organization and operation of the College, on the one hand, the social life and customs of the time, on the other, should each serve their respective purposes. Chapter VIII is devoted to this point, and the formation of an ex-students' association to preserve its tradition made itself more accessible to make itself more readily to organization on the basis of nature of subject matter than to division into chronological periods. Chapter II therefore describes the locale of Savoy as a field for educational enterprise. It relates as its setting the early Fannin County history, its growth in population and its educational development. It shows briefly that important in the more noted, however, were strictly taken by the older forms of fifty years ago—marked evidence of the strong minded, marked evidence of "compensation" or "substitution." The end of the narrative is marked by the additional comments on the trustees and faculty members of The Savoy Male and Female College. A biographical-pictorial Souvenir of Texas in 1889 reveal a constant recurrence of stories of the return and the a discouraging few years after the War set forth for Texas, arrived with nothing but ambition and energy, and within five to ten years had paid out a sizable and valuable farm and was on the way to becoming, if not affluent, by the standards of the time, even a wealthy man by middle age.

records.title: Page 18
records.text:
The Savoy Male and Female College

Chapter III therefore describes the early years of Savoy College, 1876-1880, setting forth its aims and objectives from the point of view of those immediately connected with it.

Chapter IV, the main chapter from the chronological viewpoint, traces the expansion of the College in its administration, curriculum, equipment, and enrollment—from its incorporation in 1880 to its close in 1890. Numerous original documents are recorded through photostats and transcript in the interest of completeness and authenticity.

Chapter V, of interest sociologically, undertakes to picture the student life of the College—not uncritically, not abstractly, but rather as the campus activities of the period have been brought to life for the author first hand through the memories of those who participated in and observed them themselves. The present generation will doubtless find the campus life not so different from that of today. Some things in the mores now, however, were strictly taboo by the older forms of fifty years ago. These things, brought back in reminiscent stories, were then in a transitory state and there is found in the narrative illustration of the clearly marked evidence of "compensation" or "substitution."

Chapter VI is a chapter of biography. It presents comments on the trustees and faculty members of The Savoy Male and Female College. A biographical-pictorial Souvenir of Texas in 1889 reveal a constant recurrence of stories of the return and the social foundation upon which this institution was built, a brief sketch of its origin, the list of known trustees and faculty members of the College. Other books have served as comparative data only.

records.title: Chapter II — The Locale of Savoy as a Field for Educational Enterprise
records.text:
Chapter II

The Locale of Savoy as a Field for
Educational Enterprise

Savoy Male and Female College owed its unusual growth to a combination of favorable factors, not the least of which was the nature of the locale in which it took root. Hardy pioneers had fought back the Indians a generation before the College was founded and devastating set-back of the Civil War had been overcome; and the section, a rich agricultural area, had entered upon a quarter century of economic progress and increase in population. The character of the population, too, was an important factor in the school's growth, for they who had been accustomed in an appreciation of culture and a demand for education.

ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT OF FANNIN COUNTY

FANNIN COUNTY DEED RECORDS. The Bonham News-Annual of 1884 gives the following list of pioneer history of the County of Fannin:

"Among the pioneers of Fannin County who drove back the bands of prowling Indians and opened up the way for civilization were Judge Bailey Ingish and his family, John L. German, John Thomas Ashcraft, and many other well-known, brave settlers. In 1836, R. H. Leeks, Thos. Journey, Jacob Black, Daniel Kitchens, Samuel Ligons, Isaac Newton, Thomas Ligons, James S. Baker, the Hunters, the Savoys, the Cox family, and Thomas E. Hooper and others who settled near the present site of Bonham. These are by no means all, as we have a reverence for these noble men who wore them [?] for their kindness, endurance, and bravery—armed with stout hearts and buried beneath the sod of the land they so bravely defended."

records.title: Page 20
records.text:
The Savoy Male and Female College

POST-WAR GROWTH IN POPULATION AND ITS CHARACTER

—A glance at the census figures gives a graphic picture of the growth of Fannin County following the Civil War. In 1860 the County population was 9,217; by 1870 it had reached 13,207; and during the next two decades it almost tripled, going from about 20,000 as the population was reported in 1880 and "over 40,000" by 1888. The rapid increase in population had brought in a varied family of the period. Most families had from six to eight children, families of ten children were not uncommon, and many had even more. But an equally important factor was the amount and character of the population. Like any of the less than most Southern states the economic destituteness of the war, and to many a young man who returned from the War for the Lost Cause to find his home in ruins and his financial resources gone, the opportunity of the Red River appeared as a promising land of new hope, and thither they greatly emigrated. Biographies make clear that the greatest number of Texas settlers who built up the social and economic foundation of the area brought their families from the older Southern states.

From the typical biographies it is seen that this element in the growing population of Fannin County was not of the ordinary pioneering adventurer type. Most of them, having the best culture of the Old South and were from families where good education and some wealth had prevailed. In many cases the war had interrupted the school or college career in the making of the student; there was no inclination to keep from the children what the parents had missed. Indeed, quite commonly the lack of completed education was the earnest motivation for seeing that his child should have it.

THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE 7

MANNERS AND CUSTOMS.—Equally enlightening and interesting is Mr. Carter's observation of some points of manners and customs of a people who were becoming homogeneous in their development of the section:

Native peculiarities and cosmopolitan ideas have combined to produce some strange manners and customs among the people of this county.

This peculiarity is naturally noticed in all classes. As a general thing, among lawyers for instance, a man will be consulted frankly on the merits of the society of which he is a member; but not so here. A lawyer or a doctor is an exception, and the general public is quite free to make such statement. The members of fractional class have none of the bland suave manners, peculiar to the doctor. No, they are apt to be a little rough.

The people seem to think that the professional man was made for the officers of their own class. His confidence was made for all the citizens of the rural community, not offered to any objector.

In every kind of labor, except perhaps on farms, the ten-hour system seems to prevail over all here. Men not accustomed to it, the men, during the season not accustomed to it, look, upon it something of a wonder. The sun is high in the heavens.

During a certain week in each month, the public square is a scene of busy life, and the streets around it are crowded with people. This is the day for the sale or stray stock, and since the establishment of the town on the "first Monday" to buy critics, the people have grazed from far and near, and the show of stock reaches grand proportions. Every man on the square is a trader, and trading is the principal occupation; a good time, and every man thinks he lives in the best country, if the sun is in the day's possession.

On these occasions, much of the fine stock of the county is to be seen. Those who keep stallions, jacks,

and bulls for the season bring them out on the square and exhibit them. Flaming posters containing the age, size, and pedigree of the animal are circulated. About one o'clock the sales are made, and kept up until late in the afternoon. At night a general auction of all kinds of stock is carried on.

EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT OF THE SECTION

PUBLIC SCHOOLS.—That such a population should readily take advantage of the provisions for public schools included in the Constitution of 1876 was to be expected. A cross-section of public-school development in Fannin County is quoted from Carter's History of Fannin County for this and other counties in the area:

The County Judge, by virtue of his office, is superintendent of the schools of the county, which is an ex officio district school superintendent. The annual apportionment of school funds from the State government to each of these communities is fifty-nine pupils. The apportionment of funds from the State in 1885 is $5.30 to each child of scholastic age, and, by all accounts, these facts are very revealing in their import. The annual apportionment of funds from the State government keeps pace with the increase of pupils, by reason of accrued interest on the continued use and addition to the free school fund.

The number enrolled for the district free schools enrolled for the next term of free schools, which open in September, are 3,706, from which, of course, must be deducted all for free schools. The enrollment of 781 do not know how to read; of the 1,029 colored children, there are 388 who can not read.

All the schools are presided over by competent, and most of them thorough teachers, whose testimonials and certificates from third to first degree are granted, when the applicant shows to the satisfaction of the Board of Examiners that he is well educated, and is not confined to text books, but has attended (and very properly) to the importance of clear methods of imparting knowledge, and to his thorough acquisition of the most improved modes of teaching. The directors, also, qualify the teachers of the common

schools for their work, a system of "Blue Ribbon" schools has been inaugurated, the beneficent effects of which are already felt and appreciated. These schools are taught in the summer time and consist of thorough qualifications, appointed by the State Superintendent of Public Education.

All the free schools in this section of Grayson county are attended by children from the Choctaw nation. Teachers say they learn rapidly, and some are not disposed to thoroughly comply with the rules and school discipline.

Among the Teachers' Association mentioned is one at Dodd City to meet at different places in the county at regular intervals for the benefit of all. This association seem to have been the perfection of a uniform method of teaching, and in a more efficient manner. The closing exercises of the free schools, academies, and colleges in this section are thorough. The examinations are followed by exhibitions, the exhibitions by picnics, all at the beginning of June.⁸

PRIVATE SCHOOLS AND COLLEGES.—Before the public-school system had been established and was able to take care of the needs of primary and secondary education, this section had already developed several prosperous private schools; and because the century was almost at its end before the system was firmly established in the listed in the North Texas area, the responsibility of collegiate education in the private schools and churches during the 'eighties.

In addition to this school which is the subject of this study, other colleges in operation in Fannin County during the period were a school established as the Lawyers' Institute of collegiate rank, at Ladonia; Carlton College and the Calvert Female Institute at Ladonia; and Fulton College, for boys, at Bonham; The Walcott Institute at Honey Grove; and the McKinney College at McKinney, twenty-five miles over in Grayson County, also, the long established Austin College at that time at Sherman; and the most famous of them, here, was the widely known Kidd-Key College

legs for women; and in the latter part of the period (1887) Grayson College was established at Whitewright.

THE FOUNDING AND GROWTH OF SAVOY

THE FOUNDER OF SAVOY.—The town of Savoy, which was founded in 1872, derived its classic name from its founder, William Louis Marshall Savoy, better known as Colonel William Savoy. He was born in Mississippi in 1818, and received a liberal education including training in modern languages which he never applied in practice.⁹

Colonel Savoy came to Texas when he was a very young man and settled at Bonham. The town bearing his name is not yet known as the Savoy Plantation.

Colonel Savoy was a man of adventurous spirit. In 1849 he joined the crowd in the California gold rush, making his trip to water, a professional scout. He was stricken with pick and shovel and brought back to Texas golden nuggets in a heavy commercial way.

During the Civil War Colonel Savoy enlisted in the Confederate Army, at least at a captain, but he received a wound in his foot which kept him out of active service. For the next few years he travelled on the Missouri-Pacific and the Pacific three times. His daughter, Mrs. Ada Savoy Travis, thinks the travelling was in connection with the Pony Service. She recalls that her father related many of his experiences in her when he was much older. He told how once he was left behind in an Indian attack without his hat, and once when he was in Central America he learned that yellow fever was raging, but a kind friend lent him a hat. He also left four hundred acres of rich land, but never lived to enjoy them.

It was about 1870 that Colonel Savoy moved to Fannin County. He took on the location of the new town and saw that Mr. William B. Smith was about to lose. A deed filed in Bonham, in October 1872, shows that Savoy sold to the Transcontinental Railroad (now the Texas and Pacific) forty acres of land — this is the site on which the town stands — for the occasion to have the town named for him. Part of this is the site on which the Savoy depot was built. He also gave

records.title: Page 26
records.text:
THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE 11

the road right-of-way through his land on both sides extending almost to Bells, two miles away.

On April 15, 1872, the charter for the city was filed. Deed records show that many of Colonel Savoy's town lots were sold for $150, $200, and some for $250. He donated the lot upon which the Methodist Episcopal Church was built.

Before moving to Fannin County, Colonel Savoy had been twice married. His second wife came with him to his new home where he reared a family of seven.¹⁰

In 1880 Colonel Savoy's health failed and he went to a health resort, but died on the way at the town of Johnson City and was buried there in August. Mrs. Savoy survived him two decades. His grave is dated August 7, 1908.¹¹

THE SAVOY OF THE COLLEGE PERIOD.—The richness of the surrounding territory and the advent of the railroad made the new town to grow fast. The old town, which was completely destroyed by a cyclone in 1850, it was quickly rebuilt; by 1882 it had become a lively and prosperous town.

Probably the next largest town to Honey Grove, in point of size and commerce, in Savoy. This town has built up very rapidly since the Texas and Pacific Railroad, on which it is situated, about four miles west of Sherman at a town called Bells in Grayson County, running a southeast direction. It is a chartered institution, and perhaps takes the lead of all colleges in the county. The churches and institutions of worship in the matter of church buildings are meager. One hundred still standing, the different denominations.¹²

12 THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

Savoy exports annually about 10,000 bushels of wheat, 20,000 of oats, from 7,000 to 10,000 bushels of corn, and from 3,000 to 4,000 bales of cotton. Savoy is noted for the large amount of country produce it ships annually, outside of cotton, corn, and other grain. The number of chickens and eggs and the amount of butter and fruit shipped out every year from this town is probably larger than that of any other town of its size in North Texas. Its trade from the country south, like Bonham's, was impaired by the building of the Missouri-Pacific, which crosses Texas-Pacific four miles west at a town called Bells in Grayson County, running a southeast direction through a fertile and thickly populated portion of the county. As the figures representing its trade will show, however, the town of Savoy has a solid agricultural district at her back, and one that is amply able to double her exports.

Six dry goods houses and as many groceries, a drug store, saddlery and harness, blacksmith and wood shops, a livery stable, and two mills and gins constitute the business portion of the town. The town is regularly laid off, but without the inevitable "square" in the centre. The inhabitants of Savoy, and the country surrounding it are intelligent, industrious, and quiet people. It is a rare thing to see any of them in the courts on account of a civil or criminal matter.⁸

Chapter III

The Founding and Early Years of the College

FIRST SCHOOLS IN SAVOY

Early Savoy settlers recall that the first school house was a one-roomed log cabin. The teacher was Mrs. Calkins, the depot agent's wife. The second school was taught by a one-armed man, Professor Abernathy, who the whole county had lost one arm while in service. He taught in Jackson Hall, a building with a large assembly room, more of a "Singing School."

The time and duration of these schools is uncertain; but in April of 1876 a Mr. F. J. Abernathy advertised in The Christian Messenger, a monthly religious periodical, a school in Savoy. The advertisement described the school as a "county seminary before the college." This lasted only through the brief term, you are therefore preparing a school during the next year in Savoy.

Professor R. B. Halsel, who had purchased the Abernathy school in 1882, and, perhaps in taking and moving had moved to Savoy, and, perhaps in the early part of 1876, opened the doors of a school with just thirty-eight pupils in attendance.

ASSOCIATION WITH THE REVEREND LEWIS HOLLAND

About the middle of the first school year (early in 1877), Mr. Halsel was joined in his labors, if modest, undertaking by one Lewis Holland, who is described as a well-established scholar, a minister of the Baptist Church, and a teacher of considerable experience. For a year these two men had led students together and at Ladonia College. For the ten years following 1877, Mr. Holland had been teaching and farming in the neighborhood of Whitewright.²³

Both the aforementioned men, who, for the next ten years were to work in fine harmony in building the small school in Savoy into a college, appear to have been most auspicious things. In personality and abilities each complement[ed] the other. Mr. Halsel, three years the younger, was of the more popular type, to receiving more immediate consideration and consideration. Mr. Holland was of the quieter, more reserved in nature, profoundly learned and perhaps the more to be commended consideration.

Chapter IV

The Incorporation and Expansion of the College, 1880-1890

INCORPORATION AND CHARACTERIZATION

INCORPORATION.—By 1880 the Halsel-Holland school had grown to such importance and the tracking of the students was so well appreciated that formalities could be expected. The 1880 catalog gives 1879 as the date of incorporation; the actual charter, as recorded in the state legislature. The charter, which was granted on January 22, 1880. The incorporators were James Paxton, J. B. Chenoweth, R. J. Abernathy, R. B. Halsel, and Lewis Holland, of whose photographs and biographical sketches appear in Chapter VI. The charter was filed in the Department of State February 14, 1880. It stipulated that the institution shall be called SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE; that the purpose for which it was established was "to maintain a School or Seminary of Learning for the education of Males and Females in the useful and ornamental branches of education; to employ the Faculty of said school to confer the degrees of Bachelor of Arts, Bachelor of Science, and such other degrees of Proficiency, and to Issue such Diplomas as the Institution shall be entitled to grant;" and that the charter should be for a period of fifty years; that the number of trustees should not be less than five and not more than fifteen (five are named); and that they should have power to elect their successors or to fill vacancies within the said time; should reside in Fannin County; and that the amount of capital stock of the corporation was not less than $1,500, in shares of two hundred and fifty.

A COEDUCATIONAL FEATURE.—In providing for the equal education of males and females, the charter of Savoy College appears to have recorded a dis-

records.title: Page 34
records.text:
THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE 19

tinctive forward step in the progress of coeducation; it seems to have been the first collegiate institution chartered in Texas in which both sexes took the same academic privileges without discrimination. This academic equality between the sexes had been recognized from the beginning of the College history in 1876. Coeducation was not new in Texas in 1876, but its acceptance in Texas had been rather slow.

Basque College, chartered in 1870, was one of the first in Texas to practice coeducation; then followed Waco University in 1865. But most of the early Texas colleges still maintained a separate system for the two sexes, and some schools even until the establishment of Sam Houston Normal, chartered in 1879, and in 1877, but its acceptance in Texas had been rather slow.

The catalog seems to make its appearance in years of growth in secondary education, it is evident that there is a considerable advance in secondary colleges. The growth in size of the faculty, however, may trace to their process.

with each other. With a desire to provide for the social development of young men and women, it is proper to call attention to the fact that this institution is not a "Young Ladies' Seminary." Parents who wish their daughters to have the advantages of an ideal control which some schools exercise over their pupils could not send their daughters to the University of Texas. Only earnest young women, imbued with a desire to profit by the methods of advanced education would be benefited by the institution. It is proper that young men, should attend an institution where coeducational principles prevail, as it is proper that they should attend other higher institutions of learning, open to males and females on equal terms.²⁷

GROWTH IN ENROLLMENT.—The coeducational policy doubtless served a purpose in furthering the rapid development of Savoy College in the face of its competition, for approximately forty per cent of the student body at any one moment was made up of females. Concurrent enrollment statistics for all years are not available; but those for 1884-1885 show that enrollment was well above two hundred students. Over 250 were reported by 1881; 369 were enrolled in 1880-1884; 375 were enrolled with the increase of pupils, by reason of the years.

Catalogue of Savoy College.

LOCATION.

Savoy is situated eleven miles west from Denison, in a healthy locality. Its people are largely and liberally educated, believing it their duty to educate at least their children, if not themselves.

FACULTY.

The Faculty of this college is composed of more than the average council of the students, consisting of more than one hundred students; and its results and public esteem toward their pupils have been greatly lauded by the same.

LITERARY SOCIETIES.

There are two literary societies connected with this College — the Fluvanna and the Athenian.

Board can be had at ten dollars per month. The Faculty have assured us that those desiring to board themselves can board themselves at from three to four dollars per month.

SAW HOUSTON HALL.

In addition to the large number of existing Main Streets on the ground, there will be a large building erected, at the expense of the Board of Trustees, as a dormitory for the Students—both Ladies and Gentlemen will be accommodated—it will contain at least one hall.

Our Faculty.

It is the object of the faculty to make the course of instruction not merely theoretical, but also practical. All those facilities for acquiring an education may be had at lower rates than anywhere else in this city, county, or any other county, state or other parts of Texas.

We aim to instruct students, practical, thorough work throughout.

In the future, as in the past, we shall labor with all our ability to assist our students to reach the goal of perfection, to our charges, and to arouse in them a love for learning and a desire to excel.]

    By the year 1887-1888 this curriculum had been strengthened and re-formed in a number of significant ways:

    Elocution had been added to the Freshman year’s work; Composition and Declamation to the Sophomore and Senior; and a course in Botany to the Junior. A note had added “A Select Course in Reading” to the Senior.

    Physiology, absent from Sophomore to Freshman, had become Anatomy. Physiology and Hygiene. Meteorology and Botany had been added to the second year’s schedule; Zoology to the third; and Geology to the fourth.

    Ancient History enriched the new Sophomore work, as did also Logic; Mental Philosophy had been added to the Junior Schedule, and Mental and Moral Science to the Senior.

    Juvenal had been substituted for Quintilian and Pliny in the last year’s Latin authors, and the Alcestis had been dropped from the Greek reading list.

    French, or German, as alternate choices, had been added to the Freshman and Sophomore language requirements.

    The complete program for the A.B. degree, as published in the catalog for 1887-1888, was scheduled as follows:

    Although the schedule of this course by years and terms is not available, still the amount of time devoted to some of the subjects, as for instance the Mathematics, suggests the scheduling of similar subjects for the degree courses, the comprehensiveness of subject matter, and the amount of time required to complete the entire course. The "Higher Arithmetic and University Algebra" courses took their titles from the names of the respective texts, Robinson's Higher Arithmetic and Robinson's University Algebra, which together seem to account for a year's work in mathematics. Meteorology and Trigonometry accounted for at least another one-third year's work in mathematics. Similarly, under the Natural Science subjects, the textbook basis for the courses in Chemistry and in Physics may have determined the amount of work done on them. The original of the one of which a photograph appears was used in Savoy College and was priced at five dollars. The Art work included water color and oil painting and pencil sketching; instruction was, it can be estimated, from the scheduling for the degree course, at a half year each. A language course was probably available; but when violin instruction was offered there were very limited choices—Mr. J. D.     Commercial Art.—In addition to the academic courses described above, the Savoy College curriculum included at all times a complete commercial department, and through all of its years either maintained departments of music and art or cooperated informally with private teachers of these subjects with studios in the college buildings or adjoining the campus that work in these branches was regarded as an integral part of the curriculum by many of the parents. The commercial course—including bookkeeping, business arithmetic, and business penmanship—was conducted by President Halsel and his faculty in cooperation with visiting commercial teachers. They are Kyger and George Harshaw from about 1882 to 1884, when these two are listed in Grayson County as having labeled the Gale City Commercial School.³⁴ The next year (1884-1885) Mr. J. D. Warren is listed in The Plainsman Messenger as Principal of the Commercial Department and Mr. L. J. (Lee) Montgomery as well as being listed as Professor of Business Penmanship for the year 1886-1887.     Evaluation of the Curriculum.

Its Place in the Development of American Education.—The curriculum of Savoy College, viewed in the perspective of a half-century's clarifying experience, shows an interesting cross-section of American education during the

³³Personal letter from Mr. John Glen, Odessa, Texas, July 20, 1934.
³⁴Grayson County Directory 1882-3, p. 48; and p. 64. Reynolds, July 21, 1934.

records.title: Page 67
records.text:
52      The Savoy Male and Female College

a transitional period. The preponderant increment of Latin and Greek language, literature, and composition, with a vestige of religious teaching (moral philosophy and "Evidences of Christianity") in its comprehensive A.B. degree course shows the still-abiding power of the classical American college ideal—the classic training for the clergy—while the elimination of Greek from the B.S. degree course and of all foreign language from the diploma course shows the decline of this influence and the new trend that has constituted the present high school program. But the courses close second shows the influence of a later and divergent tendency—that of the rising state universities—to make mathematics as an academically cultural or disciplinary subject had been as firmly established a course that it might well have been regarded as "classic" by the time of Savoy College's span. The emphasis on applied mathematics, carried so far as to include surveying and navigation, was perhaps inspired by what Mr. Curry calls, in his analysis of practical needs.

Typical American College Standards of the Period.—An adequate comparative evaluation of the curriculum of Savoy College, however, requires that it be measured against standards common to its time and locale. A composite measuring stick for such purposes may be found in the following nutshell characterization of post-Civil War colleges in the United States in a historical study of American higher educational standards and attainments made by Professor Andrew Fleming West's backward look at the colleges, presented in his monograph, "The American College," written in 1909:

    . . . The American college, as contrasted with European schools, is a secondary institution, the name college notwithstanding. It enrolled boys who had passed regularly of a fourteen-year course of study leading to the bachelor's degree—or who had had four years of college-preparatory training on top of eight years of secondary education, with some anticipations of university courses toward the end of the school's duration.³⁸ But these embryonic university studies were usually taught as recitations rather than real college lectures, even in the better Eastern colleges of the time. Boys entered college when they were fifteen or sixteen years of age. The course of preparation did not often exceed twenty years. Typical Lower-class Recitations.—A typical lower-class recitation began, according to descriptions of ex-students, with the teacher's command to, "Come forward, please!" This order meant that the class should step up to the "recitation benches" at the front of the room and facing the rostrum. The person reciting was expected to step up on the rostrum where he could be seen and heard by all. If the class happened to be a Spelling class, a chalk line was drawn along a plank on the floor and the pupils were called to "Toe the Line." The teachers' rules required that, in order to keep a straight and orderly line, the pupils' toes should reach to, and not over, the line at once. If a student persisted in stretching one or both arms and squirming about, the teacher sternly repeated his request to "Toe the line, please."

    The old Webster "Blue-back" Speller was used altogether and when a new spelling rule was being taught, the method is, if the word were several syllables long, then each syllable when spelled was pronounced separately, with more and more syllables after and including each syllable finished until the last syllable was spelled and pronounced, then the whole word was pronounced—and the pupil, if successful, breathed more easily. If not successful, he went to the foot to wait until his neighbor in line had succeeded and then "turned him down." If the pupil happened to be learning a primer or serial, a glib speller's recitation became a foreign-sounding succession of syllable-and-sound combinations, e. g., aigh; z, az, aigh-er; r, rlit; aigh-er(h); a, t, at; aigh-er-hat.

    In the implementation work, unless the pupils were chosen to work on mathematics for a given period, one student recalls that even in the younger children; and one student recalls that even in the advanced department there was a very young girl working algebra, geometry, trigonometry, and other mathematics problems, and the slate was used to prevent the chalk writing from being accidentally erased. College Class Methods.—Although, as the catalog rule indicates, the basic classroom method even in collegiate courses was that of orally testing the students' grasp of the assigned material in the textbook, the procedure as actually practiced was more that of classroom discussion than of mechanical question and answer. The students, being older and often highly intelligent, were capable of owners or contributing to the discussion, and questions could come from the students as well as the professor. This procedure naturally led to informal lecturing or exposition on the part of the professor.

    In science courses requiring laboratory demonstrations, students were appointed or chosen, it would seem, to go to the laboratory and make preparations for the experiment for the day's work. One of the College laboratories had students performed and explained the experiment to the class, as sufficient equipment may not have been to permit each student to perform his own experiment.

Expansion of the Plant.

    The Buildings.—By the time of the incorporation of the College, as has been noted in Chapter III, the College plant consisted of a number of frame buildings, including one very large room and one of smaller dimensions and a two-story frame building with dormitory space. The buildings, having plenty of window and door space and good ventilation, were of log construction, which were provided as bachelor's halls for young men who did not wish to room in town, living in them and doing their own housekeeping and cooking. These "back halls" as students called them, were considered the college campus on the east.

    As the College grew in size and notoriety, it was the custom to erect a temporary outdoor stage against the wall of a building and to provide temporary bench seats for the annual "exhibition" which marked the close of the year's work.

Laboratories.—The College maintained a laboratory with "sufficient Chemical and Philosophical apparatus to illustrate any of the principles usually taught in any college textbook," according to its advertising as early as 1883. It is recalled by ex-students that the department of anatomy and physiology was accompanied by dissection in which the students in the course were required to be able to assemble in its entirety, identifying each bone by name, and that dissection of animals for laboratory demonstrations was common. An original copy of the laboratory note book paper refers to the College laboratory's being thoroughly decorated and "put in order" by October 1, 1884, which would seem to indicate that the laboratory had been in use for some time previous.

In his early College he was responsible particularly for the Latin and Rhetoric, though in the earlier years he carried his share of Preparatory classes, and in the intermediate years taught Latin. A broad and versatile man, he seems to have, after a period at Savoy College, studied medicine in the Medical College at Louisville, and returned to Fannin County to the practice of the medical profession.

    The Reverend Mr. Holland was of the longest in period of service, served ten years after his first connection with the school early in 1883 to about 1893. He was actually Professor of Greek, Latin, and Mental and Moral Science. From his foundation training in the Glenville, West Virginia Institute he developed a versatility on which continued with him throughout his teaching career. In addition to this training, which suggested a superior standard, his standing in the classical languages was the hallmark of the College's classical standard—Greek was clearly his chosen worship, and his immediate successor in the chair of Greek was one of his own students who had received the A.B. degree of the College.

FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION.—A study of the financial management of the Savoy College reveals two contrasting phases of President Halbell's management: one the courage and persistence of a man who was deeply devoted to the institution, entirely without endowment and dependent on the income from tuition for its support; the other the one seen in Mr. Halbell a courageous and sagacious financial manager; he began to show in the writing the extent that the magnanimous and philanthropic activities shown in the welfare of the College.

The charge monthly tuition fees upon which the College depended for its support amounted to $2 for primary pupils, $3 for those in the preparatory department, $4

It is to be noticed that careful attention is made to the separation of the sexes: the male and female departments will be kept separate, except in recitation rooms, and no pupils of one department be permitted to associate with those of another.

The 1887-1888 catalog records them in this way, much in the order named, were very clear:

1. The male and female departments will be kept separate, except in recitation rooms, and no pupil of one department shall be permitted to associate with those of another.
2. Calling at private residences of pupils of another department is strictly forbidden, and all persons of any kind will be prohibited by the College authorities.
3. Carousing forbidden, and profane language of any kind will be prohibited.
4. All persons found in the streets or public places at unseasonable hours will be reported to the College authorities.
5. No pupil having the "serenade" or public serenading of any kind will be admitted or permitted.
6. No pupil having the privilege of the upper "house" therefore let it be resolved, that "up-town" serenading should be prohibited.
7. Cards, etc. are forbidden.
8. The standing of each pupil will be kept both as to scholarship and deportment.

As approximately fifty per cent of the students were non-boarders, boarding in private residences near the campus, the enforcement of the strict application in rule six presented some problems. President Halbell made it a point of responsibility himself, and it was his custom to walk about the village in the evening, visiting in the homes of the students. He made occasional calls to see that the students were working at their studies, so the astonished student had had time to run. Contemporaries remembered that President Halbell was wont to arrive unannounced, and in more than one remembered instance, at the home where the young men were visiting the young ladies—not in strict compliance with rules—he would clarify the disturbing matter. At other times, as may be imagined, it required the greater part of the faculty to place in his class a young man in the act of violating the rules by calling on the young ladies, and others had

On special occasions—such as holidays, end-of-school exhibitions, and trips with the debating teams to neighboring colleges—the rules were suspended, and social activity moved in an exciting whirl. These occasions were matters of high interest because the rules, strict as they were, were respected and abided by rather minutely throughout the school, and most of the students were serious-minded enough not to resent the repression. The high moral standards were kept up by wholesome precept and example on the part of the faculty, and many students remember the strong impress of the characters of the faculty members. A personal letter to the writer from Mr. T. P. Wells sums up the tenor of many conversations with ex-students:

      One of the outstanding characteristics of Savoy College students was that they left the school filled with worthy and noble ambition. As a result of this many became men and women of distinction and useful to the world in many walks of life.
      There was no athletics taught in the school. The burning desire was to burn the "mid-night oil" and become a scholar. The moral training was of a higher standard than it is in colleges today.⁶³

records.text:
Chapter V

Life On and Off the Campus

Although the major objective in a study of the history of a college may properly be that of defining its character and evaluating its contribution to the advancement of education, an important supporting aim ranking as a close second may legitimately be that of finding beneath the abstract surface of its educational aspects the lively ebb and flow of human activity in its halls and on the campus. The effective years of Savoy Male and Female College are just far enough back to permit a historical perspective in the treatment of its place in the history of education in Texas and far enough back to facilitate that research. On the other hand, its life and history are, happily, much too recent to be a matter solely of written record; for first-hand pictures of life in its environs have been available. Its story in Chapter III is told of the activities of Savoy College realistically at work and at play—and to do so wherever possible on the basis of personal recollections in response of ex-students to the author's request for reminiscences.⁶⁴

Although this material is rather of sociological than scientific interest, a different treatment might deprive it of much personal significance. Such a treatment might find its own purpose, for, in the following story will show a certain continuing and ever present side of the life at the college beyond the ordinary activities—the temperance, literary, and debating societies —then they take up the out of school activities of individual students, and finally the activities of alumni.

THE COLLEGE PUBLICATION

ORIGIN AND EXTENT—Frequent reference has been made in this study to The Platonian Messenger. This paper was a combined newspaper and literary magazine, sponsored, as the name suggests, by the Platonian Literary Society, and published monthly during the collegiate year. It was edited at Savoy by the professors and submitted students and published monthly during the collegiate year. It was edited at Savoy by the professors and contributed by the student body. From the earliest issues to the last one available, it appears to have been an effective publication, 1886-1887, the last issue available being that of November, 1886. How much longer it ran is a matter of conjecture; but the fact that the 1887-1888 catalog makes no mention of it seems to indicate that by that date it had ceased to exist by that time.

THE FORMAT—The paper was printed by the Bonham press, and distributed in sheet form. The paper was folded to make a folder of eight four-column pages eleven inches by about eight or nine inches. The front page appeared as a four-page, five-column single-fold paper measuring thirteen inches by about twenty inches. The paper was printed for the most part in 12-point standard-weight type, with poetry and other items set in larger type. The paper was named on the front page with the title, "The Platonian Messenger," and appeared in the issue of June, 1885, in the front page of November of 1885. The front page was the editorial page,

THE DAY'S ROUTINE FOR A SAVOY STUDENT

Classroom work in Savoy College went forward with earnestness and in a mood of seriousness characteristic of the dignity of professors imbued, no doubt, in the spirit of the times. Among those characteristics of Savoy College were those who kept the motto "Keep quiet back there, boys" and for the time being Bill would release his string, and in a few minutes he would commence again, to the amusement of the teacher. News items told of frequent visits of the business manager to notify delinquent subscribers. About the time he reached the College, or even a young lady, rode horseback, the latter picturesquely perched on a side-saddle, and wearing a long, black, bundlesome riding skirt, which of course was taken off before she went into the schoolroom. (A stile block, to assist young ladies in dismounting and mounting, stood on the edge of the campus.)

Again, the student may have ridden to school in a horse-drawn buggy or phaeton. In either case, there was a horse to be unsaddled or unharnessed and tied to a tree in the woods bordering the campus. At noon there was the horse to be fed and watered before the student could eat his own lunch; and in the afternoon there was the matter of saddling or harnessing the animal for the homeward ride.

Life in the bachelor halls had its own separate routine, of course. records.title: BACHELOR TOWN
records.text:
98 THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE


BACHELOR TOWN

Amid an humble shady grove
    That had lately been cut down,
In all its odd and dreary looks,
    There was a bachelor town.

At sunset, or at evening's close,
    The bachelors might be seen,
In playing marbles, other games,
    Or getting dishes clean.

When night appeared in all its shade,
    When all its inmates there,
Each one was steadily engaged
    To have at least his share.

All supper o'er and things prepared,
    All seemed to be engaged
In poring over classic lore,
    Or ancient history page.

For four long hours or more,
    The busy work went on.
Some still were busy at their books,
    And some to bed had gone.

At break of day, their spirit gay,
    And all was joy in town;
Some busy seated at their books,
    Some getting breakfast found,

To eat their breakfast at such a time,
    According to their rules;
Not very long they might be seen
    All seated in the school,

Their minds were fixed on their abstruse book,
    Nor could it well be said,
By the tutor's voice or classmate's sign,
    Won't you get your lessons, Webb?

With all the force of hero's power,
    They seem to eye their books,
And in the sequel of the class,
    Were cheered by the instructor's looks.

Many useful things they oft would learn
    By the use of each other's aid,
And would calmly return to their quiet home
    When all their lessons were said.³³

³³The Platonian Messenger, op. cit., Vol. I, No. 6, April 20, 1885.

STORIES OF THE CLASSROOM

Classroom work in Savoy College went forward with earnestness and in a mood of seriousness characteristic of the dignity of professors imbued, no doubt, in the spirit of the times. Among the students there were always the irrepressible spirits who kept the motto "Keep quiet back there, boys" constantly ringing in the Professor's ears. The following stories related about individual students are characteristic of these conditions.

About the year of 1884, in order to meet the needs of the fast-growing institution the College building had been greatly enlarged; and when completed it was quite a new and commodious structure (it was later called the East addition, and when completed it was quite a valuable building of which we were all justly proud). The lower part was used for recitations, with the upper story arranged and fitted to accommodate the Business and Commercial department; and the basement was to be occupied by the intermediate department with Prof. F. Montgomery as its teacher.

The lower story was fitted up with good taste, with the inside wall being shiplapped with white pine lumber. Among the full quota of students in the department were tables arranged in rows with aisles running between each row.

Now as Bill passed in silent meditation upon the soft white pine planks, so he had made in the wall—just large enough to insert a string with a row of nails in it one end of which was hidden on his desk. As just the size of the hole he had made in the wall, about six or eight inches—in such a manner that the string would make a sound the moment anyone would notice more. The College's official advertisement, however, accused him on the ownership of the wall. A long wrangle among the confederates as to the ownership of the string issued, and nobody, being a person of high noble, took his place, and Mark continued the recitation. There was some giggling quietly to his book, continued the recitation. There was some discussion among his classmates about it, and then, at last and determined in his search, after a close scrutiny to find the maker of the prank, called on his coterie on the wall; and with it the solution of the mystery.

The teacher, with a look of amazement upon his face, would call out, "Keep quiet back there, boys!" and for the time being Bill would release his string, and in a few minutes he would commence again, to the amusement of the teacher. News items told of frequent visits of the business manager to notify delinquent subscribers. About the time the teacher faced around, looking squarely at the class, the noise would cease, and even search the desks to find the origin of it. Bill replied, "Yes, Sir."

Montgomery challenged, "Then let us hear it." Bill arose and commenced with a ring of inflection on each "Woe" and delivered his recitation in such a decided note of awareness, stand out more boldly in the memory.

Finally Montgomery stopped and listened at it for a moment and then said, "What is that making that noise?"

Bill replied, "I do not know, Sir; it is in the wall, I reckon."

Finally the mystery was solved and turned out to be Bill's; and the entire class was given a sound thrashing. This was duly written to the episode of the scholar in The Platonian Messenger.

THE INIMITABLE PROFESSOR HOLLAND—Miss Lou Montgomery, writing in a commemorative tribute on Holland in the 1937 Anniversary Edition of The Savoy Star touches on a particular individual with characteristic Holland.

Mr. Holland was a man of a tranquil, philosophic mentality; not given to magnification of the law in its sternest aspects; free from bluster, stern, excitability, peculiar tribe, unreasonable expectations and petty grievances. He had a happy faculty of getting along with students one day, and that easily might have terminated in looking out of the room just once took his place, sat quite calmly in his chair, had him seated in the school one day, and as members of a family helped some students towards a better form of life—a way of taking their lessons easily, and as all members of a family helped some students their afternoon time well-scheduled in advance.

Our Vice President, Professor Holland, a great student-lover, was always quiet, slow and kind, but one day, now, at the young students' recitation, "The Ciceronian," was organized. Whether this organization supplanted one of the older societies or supplemented the work of both is not remembered.

We country girls brought our dinners (noon meals) to the school, and at noon, when I have forgotten exactly when it was, it was embarrassing, but we made the best of it by the time it was often embarrassing, but we made the best of it—Con Thomasson, E. A. McMahon, W. F. Holland, Bill Harris, Joe Thompson, W. H. Lacy, E. A. McMahon, and others whose names I do not recall. This group is well remembered as good and amiable and By-Laws were copied after other older organizations of the area. Their motto taken from the preamble to the Constitution of the Platonic Society was "Life is Given for Noble Deeds" by Julia Montgomery: "On Other Thoughts By Stonewall Jackson," which was given a sound thrashing.

Of course, we thought the picnic was very great. It was recalled with surprise and a prayer of thankfulness that their side was six members of the class, the party broke up the middle, deposited it in a far corner of the room, returned to their seats, and without batting an eye, sat quietly to his book, continued the recitation for the balance of the hour without any appreciable loss of time.

NO WANT-TO-GO-HOME HEADACHE CURES—Mrs. E. A. McMahon remembers that disciplinary touches of the gentler and more nurturing variety began with the earliest school days.

Mattie Patton (Mattie Patton) and I first started to school, and we had a game that we played on Mr. Dick Gay, our teacher, each day to get to go home early; that is, each day (by the time it was often embarrassing, but we made the best of it by the time it was often embarrassing, but we made the best of it—we had become such good friends) that we would tell Mr. Dick Gay, our teacher, each day that we had a headache and wanted to go home. For a month we did this, and the teacher, of course, was very soon disgusted with our game of truancy every day that they played truant daily together. After that Mattie gave Mattie a little whipping one morning before we left for school, and after that each morning before we left with me, and of course we had no more headaches.

Miss Ella Scott was at our house and I think Mattie Scott must have known about it too. When Mattie's mother came home, we told her "Mattie is sick." So she came in and was very sorry for us too. They all sat in the sitting room until nearly supper time. When we really got pot[?], until we really got pot[?], and had our supper without him, returned to their seats, and without batting an eye, sat down and had our supper until finally nearly supper time.

†Personal items from Mrs. E. A. McMahon (Gala Chenault), Dallas, Texas, June 20, 1938.

He and mother were fearful of letting us go, as the water was quite deep and none of us could swim. On this one particular occasion mother and father were away all day. On this one particular occasion I asked him and his reply was that we should all go, and that Mark continued the recitation for the balance of the hour as he called it only at break, took his place, his pocket, and determined in his search, after a close scrutiny to find the maker of the prank, called on his coterie on the wall.

I asked him how Mark would know about the way to go from the prank, and his reply was that he called us all up before him and had us take our right hands and swear that we had not told anyone about the matter. The "Suspension of Rules"—Social visits between young gentlemen and ladies were not always clandestine, however. On special occasions there was a general standing announcement of the "suspension of the rules"—and that announcement was more stirring to the students than the making of dates. For some occasions, such as for "exhibitions" and scheduled holidays, the suspension of rules was anticipated for some time in advance. Sometimes, for unexpected occasions, the announcement was a partial surprise, and as a consequence all the more exciting. The college paper tells of one instance when the rule had been suspended: man had successfully presented a request for "suspension of rules" and this produced this result:

The young girls were so hilarious over the suspension of the rules that as I hurried past I almost felt the suspension of the rules! I met B. M. and little M. is a small man in stature; they wanted me to play a little too; so I went into the situation with all my heart. But something happened: I was brought up short.

Date making was a formal affair. The gentleman sent his "compliments" (by which name the whole written message was called) to the young lady, a carefully worded note asking her company for the occasion. In the note book, the young lady had her carefully phrased note accepting or rejecting the date. In one of her note books still in existence, the date, if other demands that means of transportation than walking, and the young gentleman had to provide it; the two literary societies kept rosters of the dates by the two lively stables of Savoy.

"Exhibitions" and "Levees."—Savoy made most of its own entertainment, as traveling shows and concerts came to Sherman or Bonham but not to smaller towns in the region. The types of local entertainment were mostly open programs and the exhibition affairs of the literary societies. The "exhibition" was one week of "showing off" similar to Commencement Exercises of longer duration; there was a program each night. Musicals, debates, speeches, orations, plays, "exercises" in one quarter, there was always the large family picture album (elaborate in plush or embossed, with music box), and at the exhibition the class walked in with their partner. In the students' language, they "spoke their pieces" and came upon the rostrum with their platform eloquence. The citizens came to the exhibitions with arm loads of lovely bouquets to offer compliments to their friends, and the group frequently demanded renditions by those who could sing, play an instrument, or recite. Eulogies and bouquets were thrown to the "rostrum."

Mrs. W. B. (Bennetta Connally) Duncan stated, in an interview with the author more than half a century since she stood at her mother's side and listened to the story of the tornado as it bore down upon the little town of Savoy, 1888, carrying death and destruction in its path. It was the most distressing calamity ever witnessed in this section. Lives were lost, property destroyed, and bodies bruised and mangled in every conceivable manner. The storm struck the town at 10 o'clock and lasted all night. The storm struck the town at 10 o'clock and lasted all night. The foundations of the houses were swept away. About twelve houses, besides many outhouses, were demolished. The storm, it seemed, needing to come down from the clouds, in a frenzied and concentrated rush of lightning, thunder and hail at the same time. The trees were uprooted and electricity seemed to be flying through and through the dark and heavy atmosphere. The intensity of the darkness and the density of the atmosphere was almost indescribable. The passenger train on the T. and P. railroad passed through in the midst of the tornado, and was the means of carrying the news to the outside world. At one time it was thought that over two thousand persons were on the ground. Physicians from Sherman and Denison came at once with money and medicine.

Chapter VI

The Founder and Faculty of Savoy College

If this history of Savoy Male and Female College is to be regarded as an examination of a forward step in the program of education in Texas, something more must be given than the external facts of school plant, enrollment, and the human interest of campus life, for obviously the development of such a college was an expression of the character of a wide-reaching neighborhood of people of advanced ideals, and its success was rooted in the support of the community's leading citizens. There is additional significance, therefore, in the personnel of the founders and the faculty which was drawn to the work under the leadership of President Halsell. For a more adequate understanding of the significance of the College, therefore, this biographical chapter includes sketches of three trustees, as representative of the citizenship of the section, in addition to biographies of the three principals who are the central figures in the story of Savoy Male and Female College.

J. L. German, Thomas J. Chenoweth, and James Paxton married sisters of Miss Eliza German and Mr. Paxton had married sister of Mr. Chenoweth. SEND CONGRATULATIONS
Prof. R. R. Halsell Remembered by His Old Pupils

The following communication was sent to Prof. R. R. Halsell, who has been elected a member of the Oklahoma legislature. Prof. Halsell many years ago conducted the Savoy College and is remembered by many former students.

Dear Prof. Halsell: We, the undersigned, extend to you our heartfelt congratulations on your election to the legislature of Oklahoma. It would be impossible for us to express how dear and precious to our hearts are the memories of those pleasant days spent under your guidance and instruction at the Savoy College. I have further to congratulate you as a man, for your devotion to your home, your State, and your fellow men.

Oklahoma is certainly fortunate to have the services of your scholarship, and we trust that your government can bring to her counties.

Well do we appreciate those years of self-sacrifice and devotion, with which you inspired and aided us when we were struggling against almost insurmountable odds. Our state was new, her progress had been stopped by the devastation of the war, and was but poorly equipped, and those of you who devoted your lives to building institutions of learning were few and poorly equipped, and the fields from which to derive support were limited. Yet such men as you and your co-laborers among us were deeper, the less higher, and the fields larger than they are now. Without the foundation built by you and those working with you in establishing and maintaining our higher institutions of learning, proper education would have been practically impossible.

We wish you all the joys, comforts, and blessings that life can give you in the remaining days that shall remain, and trust that you have not forgotten them.

I am, with the sincerest of all wishes for your future,
Ed. A. McMaron.

RICHARD A. "DICK" GAY

Richard A. Gay, one of the earliest members of the faculty to be discussed, is among the most interesting to be included, if one is to judge by the number of sincere and affectionate references to him. His schoolmates say that he was known to all his friends and schoolmates as 'Dick' Gay, and came to Texas at the age of four from Georgia, with his family, and attended the public schools in Fannin County. When Savoy College opened he continued as a student there for a year or two, then went on to make his minister in 1880, at Ladonia, Fannin County. He conducted the Primary Department of the College as early as 1881-1882, and taught several years, all the while advanced work as a student in connection with his teaching.

For the years 1885-1886 he served in the State Normal College at Athens, Texas, where he was a member of the faculty and teacher of mathematics. During his latter days he recited from memory many times Tennyson's 'Crossing the Bar'—which at the close of his public life on earth was his wish—and that at the moment of his de-mise he preached the 11 o'clock service last at 891 Main St., Dallas, and then attended the night service. LEONIDAS WILLIAM PIERCE

The story of Professor W. Pierce's life as a student and teacher in Savoy College is well marked by references in the Cotton student papers of that day. Space must be left for a record of his subsequent career as a missionary in China the writer has been helped in this work more than by him by sixteen years and now lives with their daughter, Miss Ethel M. Pierce, at 1416 Oak Lawn Avenue.

Leonidas William Pierce was born of hardy forbears. His father, Sidney Pierce, a native of Virginia, born in 1833, had gone at the age of eleven years with his widowed mother to Tennessee, and when he was twenty years old made the journey overland to California, arriving there in 1854. Starting with nothing, he became well-to-do. In 1869 he married Miss Cornelia J. Brown. His wife was a native of Nancy (Addina) Brown, and to them Leonidas William was born, on October 15, 1870. Through the years the family grew to include ten children.

Young Lee Pierce spent his boyhood on the farm and began his education in a little log school house. Later he entered the Savoy College, was a good student, showed scholarship, and was a leader in student activities. He joined the Victorian Literary Society and became interested in journalism in writing for its paper, the Philomean Messen-

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
per. Receiving his A.B. degree in 1883, he was given a position as teacher of English and German in the College in addition to some preparatory subjects and was retained the next year to teach natural science. He told that he was Senior assistant editor of one of the paper's early issues and was Business Manager later in the year.

The following account of Mr. Pierce's service after he left Savoy College (in 1887) is quoted through the courtesy of Mrs. Pierce:

Leonidas William Pierce . . . attended the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary at Louisville, Kentucky, finishing the course in 1892. He and a party of young volunteers who were sent by the Foreign Board of the Southern Baptist Convention as missionaries to Yangchow, China.

For months after his arrival in China, he and Miss Molly E. Tupper of the mission were married in 1893. He spent his entire missionary career with the missionaries in Yanochow, a city, at that time, of about four hundred thousand people and whose inhabitants did not know whether they wanted the Saviour who saves for eternity, or of the God who had saved them.

The first few years were very difficult years. The Chinese language was not easy to learn. It was in fact a discouraging undertaking. Mr. Pierce, though he has signally failed in this) was difficult, and required hours of study; yet a Chinese scholar, who, you knew little about teaching! On one occasion Mr. Pierce discouraged to the extent that he was not able to see how he could continue his work. His wife, however, took a brighter view of the matter, and she encouraged him as best she could. He again turned to the Bible, and on his knees he sought the Lord to enable them to learn the language that they might give the story of Life to those who knew Him not. God graciously answered that prayer, and he became an accomplished Chinese scholar, and could speak and write the language without difficulty.

He was tireless in his efforts to give the Gospel to the people. He visited all the neighboring villages, and their adjacent country-sides, in towns and villages with a pen of seven thousand square miles of territory in and around Yangchow. On these circuits, accompanied by his Chinese helper, he preached

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
to the surging crowds which surrounded him in the market places and the tea-shops. He was the pioneer missionary in that section of the country, not only of the Baptist denomination but of any there. During those long years he had made himself—in a word—a half a hand of friendly Chinese. They learned to love him because they realized he was true, and felt constrained by that love which was shed abroad. If, on arriving at a town, he went to the market-place and cried out with a loud voice, "Tin ming! Jin ming!" which means "Save life!" As a result, great crowds of people came running from every direction. The object was not that any danger was at hand; but where there seemed to be no danger. When the excitement had somewhat quieted, he said, "Friends, I did not call because I wanted you to save my life, but because I want you to know that the Living God wishes to save your lives for eternity, for ever and ever."

Mr. Pierce was a man much given to Bible study and prayer, rising often at 4 o'clock to read the Bible and to pray. He believed that the strength for day's work was done often reading God's Word far into the night. He was earnest in all that he did. A childhood incident illustrates this attitude. They were requiring a work at the hay field. When darkness came on, he suggested that they stop. His father frowned, and said to his father, "I'll go down if you will hold the rope." The same earnest and compelling faith was characteristic of his attitude toward life.

In his preaching trips he traveled the country: on sail-boat, on donkey-back, or by wheelbarrow. On a journey, once, to China, some thirty or forty miles from Yangchow, he met a servant of the people, traveling with a foreign face. A Chinese gentleman fell to looking at him and decided to converse with that servant. He looked not on the outward form but reproached the foreigners of his condition. If Mr. Pierce needed rest, he would take a short sleep, and he would improvise a bed from a table or some planks placed across chairs. On one occasion, a Bible-woman was visiting a place at the same time and seeing the condition in which he slept, she reported to some of the Chinese Christian women who love ease and comfort. If this foreigner can come to our land and sleep on a hard bed that to exemplify the Gospel, we Chinese Christians surely should be more faithful than we are." Mr. Pierce organized

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
two churches in Yangchow, and twelve others in as many cities and towns outside Yangchow, during his missionary career. In all, it is said, some sixty-five were Christian schools established.

Thirty-one years of missionary service ended with his death at Soochow, China, on July 16, 1922, when a launch on which he was traveling capsized, and he was drowned. His mortal remains lie buried in Chinkiang, his body lies, awaiting the Resurrection Day, and on the black granite tombstone, in English and Chinese is inscribed these words: "Greater love hath man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." I fitting epitaph for the man who lost not himself, that he might win lost men to God."


WILL I. HUNT

Will I. Hunt was the second alumnus of the Savoy College to reach the signal honor of being a member of its collegiate department upon his completion of the A.B. course in 1887, and later it was to claim as one of its professors whose enthusiasm and energetic labors were enhancing the growing reputation of that institution during the middle 'eighties. His subsequent career shows that this association may have left its marks on the work of both the administration and the young teacher, for an observant residence has said that it was the influence of professors Halsel and Holland in inspiring young men and women to undertake ambitious endeavors and to serve for the student bed was to be observed in the achievements of the young faculty members of that period. If the College was in this manner to plant seeds of service in the hearts of young men—one in the ministry, one in missionary service, one in journalism, one in law, one in education, one in medicine—there may be traced the touch of the College and the character of its faculty members.

Back of Mr. Hunt were two generations of Baptist ministers. His father, W. S. Hunt, or M. Hunt, was fourteen years old when, in 1853, his family moved from Kentucky to Texas and settled in Savoy. His mother was Florence Noblitt, daughter of Seneca Noblitt, who had moved his family from Indiana to Texas, settling in Kentuckytown in

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
about 1855. W. I. Hunt was born May 9, 1861, near the present town of Whitewright and attended rural schools in that locality. He had just reached man's estate when he entered the College in 1882. He was first in the Preparatory Department a year before entering on the stringent course for the A.B. degree. The Victorian Literary Society attracted him to membership, and he became a leader in student affairs, serving as editor of the Philomean Messenger during his last year in College. He was Julia S. Fielder, Miss John Mayer, of Eastland, Texas, was also a popular student at the College during this period, and teacher in that college.

Upon his graduation with the A.B. degree in the spring of 1887, he was invited to join the teaching staff and became a stockholder in the institution, for Professor Holland was seeking to strengthen his faculty at this time as there was need for an instructor in Greek. After teaching one year at higher math and Greek in the College, in the fall of 1888, Mr. Hunt shifted his teaching field to Trenton, Texas, where he was principal of the academy for one year. It was there that he had met and wooed Miss Mollie Lee, whose family lived on a farm near by, and they were duly married on August 9, 1888, at the beginning of his period of teaching.

In 1890 Mr. Hunt moved his family, which now included two children, to Stephenville, Texas, where he made many friends readily, and found public office an attractive career. In the more than forty years spent in Stephenville, he served variously as County Surveyor, County Clerk, District Clerk, and County Commissioner. He was also at one time City County Surveyor and a civil engineer.

When Mr. and Mrs. Hunt celebrated their golden wedding anniversary on August 9, 1938, they were surrounded by their four children and six of their twenty-six living grandons. Their children, who all live in Breckenridge, are Homer Hunt, who is a dentist; Mrs. Lessie Maddux; Mrs. Della Pitcher, whose husband is a salesman; Mrs. Ina Boomquist, a teacher in the city school; and Mrs. Eula Lockett, whose husband is an electrician.
