ELBU BENNETT HINSHAW

Elbu B. Hinshaw, who came to the Savoy College faculty early in 1887 to fill the vacancy in classical languages when Professor Holland retired, was of Pennsylvania Quaker ancestry, the son of Jacob and Elizabeth (Barker) Hinshaw of the Keystone State. Elbu Bennett Hinshaw was born October 14, 1860, in Indiana. Indian. The following account from D. C. Gideon's History of the Indian Territory gives a picture of Mr. Hinshaw's training and abilities during the last three years of Savoy College:

Professor Hinshaw, of this review, completed his education in Hiwasee College, in Tennessee, where he was graduated in 1884 with the degree of Bachelor of Science. Since then the degree of Master of Arts has been conferred upon him by his alma mater, which is one of the oldest institutions of learning in the mountain sections of the middle South. After his graduation Professor Hinshaw entered upon the work of instruction, having taken charge of a high school in East Tennessee for two years, after which he became connected with Savoy College in Grayson County, Texas. For five years work there becoming known, in 1887 he was selected to accept the position of president of the Bloomfield Seminary in Panola County, in the Chickasaw Nation. He accepted this and has been in continuous service in this institution for some twenty years. Bloomfield Seminary is an educational institution established by the Chickasaw government for the education of the young Indian women and the children of new citizens. It was established before the war at its present location in Chickasaw Nation, and has been in existence for fifty years. . . . The number of pupils in attendance is two hundred and twenty, including all departments, and the list of applicants is very large in number, so many being desirous of entering the institution. . . . Careful and efficient work is required in all departments and the students who have graduated at Bloomfield Seminary on the advice of State

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
ter of Literature will compare favorably in equipment with those of any other institution of a similar character. . . . Professor Hinshaw is a very enthusiastic teacher and an untiring worker, laboring for the upbuilding of the Seminary, his work being thorough and exhaustive. He prepares himself thoroughly in the work and he seems tireless in his efforts. He has adopted the branches of study not only beneficial but attractive and pleasant, and is continually on the alert to promote the usefulness of the school. He is a pleasant gentlemen, and is also a factor in advancing culture and intellectuality in the community in which it is located.

Professor Hinshaw was united in marriage to Miss Mary Hianott, a teacher of Bloomfield who had educated in Victoria College in that State. Both the Professor and his wife are consistent members of the Cumberland Presbyterian Church, whose lives together have been an exemplification of its teachings, an example which has been held up before the pupils of the Seminary. He is a very prominent and exemplary member of the Masonic Lodge. He is a musician of ability, having completed his music under the second degree in the Scottish Rite and is also a noble of the Mystic Shrine. . . . His home life is one of the models of broad culture, refined intercourse, charming conversation—all that is of domestic companionship and culture and all that is good and fine in social life.

Mr. Hinshaw remained in his position as superintendent of the Bloomfield Seminary for eighteen years, up to the close of the tribal government, marrying and remaining in the Chickasaw territory, married Mrs. Henry Naylor, and continued in educational work up to the time of his death. Later he married for the second time and after that was connected with the Southeastern State Normal School at Durant, and became one of its teachers. He was a close friend of Governor Johnston, the last chief of the Chickasaw Nation. Mr. Hinshaw died in Oklahoma City, June 27, 1920, and was buried in Collinsville, Texas, where his widow still lives.

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
ALEXANDER C. BOHANNON

Alexander C. Bohannon was a Virginian who in the course of a long career as a college teacher had followed the westward development of educational institutions and had been attracted to Savoy by 1881. Some of his earlier life as a teacher is sketched in the following brief biography:

Alexander C. Bohannon, professor at Christian College, Texas, was born in Mathews County, Virginia, July 22, 1820, and was a son of Reuben W. and Nancy Bohannon, both of whom were born in the same place. He Bohanny in 1820. Reuben W. Bohannon was a man of mark in his section; he was a patriot of his country; he held the respect of everybody; was a man of Christian character. Reuben W. was a member of the Christian Church.

Professor Alexander C. Bohannon is the second graduate of Hampden-Sidney, and was raised on the home farm in Virginia. After a preliminary common-school and academic education, and after pursuing a course of seventy studies, Virginia College, then located at Portsmouth, finished his education, when studied with Professor J. A. Cocke, of Virginia. He was, however, compelled him to relinquish his studies, but he soon recovered and studied law with Judge Harris, of Mathews, until 1861. He then taught school until the outbreak of the war, when he enlisted in the Confederate cavalry. He was taken and sometime a prisoner in 1862 he was honorably discharged on account of ill health. He was then occupied in various pursuits, but in 1864 again entered the Confederate service and taught until 1864. The war having come to a close, in company with others, established a high school at Concord, North Carolina, and organized a school, but in 1868 the school was broken up. He continued his teaching.

In 1869 he returned to the place of his birth, and after his father's death left Virginia, and moved to Indiana; then taught at various places; went from there to Hopkinsville, Kentucky, where he was connected with the South Kentucky College. He came to Texas, where he taught at the Christian College, Columbia, Kentucky, and then taught at Sherman, Texas, before accepting the invitation of Professor Holland to fill the chair of logic and rhetoric at the Savoy College, Savoy, Texas.

September 3, 1871, Professor Bohannon married

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
Miss Maria Donovan, daughter of Cornelius and Harriet (Jones) Donovan, of Gloucester County, Virginia. Three children were born to this union. The names of the children—Hattie, Annie D., Edith B., and Connie. The professor is recognized as a gentleman of unusual experience, and his record gives good cause for such recognition as a member of the Christian Church, he has been a helpful factor in the Christian community.

One of his former students, Miss Lou Arterberry, furnishes the following information about the remainder of Professor Bohannon's service:

Mr. Bohannon was a very able instructor; one of the best the community ever had. He remained at Savoy until the College closed in 1890, when he became superintendent of schools at Bells, Texas. He taught there two years and then moved to Gainesville, where his son-in-law lived. Nothing is known after his death, which occurred in about 1895 or 1896.

Perhaps it is not insignificant to notice that his oldest daughter, Hattie Donovan Bohannon, became the author of a fairly well-known novel, "A Second Marriage: A story of Society" (G. W. Dillingham, New York, 1909), which, being a first novel, indicated a high order of literary ability. I have not found anything inferior in it written by authors of wide reputation. But after the first published novel, Miss Donovan is said to have gone South, and I have been told unable to trace her whereabouts.


PRINCIPAL AND PREPARATORY TEACHERS

Except for the references to Reverend J. H. Gay which appears earlier in this chapter, scant information has been available concerning the preparatory teachers of the Savoy College. They are such important members of the faculty, that their personalities are stamped as pleasant memories in the minds of the alumni who received their earliest and most patient training during impressionable years of childhood. The complete roll of these teachers, as far as the author has been able to compile it, includes, in the approximate order of their time of service, these teachers: Georgiana Wells White, Mr. Gay, Mr. John S. Barratt, Mr. Burke, Mr. Hud-

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
son, Miss Tennie Deatherage, Miss Emma Lacy, Mr. E. L. Trottier, Mr. Ike Hughes, and Miss Minnie Halsell.

Mr. John S. Barratt belonged to a family of cultured and prominent people in Fannin County. A brother, T. E. Barratt, was a minister of the Christian Church and editor of the Christian Messenger. Dr. Lassiter, the footsteps of a former teacher at Savoy, recalls that in 1875 or 1876, Mr. S. Barratt taught school at Lamius, near Dodd City, in Fannin County, and that his school-house was destroyed by a storm. From 1878 until the cyclone of 1880 he taught in Savoy. His home there was wrecked just a week before the cyclone, and with his family he was domiciled in the section house of the railroad company when the storm struck; left Savoy to accept the principalship of the Oak Cliff high school in Dallas. He died in Dallas about 1898, leaving three sons, J. J. and Foster Barratt, now in Dallas, and W. T. Barratt, who is now a druggist now in Sherman, in 1938.

Miss Tennie Deatherage, the daughter of John E. and Hannah (Campbell) Deatherage, was raised in the neighborhood of Savoy and was probably a student in the College before her teaching. She married a successful farmer, William J. Hood, the husband of her deceased sister, Mary, and helped him to farm a large acreage in this area.

Miss Emma Lacy was likewise a member of a well-known Savoy family, as she was the daughter of R. W. Lacy and his wife, Nancy (Thompson) Lacy. Both of both families had been in the area since before the War. She was a teacher in the preparatory department from approximately 1882-1884, according to the recollection of her sister, Mrs. Y. E. Conner. She married George E. Standifer some ten years after her work in Savoy, and died in Whitewright, Texas, in 1920.

E. L. Trottier, who did part-time teaching in 1884-1885 while helping to look after his parents' property in the Savoy neighborhood, obtained his training at the College, and continued teaching later in Bonham, where he died at a

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
same occurs in a catalog of the Savoy School in 1885, and a few years later he was principal of the high school there.

Miss Minnie Halsell, who served as primary assistant during the last year, or perhaps the last two years, of the history of the school, was the daughter of President Halsell and had received her training in the College under the administration of her father. Soon after the dissolution of the institution, she married Mr. William Phipps, and they moved to the Indian Territory, where she died about 1894.


MUSIC AND ART TEACHERS

Of the teachers of the fine arts in connection with the Savoy College the two who remained longest were connected with the institution in its early years—Madame Michely and Mrs. Jnd Mathison.

Miss Lou Arterberry of Savoy gives a brief but striking picture of Madame Michely in the following excerpts from letters to the author:

Madame Michely was of pure Spanish stock, born, reared, and educated in Madrid, was highly accomplished in music, she played everything—guitar, violin, harp, and piano—in any key, transposing and playing them all with equal fluency. She had married a Frenchman and lived for a long time in Havana, Cuba, before coming to this country. . . .

She came to Savoy with a colony of educated people to establish a school there, bringing with them this part of their plan. However, they were unable to secure their plan, and the colony met with reverses and the school was never founded. . . . She made her home at Burmida's hotel in Savoy, where she did private teaching and supported herself for a time by running a modest little store. She died a few years later from injuries sustained in the storm in the year of the cyclone.

I was right intimately associated with her during the time she was here, having studied French under her. I regret that I cannot give you valuable information regarding her biography or musical attainments; I do not remember ever hearing say she

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
was a painter of pictures. . . . She was one of the most intelligent women I ever knew.

Mrs. Jnd Mathison, who taught private classes in piano for College students for the first three years of the school's life, was the granddaughter of John Sevier, the first governor of the "State of Franklin" (later Tennessee), United States Senator, and famous as a Revolutionary hero. She was born December 21, 1840, in Henry County, Tennessee, the daughter of James A. and Sabra (Elliston) Yowell, and reared and educated in Tennessee. She married E. J. Mathison, a Northern educator and philanthropist, and left Texas in 1870. Her work as a teacher in Savoy was closely connected with the college, since most of her piano pupils were drawn from the school. Her son-in-law, Mr. George Lindsay, of Houston, recalls the spell-binding thrill of the programs given by Professor Holland's students at the College, and the musical background and accompaniment which Mrs. Mathison provided. When the Mathisons moved from Savoy they went first to Whitewright and then to Nashville, Tennessee, and then to different places on their ler and Susie. Some years later they came back to Texas and settled in Greenville, where Mrs. Mathison died October 18, 1926.

Miss Kate Hunderhult, who was advertised in the Philomean Messenger as being head of the Music Department of the College during approximately 1883-86, was a graduate of Ward's Seminary at Nashville.

Miss Frankie Chesworth, one of the later teachers of music, was the daughter of George F. and Mary E. (Patty) Chesworth. She was born July 1, 1871, and graduated from Savoy College in 1888 with a diploma in Music and the A. B. degree. She then returned to teach in the College. Her

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
After living for a time in Bonham, they moved to Oklahoma. They now live in Oklahoma City, where Mrs. Smith continues to teach music and the art of dancing. They have one son, Dee Smith, and three daughters, Lela Mae, Elizabeth, and Janetta Lou.

Miss Lily Lacy, one of the later art teachers, began her work at the College when she was only eighteen years old and just out of Carlton College in Bonham. Since then she has continued the study of art widely, and has taught in Grayson College at Whitewright, Carlton College in Bonham, Carr-Burdette College in Sherman, and Kendall College, Enid, Oklahoma. She lives in Bonham and is teaching a private class.


COMMERCIAL TEACHERS

Except in the single case of Mr. Leon C. Reynolds, scant information is available on the men who established the commercial department of the Savoy College in the seventies and carried the work forward effectively. Mr. George Hardsaw, Mr. J. E. of Finger, Mr. James L. George, Mr. J. D. Warren, and Mr. W. P. Marcy, all left the impress of their capable teaching on a generation of Savoy graduates and their business training successfully, but Mr. Reynolds is the only one with whom contact has been established or concerning whom much information is available. He still lives and at the age of seventy-four years is actively engaged in the printing business in Dallas. Because his connection with the Savoy College is thus continuing and is broadly represented in the printing and publishing traditions that bind him in so intimately with the College history, his life sketch, written by him out himself, is given as a fitting conclusion to this biographical chapter.


PERSONAL SKETCH OF L. J. REYNOLDS

I was born in a log cabin in Polk County, Texas, at Livingston, the county seat, on November 6, 1864. My father, Jasper P. Reynolds, was born and reared near Lynchburg, Virginia, and my mother, Addie Anne (Fanning) Reynolds, was a native

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
West Virginia. They were married in 1857, and I was their third child.

During my early childhood we lived in various towns in North Texas, where my father worked first as a store clerk, then as a teacher of literary schools and of special schools in penmanship, until his health failed. My mother also taught a private school in Celeste, Texas; and later—when I was perhaps ten—for a time in Galveston, where I had a hilarious time jumping into the in-rolling waves down on the beach.

My first school experience was in the winter of 1871-872, in Whitewright, where there was rather good subscription school. Later there were schools, many of which were taught by my father, but it was in 1878, while we were living in Mount Pleasant (a little village on a branch of the L. & A. railroad), that I began to experience my first real thirst for knowledge. Up to that time I did not know that the field of learning extended beyond the "three R's." The school at Custer City employed a real teacher, a University of Virginia graduate, B. F. Dean, who was reputed to have it that he could teach Greek, Latin, algebra, geometry, philosophy, logic, and what not. A well-meaning people, the Goldsmith, wondered how one small head could hold all he was reported to know. He came and I went to school to him—and was electrified after only six weeks info. Although I had never seen a Latin book, I persuaded him to read with me the Latin, and in the spring of the year I had thirty-two scholars in the Latin class of students from twenty to twenty-five years of age. He was a great teacher; on one occasion when I was with him I was reading Roman history. In order to give me a little help the first day I took the book he called for the story of the founding of Rome and the careers of Romulus and Remus; and the next day, entirely on account of this concentrated twelve-hours work and exceptional memory, I read the entire page without missing a word. . . . Of course this was exceptional; but it shows what concentration of mind will do. Going on in read Caesar it took me almost a day to realize definitely just how great Caesar really was. This was to me great inspiration, and that year, in addition to keeping up my Latin, I had learned, or was learning, in a self-taught way, German, Greek, mathematics, and composition. Since then I have been longing for theught from the Savoy teachers.

In November, 1879, my parents moved to Sher-

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
topics: T. and F. B. R. railroad
records.text:
man again, where I secured a job as "devil" in a newspaper office. The next spring the family bought a home in Savoy and had lived there two or three months when the terrible tornado swept away three-quarters of Savoy, only leaving intact a small part of the village. The morning after the catastrophe, while waiting for the T. and F. B. R. to repair a broken rail, I, following some newspaper instinct, issued what might be called as a "special edition" of the paper for which I was working a circular giving all the information I could get about the storm. My hours of deep anxiety about my parents were soon eased by news from them, and I was soon again at work, glad that they were safe and unhurt.

I soon gave up my job in Sherman and joined my family in Savoy for the purpose of attending school. The school had been chartered a few months previous to the tornado, and could therefore be styled a legal institution of learning, but was not officially raised to the rank of a college until two years later, when it was chartered as a college. During the entire first session after the charter was issued, I was on hand and, enthusiastic student and good one. I attended the first college year without the loss of a day, but unfortunately my father died the second year, and the family was looking to me for support; money was failing, and I had to help make a living for the family. He died in May, 1882, leaving my mother and sister; then on I had to support my mother and sister and put my little sisters through college. When Mr. P. W. Halsel had heard of my circumstances, he was very graciously insistent that I go on to school and forget about the immediate money needs—help in later failure as I felt to study to repay. With nature and these kind encouragements I still attended, though by necessity of part-time work it took me until 1889 to wear today; so I had to get out and go to work. It was only by the kindly help of Mr. Halsel that I was able to round out the full requirements for the B.S. During the seven years in which I was working for an education, I taught in about six different schools of four, five, and eight months respectively; in addition to this I pursued a course in penmanship in my spare hours, helped survey land one summer in the fall, cut cord wood in winter, and taught penmanship at odd hours, and I had one year of six paying teachers in class work. In the spring of 1887, the year I graduated, I was called to teach the remainder

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
of the term in a country school where a teacher had been dismissed. During those three months I kept up my college work as well, and at the end stood up right along with my class and took my final exams with the others.

After finishing my school days I taught two years and then went back to my first love—printer's ink—and secured a position in a printing office where I was foreman of the Van Alstyne News; then, in August, 1892, I established the Van Alstyne Leader and presently took in a partner, Mr. W. E. Donnan, who was a chemistry student at Grayson College and subsequently became a teacher in the Chemistry Department of the State University. In 1897 we sold the Leader to R. S. Fulton (who still owns it being 81). Then for a short time I was advertising solicitor and manager of the Sherman Daily Register. That year we started as the W. P. Forest. We incorporated the Reynolds-Parker Company as a stock company for commercial printing. For some years I was the manager of the office here, and in 1907 established The Office Supply Store, which I ran for ten years. From 1920 to 1923 I was linotype man on a Tribune, and since 1923 I have managed the Guar-anty Printing Company in Dallas.

In personal matters, I married Miss Dora Lee Johnson, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Johnson of Van Alstyne, Texas. We were married on April 4, 1895, and both were born to us; Harold Johnson was born July 30, 1900. After thirty years of poor health and long suffering, Dora died in 1924. I married to Miss Fannie Mae Ball, daughter of the Reverend and Mrs. S. A. Ball, an old and well-to-do family in Mississippi, on December 29, 1925. A son, Leon Ball, born April 21, 1921, and adopted by us when he was four years of age.

In Van Alstyne in August, 1892, I joined the Methodist Church, and in all the succeeding years have been active in church affairs. I was Sunday School Lay Leader, as Bible-class Teacher and Sunday School Superintendent, and for two years was president of Epworth League. In civic life I was for two years an alderman and one year a member of the Citizens Water and Light Committee in Van Alstyne; I have for two two years, president of the Retail Merchants Association one year, on the Board of Trade for two years, and secretary of Rotary as long as I held my membership. I became a Mason in 1902 and have

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
taken every degree in both rites except the 33rd; in 1918 or 1919 I was Deputy District Grand Master under Grand Master A. L. Randell.

During the recent reunion of the ex-students at Savoy, I re-lived many happy hours, yes, years, in meeting and communing with many of my old school friends, chums, and classmates, some of whom I had not seen for more than fifty years, as I moved from Savoy in 1888. In a troop they are passing before my vision now—Matt Harder, Oliver Mulkey, Lee Clark, W. I., Julia and John Hunt, Clint Mays; Nat, Lee, Pree and Lillie Hampton; Kate King, Maggie Jones, Lee Lindsey, Lee Gorrell, Sam and Edna McKee, Barlow Roberts; Doke, Maggie and Mattie Halsell; and many, many others.

I can recall many incidents of our school life, some extremely ludicrous, some semi-pathetic, all interesting, but perhaps they would be out of place in this sketch, which I fear is already far too long for our very busy but most excellent little historian, who "asked for it."

records.title: Chapter VII: Transition from a College to a Public School
records.text:
Chapter VII

Transition from a College to a Public School

THE BURNING OF THE COLLEGE PLANT

Savoy College came to an abrupt and untimely end with the burning of its plant on the night of July 3, 1890. The destruction was complete. Savoy had no fire department, and bucket-brigade methods were ineffectual to combat the flames in the close group of wooden buildings. Ex-students who lived in Savoy remember vividly the scene as faculty members and citizens strove to save the town's chief enterprise and claim to distinction and finally had to stand back out of range of explosions as the flames reached the chemistry laboratory and burst out in varicolored displays of fireworks. The library smoldered until the break of day.

PLANS FOR REBUILDING

The restoration of the plant was obviously beyond the financial abilities of the faculty members who owned it, but an effort was made to re-establish an equivalent preparatory school on some basis. A news story in The Dallas Morning News a few days after the fire reported the situation optimistically:

Savoy, Fannin County, Texas, July 10.—The citizens of this place have held several meetings for the purpose of building a college since the burning of the old one on the night of the 3rd. They met last night and raised $4,000 in subscriptions. They are building on the old foundations. The school has 200 or more pupils and will have it completed so as to be ready for the term commencing September 1. The town will doubtless have a boom they have never before witnessed, and property has already advanced in price from 20 to 25 per cent. The surrounding country expects of a fine yield of both corn and cotton, but they are greatly needed since the fire.

[184]

records.title: The Savoy Male and Female College
records.text:
[Photograph: A two-story wooden building with a bell tower or cupola at the top, decorated with ornamental trim. A sign on the building reads "Savoy Tea" or similar. Caption below the image is not fully legible.]

The building as actually erected was a two-story wooden structure of about six rooms, adorned at the top with a decorative belfry in the center (shown above).

In this belfry, later, was placed a bell purchased through the efforts of a group of students organizing themselves as "The Squintus Dramatic Club," a brief history of which appears in Part II, page 5, with a picture of the bell on page 14.

The bell (see picture on page —) contains an inscription reading as follows: "1901. Presented to Savoy College by Squintus Dramatic Club. E. K. Noseworthy (now deceased), Manager; Guy W. Thompson, now living at Dallas, Secretary; Prakney E. Durrett, now Mrs. W. H. Davis and living at Wichita Falls, Texas."

This bell is rung during each reunion of former students, but is not otherwise used by the present school.


EFFORTS TO REORGANIZE A COLLEGE

The old College faculty, in discouragement, had scattered variously toward new places or more definite incomes in the rapidly developing public schools or other colleges. Pro-

records.title: THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE
records.text:
fessor Halsell had moved his family to West Texas and he was superintendent of the school at Anson for the next two years. Professor Pritchett had returned to Bonham to teach in Fannie College; and Professor Simmons presently became superintendent of the Bells school.

No record has been found of the teachers who carried on the school for the first two years after the fire, but the citizens apparently did not give up hope of re-establishing a private college, according to the following statement by Mr. L. G. Gee:

In 1892 I went to Anson in search of a school. While there I met Mr. W. B. Halsell. He told me then that the citizens of Savoy wanted him to return there to try to rebuild Savoy College, and that if he would come back to Savoy he could have the headship of it for five years. He persuaded me to join him in this enterprise. Halsell took the principalship, and I was employed as an assistant in mathematics and history.

Mr. Halsell, with Mr. Gee, did return to Savoy, but after two years Mr. Halsell moved to Durant, Indian Territory. Mr. Gee stayed and carried on. A pamphlet for 1897-98 reveals the following designations of teachers: L. G. Gee, principal and teacher of ancient languages and Bible; Professor H. A. Henderson, natural science (former F.A.M.E. teacher), mathematics and history; W. E. McMahan (also a former college teacher), Latin, physics, and chemistry; and Miss Martha Buford (likewise a Savoy College ex-student), primary. Mr. S. I. Chesworth, a Savoy graduate who married Miss Frankie Chesworth (graduate and former piano teacher of the College, a daughter of Mr. J. W. Chesworth, one of the founders), was principal of the school for the next several years.

Although the institution was evidently operated as a public school during these years, it seems to have carried the name of Savoy College, for in the report of the United States Commissioner of Education for 1897-1898 (the only year in which the Savoy school was reported) the name "Savoy College" appears in the statistical tabulations of high schools.

records.title: THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE
records.text:
LATER DEVELOPMENT OF THE SAVOY PUBLIC SCHOOLS

The Savoy school continued a progressive development. The wooden structure built subsequent to the fire of 1890 was, in course of time, replaced by a modern brick building. When this building, in a few years, became both unsafe and inadequate for the district's needs, the commodious structure which now stands in Savoy was erected. The present building is modern in equipment, with gas heating, electric lights, and drinking fountains. The school has a good library, laboratory, and an auditorium. The district has incorporated several of the surrounding communities through annexation or consolidation with outlying districts, and now maintains three buses to transport the rural children to school. There is now an average enrollment of 275 pupils. Both white and colored schools have efficient teachers.

Mr. W. F. Carter is president of the present School Board. The current faculty listing with subjects taught and the number of years in Savoy follow:

Mr. J. W. Moulton, Superintendent, nine years, Latin.
Mr. Walter McCollum, principal, two years, Science and History.
Miss Alma Witherspoon, two years, English.
Miss Pauline Barnett, three years, History and Commercial Work.
Mr. Tom Garner, one year, Sixth and Seventh Grades.
Mrs. Mary Morgan, twelve years, Fourth and Fifth Grades.
Mrs. Lakah Baker, twelve years, Second and Third Grades.
Miss Beulah Fulson, fourteen years, Primary.
Mr. K. Y. Edwards, two years, Vocational Agriculture.
Miss Tommie Chesworth (daughter of T. J. Chesworth, one of the founders of Savoy College), three years, Music.
Miss Bonnie Lee Roberts, three years, Librarian.
Irene Carr, colored teacher, three years.**

records.title: Chapter VIII
records.text:
Chapter VIII

The Preservation of Savoy College Tradition

ACTIVITIES PRECEDING THE REUNION OF 1938

REVIVAL OF THE REUNION IDEA.—For years Savoy College ex-students talked among themselves about the possibility of having a Reunion. It had been hoped that such plans might materialize during the life times of the founder, Professor R. B. Halsell, and his comrades in the work for many years, Professor Simmons. They had such plans come to a realization, many other beloved faculty members, who have now passed on, could have been present, too.

In the summer of 1937, when with the aid of Federal funds through the Works Progress Administration the Savoy Independent School District was holding a new gymnasium, Mr. Gus W. Thomasson, a WPA foreman in charge of a part of the work, happened to be a grandson of Thomas J., a Savoy College founder and using the occasion of the building's dedication, originated a plan for a reunion of ex-students of the old College.

On August 15, 1937, Mr. Thomasson sent a circular letter to as large a mailing list of former students as he could compile, giving in the letter the history of the old school and suggesting that Mr. W. F. Carter, president of the Savoy School Board and an old Savoy school man himself, was even then ready to begin making plans for a gathering of ex-students to take place at the dedication of the gymnasium planned for the fall. A date in November was set for this. It was also mentioned, incidentally, that the Works Progress Administration, through Mr. Gaber, was even then engaged in compiling a history of Fannin County, of Savoy, and of the old Savoy school. A plea was made that documents, photographs, or relics of interest of the old school to be sent to Mr. Thomasson or Carter.

ORGANIZATION OF A GENERAL REUNION COMMITTEE.—Enthusiastic responses to Mr. Thomasson's letter brought such

( 188 )

records.title: THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE
records.text:
interest that when invitations were sent urging the former Savoy College students to attend the cornerstone laying of the Halsell Gymnasium, WPA project No. 2022, more than fifty ex-students of the old College were in attendance. Many others wrote letters expressing warm interest. The roster and the names of the forty-eight ex-students who did were copied from the official register and placed in the cornerstone with some relics of the College that had been brought for that purpose. The names of these appear in the roster on page 233.

Notice of a called meeting of former Savoy College ex-students following immediately after the cornerstone-laying program was placed on the program. That meeting was the first official group of ex-students to undertake plans for an all-college reunion. It set up a general committee on reunion plans, which began work immediately. The members of the committee were:

Their cordiality was such that each welcomed the others and the committee members, as they expressed it, had fun among themselves far above and beyond the duties of the work. Excerpts from a few letters are quoted below just as a sample of their "preliminary pleasures":

Dear Old Savoy friends:
I am enclosing herewith copies of letters from Harlow Roberts and Albert Galbraith concerning the proposed Savoy College School reunion and am particularly directing your attention to what is said about the boys headed for a camp to be organized to protect us from Mr. Hitler. I haven't read much that is pathetic about the love but it may be mostly in their heads

records.title: THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE
records.text:
rather than their feet. Those letters I have sent on to the secretary, Mrs. J. B. May, editor of the "Savoy Star," for she will know how to handle them. If she is off the press you will find out how much they all think of you boys and the love. Little (my wife) I can recall ever taking an active part in a love—just stood around and watched others. Little (my wife) may not agree with me but I can recall that the night she was going out with the boys a long time before I quit going barefooted. I went barefooted so long waiting, playing first base, that I made it through those old outfield shoes by stepping on a groundball while knowing a woman was watching, and then spiked my feet so that other boys just couldn't follow me. I would rest up and come right back. You may also notice that some of the mothers of these same love boys had their tongues hanging out.

Gus says you are busy but too old to furnish the music, but I think at least you could manage the affair, and give your personal touch to help us get up a show even though it doesn't make music. You know it is a comedy act in which I played the role of a bashful country cousin in which you and Barry acted the part of the fresh city cousin, and as the script called for it you were given a scheme to exploit me and I recall that when the young lady in question heard of way said that I wouldn't let her do it even though she wanted to. Our problem seems to be to round up the actors, put in a night or so doing something less than a dance, and make as though they believe it was really worth while. Take it calmly old boy and have.

Please write the "Savoy Star" what you boys think about it. Is it right enough? Do you think a dance on the 13th instant may comment on your attitude."

Affectionately,*

My wife good read my letter of yesterday after it was that Mrs. Montgomery "suggested that we have a meeting, drawing on ourselves." The plans were so far advanced at that time that you could hardly push anything farther than committee business, without even the boys being too embarrassed in order to be pleased. The idea of a possible banquet was far from it.

*Letter to Messrs. Barry and Bob Taylor from Mr. E. A. McMahon, Dallas, Texas, December 1, 1937.

The two Whitworth committeewomen have ceased acquaintances, it would have been a good guard to make in secrecy. As a new committee man, editor may not be aware of the background of my touch with the Jones and King family of "Ginger Joe" and of others who have lived here. An interesting reminiscent mention of them was made in my home, and I stayed awhile in Jim Jones' drug store when rather small. My recollection is very distinct and clear about a professional visit by. King made in my home. As to the King family affair, but I can go this one better. I was listening to a conversation between Dr. K. and my father. In the discussion was the stone of the church across the street of "Come Argel Road," the observation was made, that if it were a window, so much the better. My father, and I heard him, remarked that: "Were a band of angels to really appear, there would not be a window sash left in the building!" The speaker's graphic description of the fancy built a vast scene of the results and in later years there is not a window intact! In memory, I was shocked at the visions of the little pickaxinettes as many appeared to be present. As a businessman now, I am no less realistic, and I hope the visions went with me down to old age. Even now my voice is very weak and faltering.

"Lord I care not for riches, neither silver nor gold," and I do not find himself in trouble while he held the fold.

"I would make sure of Heaven, I would enter the fold."

With a background like that I should not be surprised at almost anything but it also ended with a vision of the youth in those days that would hold "Mag." Anyway, the members of the committee are free to act as they see fit. I have told you of the ideas that I have put in the way of the affair. The object before the committee is the really important thing and earth-bound policies and a banquet might inhibit wise deliberations of the committee.

I am in receipt of your (Mac Ed's letter in which he listens your letter to him and I certainly appreciate his thoughts about the matter and I am very much as you stated the same feeling about the way you handled the matter and the keen interest

COMPILING THE EX-STUDENTS ROSTER.—The first big task of the Committee was to compile a list of living ex-students, for the burning of the College had destroyed all of the records, and the lapse of forty-eight years added to the difficulty. To start with, besides the names used at the cornerstone laying, as a nucleus, a few other names were added to form a list from which to work. A letter was sent to each asking for names. Mr. L. G. Gee compiled a roster from memory as much as possible. This was sent out about July 20, 1938, when the ex-students' list had grown to twenty to thirty names, though some were duplicates. Presently a completion of the alumni catalog of 1887-1888 came to light and furnished more than two hundred extra names but some bore for current address. NEWSPAPER PUBLICITY.—Advance newspaper publicity for the reunion was generous. The largest amount of space was, naturally, given by The Savoy Star. In December, 1937, the Thirty-fifth Anniversary edition, with an entire section devoted to the College, was given wide circulation.

Earlier, when it was thought that the gymnasium would be completed during the fall, Mr. Gee sent notice of the forthcoming reunion to several papers for advance promotion. As it turned out, the issue was perhaps more effective in turning minds to the reunion, however.

Quite a lot of advance reunion publicity appeared in The Dallas Morning News, which carried pictures of two Savoy College men (now Dallas residents), E. A. McMahon, and and former student, and the George Elliot Coleric, the rather brief biography of Savoy College's early days.

One article of unusual news interest is quoted below as it was furbished to the Dallas Journal from Mr. Gus W. Thomasson of Dallas on July 29, 1938:

The article in the Dallas Journal of August 3, 1937, describing the interesting story was: (1937-1938)

SAVOY GYMNASIUM IS SUBJECT OF FIRST PRINTED PICTURE EVER SENT FROM TEXAS TOWN

The Journal is permitted to announce the introduction of the first photograph ever sent over telephone wires from one Texas point to another in the state's newspaper.

The picture was made in Savoy, Texas, about eleven o'clock this morning by Karl Moore, staff photographer of The Journal. Mr. Moore left Dallas this morning with The Journal's new portable wired picture machine. After taking the picture at Savoy, developed it and mounted it, he placed the print on the cylinder of the portable, hooked it up to a long distance telephone, called The Journal dark room and began sending the pictures.

records.title: THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE
records.text:
NEW WIRED PICTURE SERVICE FOR THE JOURNAL INTRODUCES PORTABLE SENDING MACHINE

Within fifteen minutes after his connection was established with this office, the completed duplicate of the Savoy picture was in The Journal dark room ready for printing.

This view was made in the photograph studio of Geo. W. Wear at Sherman while the picture on page 201 was being transmitted by telephone wire from Sherman to Dallas.

CORRESPONDENCE WITH EX-STUDENTS.—In addition to newspaper publicity, the advance planning included the sending out of a questionnaire to ex-students, to be filled out and returned to the secretary by every ex-student of the Savoy College who could be found; a printed booklet of the tentative two-day reunion program; and a final card of invitation on July 20, 1938, urging all ex-students and friends of the College to attend the reunion in Savoy, August 6 and 7, 1938. The response to the mailing of the questionnaire and application for banquet reservations (the only mailing asking a written answer) was encouraging to the committee as 124 forms were returned.

THE REUNION OF AUGUST 6 AND 7, 1938

ASSEMBLY AND REGISTRATION.—All plans worked out almost to the mark of perfection, and on Saturday morning, August 6, 1938, a large group of ex-students and friends of old Savoy College arrived at the new Halsell Gymnasium in Savoy for the informal greeting time which was scheduled to extend to the two o'clock business meeting hour.

A news reporter described the morning's activities thus:

Remarking on the enthusiasm of the celebrants one observer said: "Why, they went on like a school reunion!"

Handshakes were warm and kisses were noted in profusion. Eyes sparkled with memories renewed, friendships of bygone years.*

Much of the morning was spent in enjoying the exhibit of old photographs, diplomas, textbooks, autograph albums, and other cherished College mementos. At noon the registration began under the supervision of Mr. Lew Reynolds, former professor of music and leadership in the College. The hand-made frontispiece for the list of registrants shown by photostats in this chapter is a work of art done by Mr. Reynolds himself for the occasion at the author's request.**

THE FORMATION OF A PERMANENT EX-STUDENTS' ASSOCIATION.—From the standpoint of long-time perpetuation of interest in the old Savoy College tradition, the most significant activity of the whole reunion period was the crystallization of the reunion occasion into a permanent association of ex-students and the provision for annual reunions in the future. The complete official minutes are herewith given. The official minutes of the afternoon business session kept by Mrs. J. B. May, the secretary of the General Committee on the Reunion:

*Sherman Democrat, Sherman, Texas, Vol. LIX, No. 102, August 7, 1938.

    After the last course was served, a waiting crowd of perhaps five hundred more people was admitted to the gymnasium seats to witness and hear the program which followed, and still others remained on open-air seats erected in front of the building and heard the program through loudspeaker extensions.

    Facing this combined crowd of well over seven hundred people, Mr. Gus W. Thomasson proved a most capable and spirited toastmaster. After the invocation by Judge Oliver C. Mulkey, of Commerce, Texas, Mr. Thomasson delivered the keynote address entitled "After Fifty Years."

records.title: Page 225
records.text:
210  THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

AFTER FIFTY YEARS

    We are making history here, today, in a reunion of old students of Savoy College, meeting for the first time fifty years after their old school has passed out of existence.

    The incorporated name of our old school was "The Savoy Male and Female College." It had elementary and college departments. The transition from the grades into the college department was no more than changing from one classroom into another. There was no such thing in those days as "going off to college." The college was right at home, and mother stayed at home too.

    I do not think that reunions were thought worthwhile, and certainly not practicable, until now, for several reasons. One reason is that students came from long distances to attend school, did not go home until the end of school, had little roads over which to travel in wagons and lighter vehicles with but little money to spare for the purpose. After graduation or leaving school, they scattered. It was difficult to get together for a reunion, as now with good roads, automobiles, and a better economic condition for all concerned.

    Another reason, I think, why our students made no effort at a reunion for fifty years, is that when Mr. Halsell moved away from Savoy and Texas, and there remained no nucleus about which to form such a reunion. So, the reunion spirit has been allowed to lie dormant for almost half a century. Happily, however, the grandchildren and great-grandchildren, as those of the old student body who are still living come together to show their respect for early struggles for an education, and live over in our memories the scenes, the experiences of those days in a school half a century ago. As I see this large gathering here it is a matter of significant historical interest, as I do not know about the life of the individual.

    In this reunion there is an outstanding difference to be noted in its purpose. There is no effort being made to evaluate or discover whether or not the Almighty involved as to the success or failure in life of the individual student, for the court of final review has already either made good or has not. For the most part the old students who have gathered around their old school have attained reasonable success in life.

records.title: Page 226
records.text:
THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE  211

    There was something in the character and personalities of Mr. Halsell and his associates, and did they not strive to inculcate the idea of surrounding himself with competent and efficient men and women as teachers? I never knew of the old school to have created in the heart and mind of every pupil a desire to go forward in life and make the world better for having lived in it.

    The old school had another characteristic: it was a poor boy's and girl's school. There were no fancy and expensive frills to it. There was but one serious purpose, and that was to get an education. If any boy or girl failed to get an education from this school it was because he or she was unable to pay tuition. Although there was a strong effort Mr. Halsell always found way to provide tuition for those deserving it. I think of old this through his conversation instructed me that he was able to extend the advantages of the school to those who were not able to pay for it. Of this there were many who are here today, and they are grateful and honest.

    So, I again say, we are making history today in holding this reunion, and, for one, I am glad of the opportunity thus to pay tribute to the great men and women who made this school what it was.

    Much credit is due Ed McMahon for both the holding of this reunion and its success. He and I had long talks about this fine enterprise for several years, even before the death of our greatly beloved President and General Chairman, Warren Halsell. As a matter of fact, Ed and I made several visits when the construction of this gymnasium was under way, and when erected here as a suitable and fitting memorial to this noble man who is entitled to this fond memory. Even then my official duties were of such a onerous nature that I could not do more than assume more than a nominal relationship to the enterprise. The members of this Ex-Students body who planned, organized, raised funds, and spent their time and money in bringing the undertaking to its full fruition.

    Before Mr. Thomasson had finished his address, the banquet group had enthusiastically caught the reunion spirit of the occasion. The sing-song which followed—led by a kinsman

records.title: Page 227
records.text:
212  THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

of Prof. R. R. Halsell, Mr. Ben Halsell of Bonham—heightened the enthusiasm so much that the reminiscent ex-students were loath to quit singing. But the program was full and had to move fast.

    Mr. W. P. Carter, president of the Savoy School Board, gave a word of greeting.

    One of the most enjoyable surprises to the ex-students, as during the day it had been secretly planned between Mrs. J. B. May and the grandchildren of the founders. About twenty of them gathered around the microphone and gave this toast in animated fashion:

            Rah  Rah  Rah
            Rah  Rah  Rah
            Rah  Rah  Rah
        Savoy College Exes
        Gathered here from over Texas
        To honor old Savoy College,
        The place where we received your knowledge,
        Halsell! Halsell! Halsell!
        Hurr-ah! Hurr-ah!
            OUR DEAR PRESIDENT!

    Reminiscent talks of Old Savoy Days were made by Judge J. Benton Maxey of Atoka, Oklahoma; Judge Lee A. Clark of Greenville, Texas; Mr. Jno. M. Gist of Odessa, Texas; Judge W. E. McMahon of Mexico City; Judge N. E. Peak of Greenville, Texas; Mr. Jim J. Gallagher of Waco, Texas; and others. These stories ranged from humorous references to "the boy in the apple tree" in the old "Blue-Back" to poems of touching sentiment.

    An effective rendition of songs, made the more sentimental by the special setting, was given by Miss Mary Alice Pritchett, daughter of former Professor E. H. Pritchett. Mrs. E. H. Pritchett, herself a former student and teacher, was present and assisted her daughter at the piano, but becoming rather touched by the occasion, eventually gave way to Miss Mary Alice Pritchett.

    Coming next on the program as a humorous contrast, was the "Lew" Reynolds, who gave a recitation of everybody's classic poem, "My Breeches, Oh, My Sunday Breeches!"

    The banquet program was concluded with the singing (to the tune of Auld Lang Syne) the words of a song, Savoy

College Days, sent in by Mrs. Lena Pace Hodges, of Hollywood, California, who was unable to attend the reunion.

    The banquet ended and the room was quickly cleared to make room for the staging of an old-time "levee" designed to give pleasure to the young people who attended the banquet as well as to provide the ex-students extra time for long-wished-for-visits among the participants. The levee, carried on under the direction of Robert and Harry Naylor of Sherman in the absence of the Naylor boys of Collinsville, afforded an excellent means of adding to the socialization of the ex-students, who were the "onlookers only" as no one was permitted to be on the floor but those who wore the official ex-student registration badge. The dignity and solemnity with which Robert Naylor directed the old Scotch Reel, lent all the more jollity to the affair. With the approach of midnight it was "goodnight, ladies" and the crowd left the Halsell Memorial Gymnasium not to return until two o'clock dedication ceremonies the next day.

THE DEDICATION OF THE HALSELL MEMORIAL GYMNASIUM—Sunday morning, August 7, 1938, services at all the churches in Savoy were attended by many ex-students, and the Reverend May, pastor of the Sherman Avenue Church, preached at the Baptist Church. In addition to attending these services, many of the visitors took advantage of opportunity to visit in the town of Savoy in search of familiar landmarks of the past. Many of the participants in the reunion marked their first return to these scenes in forty or fifty years.

    At two o'clock, in the gymnasium, the formal dedication program began. Dr. William Deatherage of Dallas, delivered the invocation. He is the only son of Dr. J. R., living, being then an octogenarian.

    Honorable J. B. May, Mayor of Savoy, made the address of welcome and Honorable Mark McMahon, of Fort Worth, responded.

    Recognition was made of the Descendants of the Founders, who were called to the front as each of the names of founders was named. When the members of Professor Halsell's first family of forty-eight pupils were asked to stand, ten responded. They were:

DEDICATION OF SAVOY GYMNASIUM

WPA PROJECTS 5023 AND 9708

By Gus W. Thomasson, Administrative Field Officer, Works Progress Administration, Dallas Area

    Mr. Chairman, Ladies, and Gentlemen:

    It has been my good fortune as the Works Progress Administration, when requested so to do by sponsors, to dedicate its major projects, for many purposes. In the course of that duty, I have attended many dedications, but I have considered not only a major but an outstanding major project.


HISTORY OF THE PROJECT

    This project was originally started on May 17, 1937, estimated at that time to cost $16,417.65, of which the Government was to pay $13,364.52, and Savoy Independent School District, as sponsor, was to pay $4,051.13. This period of operation was allocated for 106 workers, 94 unskilled and 12 skilled. Various changes in the project due to some delays in materials due principally to bad weather conditions, plus an increased cost by increased wage scale effective October 1, 1937, and additional work ordered by WPA to complete the project, caused a suspension of operations on February 15, 1938, at which time a supplemental project was submitted to Washington. It was not until May 11, 1938, that the total approval of the new project was finally obtained. The new project as approved and put into a complete place called for an additional outlay of funds of $15,549.52, making a total of $31,997.27, of which the Government agreed to supply $30,063.61 (61.8¢) and the sponsor agreed to supply $11,539.35 (38.2¢).

    On September 19, 1937, the cornerstone of this building was laid with appropriate ceremonies, at which a group of citizens who were students and supporters of this college, and whose names were placed in the stone, and a number of other honored out-of-tellers, their friends and interested parties, attended. The number of number of persons present being estimated as 500 to 600.

records.title: Page 231
records.text:
216  THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

CHARACTER OF THE PROJECT

    The material of which the walls are built is a native stone, found a few miles north of town. It is described by competent builders as being a very superior building stone because of its flint-like nature. A building properly constructed as it is of this firm texture stone and reinforced concrete, will last indefinitely. There has been no finer building, based on the over-all cost, constructed in recent years in the Dallas areas by the Works Progress Administration.

    The revised project includes much ground work in the way of leveling and landscaping, with football and baseball fields, tennis courts, etc.

    The building as it stands today is practically completed, and the project as a whole is expected to be completed within two weeks. I desire in a formal way to call briefly to your attention to a few items: (1) Number one quality of native flooring has been used in this building, whereas a number two or three quality is usually used; (2) Bolts instead of nails are used throughout in the construction of the roof and bleachers, making it far more substantial; (3) All mill work is of prime quality and design; and (4) The seating arrangement is permanent bleachers with seating capacity of 600. In fact, no important detail has been overlooked. It has been an object of our earnestness in the performance of this work.


AS A MEMORIAL

    At the time of the laying of the cornerstone on September 19, 1937, the Board of Trustees of the Savoy Independent School District, and by formal resolution, named the building aside and dedicated of this building. This completed as a memorial to the late Warren Halsell, founder of the original school. Over the main entrance there has been placed a stone nameplate bearing the words Halsell Memorial. In addition to this, over the entrance there has been placed another stone bearing a dedicatory inscription.


AN UNUSUAL PROJECT

    These features therefore characterize an unusual project. The fact that a reunion of ex-students of the old school is being held at time of the dedication is also unusual in the history of WPA. This was deemed of sufficient of the National News Service as noteworthy, and both news gathering associations in the field have not out over their wires to all sections of the United States.

records.title: Page 232
records.text:
THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE  217

ROBERT ROBINSON HALSELL

    I spoke briefly on the life of Mr. Halsell at the time of the laying of the cornerstone of this building, and wish to repeat on this occasion what I said about him then, since some reference to him seems most appropriate.

    There are four or five outstanding facts about Mr. Halsell which I especially remember, the first of which is that he was a great disciplinarian. Eight o'clock was the opening hour for our morning exercises, not 8:00 nor 8:10, or any later period, but woe to any student who came in after the opening bell rang. Every morning about 7:50 or 8:00 o'clock, when Mr. Halsell would come into the room and begin calling and checking exercises, you were supposed to have pencil and paper ready and when to copy the exercises, and when after he had given them, they were handed in at the close of morning exercises and a grade was given for it, and those who failed to submit a report were also called to account. These morning exercises were in keeping his record keeping so accurate and complete as one of the greatest I have ever known.

    I want to second, he a great humanitarian. Every student felt free to take his troubles to him, and when some of the boys could not find the money to meet tuition, those who had money were not made aware of it, by what he called "Back halls." I do not know whether he charged anything or the use of these back halls. I know Mr. Halsell never refused to allow any boy or any girl without money from what I have not done from their own to come to his school.

    Third, he was a real Christian gentleman, a real Christian gentleman, and when you can say that about any man you are saying a lot. He was a man well liked of the community, and I do not recall that I ever heard of anything but an unbecoming conduct on the school premises or among his students at any time.

    Fourth, he was a great educator. He knew how to teach, and teaching in a small school is a very much harder job than teaching in a large school. The small school teacher must know how to teach. The test of Mr. Halsell's teaching was that his students got results. I believe that it is safe to say that a greater number of students and a more self-reliant boy or girl who ever went to Mr. Halsell arose out in life than any boy or girl I have ever known.

    Fifth, Mr. Halsell was an ideal family man. He reared a family in a little town of Savoy that was one of those outstanding families. I knew all of his children, and when you just say something to the son or those two daughters who are reading on the platform and hear them extol the virtues of their father.

records.title: Page 233
records.text:
218  THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

    Sixth, and last, Mr. Halsell was a philanthropist in an unusual way. He was the poor boys' and poor girls' friend. I never knew of him to turn any boy or girl away who was otherwise unable to pay for it, being turned away who came to Mr. Halsell. He probably often went with money out of his own pocket. It is true that he had a hard time working teachers their salaries, but he always took care of the boys and girls who wanted an education.

STUDENTS AND EX-STUDENTS

    We have in our audience today a most unusual group of persons, being a large number of the present student body, and a considerable audience comprising the surrounding citizens. I speak with greater freedom before ex-students of the latter group, and therefore can speak advisedly in saying that it is very desirable for the ex-students and the students to visualize the sacrifices, hardships, privations and personal discomforts through which those students of the old days went in those days to get their education, and in their efforts to secure an education.

    To much credit should be given to Mr. Halsell and his associates for their sacrificial leadership in those days when an education was not so easily obtained as it is today. I want you of the present generation to think well upon the fine character and achievement of the present-day student body of the Savoy School, and I to those who may hear me who are of the school age to think well. You might not enjoy the conveniences which are provided here. We make no sacrifice and went to no hardship like the students of other days, and yet, if you were forced to go through what they went through to get an education, most of you present would get along with your education then. I think we lacked conveniences and that we lacked comforts and that we lacked opportunities to get a good education. In our day we were greatly in advance of the day of our forefathers, and so it is in the day that we live in.

    To him who is so fortunate as to have nearly completed education in an institution but who has had to depend upon one's efforts to get a good education, the education has been more enduring. To those who are either untrained person in life, I should like to encourage you to take advantage of every opportunity which you have in trying to secure a complete education, to encourage you, if I may, to continue your own education until it is completed. How does it benefit a man or woman who is not mentally fully equipped to compete with others who are fully trained and who experienced such and such as the case, wait until he is not too late that you have thrown away the greatest asset now available to you.

records.title: Page 234
topics: House by the Side of the Road
records.text:
THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE  219

CEREMONY OF DEDICATION

    We have now finished our task. This building has been completed. Acting upon the authority of Honorable Harry P. Dwight, State Administrator of Works Progress Administration for Texas, who but for the limitations of time which would permit him to participate in the numerous dedicatory events which are taking place throughout Texas today and hence delegated me to represent him and who is pleased to be here in person, but who, in his absence, authorizes me to extend to you his heartiest felicitations and greetings and best wishes for the success of this building.

    The primary purpose of this building is to form a useful adjunct of your system of education and especially for your student body. But it goes further than that. It is designed to form a community center in which all activities, not alone your student body but of your parents, not of your municipality but of your citizenship in its entirety, as well, may be served. It is not in the building's secondary another building to be used incidentally for such purposes as may for the moment be obvious. It is a building which at all times and for all purposes should be kept open and always available to include all of the welfare needs of your community.

    It bears the name of Warren Halsell, a person who was a great influence in this community. I know of no more fitting manner in which to express the spirit of the full life of Warren Halsell than by repeating a portion of the story and words of a poem with which I am sure many of you are more or less familiar. The story is as follows: A man named Sam Walter Foss was traveling along the road one day to a shaded nook by the road, stopped momentarily to rest, and in shaded tones had a sign, which read: "If you are weary, have a seat; if you are thirsty, have a drink; and if you are hungry, help yourself." He found an open road, and he found a spring, beside the spring he found a basket well filled with luscious apples. He partook of the hospitality that was there on the road side, and took away with him this poem. A very vital and moving part of the poem which he wrote, as a result of this experience, are these words:

        "Let me live in my house by the side of the road,
            Where the race of men go by;
        The men who are good and the men who are bad,
            They are weak, they are strong,
        Wise, foolish,—so am I.

        'Then why should I sit in the scorner's seat
            Or hurl the cynic's ban?
        Let me live in my house by the side of the road
            And BE A FRIEND TO MAN."

records.title: Page 235
topics: acceptance address on behalf of founders
records.text:
220  THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

    It is therefore my happy privilege, as a representative of our Government in the capacity of Administrative Field Officer of Works Progress Administration, Dallas Areas No. 4, to now dedicate this building in the spirit of this poem, to serve for all time to come the welfare of the young and old— as a place of wholesome learning and wholesome recreation, may be developed into a community center in all that the term means and, as such, inspire and encourage to nobler thinking and higher ambition in life all who may enjoy its benefits, and I now so dedicate it.


ACCEPTANCE ADDRESS ON BEHALF OF THE FOUNDERS

By Mrs. Annie Halsell Woodward

    Mr. Chairman, Ladies, and Gentlemen:

    Little did I ever think that the day would come in my life when I would stand here to pay public tribute to my father—my beloved father—Warren Halsell. It is with deep appreciation that I am permitted to be here today, and while many of you know of him by the gracious acts he performed and the noble things he stood for, I knew him as a loving and tender father, with all the meaning that implies, and therefore well realize the feeling that is in my heart today as I speak. None of the other children of his are present, my taking part, in some small way, in paying tribute to the memory of him was first and foremost the reason for being here today.

    It seems to us, in whose veins courses his blood, that today we stand on the threshold of a greater era. It is out of a century that he dedicated some of the best years of his life to the service of his fellow-man, and it was most fitting that here, where he gave gratefully his best efforts to know and that men making a school in this little town and in this county, a place of service, for in serving others he had in mind the knowledge of living.

    If there could be gathered a roll of those who were at one time or another his pupils, there would be found embodied in that list a large number of those who have become leaders in their respective communities and who, the servants of their fellow men—men who became leaders in all that stood for better life in the community, the county, in the society in which they move and have their being.

    First, I call your kind attention to the fact Honorable John T. Ashcraft, who was a member of the faculty while

records.title: Page 236
records.text:
THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE  221

our father was the head of this school, later returned to Florence, Alabama, his native state and there became one of its most distinguished citizens, a member of and leader in the Alabama Constitution Convention of 1901. His service to his people was the culmination of that principle of good government inculcated in his association with, and admiration for, the man you remember and love as Professor Robert Halsell.

    When our father left the great State of Texas and moved to the Indian Territory, that is now a part of the State of Oklahoma, he gave another quarter of a century to a profession he loved. He founded the city of Bryan County— Durant, Oklahoma—and his associates had sent him back to the State Legislature as their representative in that lawmaking body. It was among the duties of Bryan County that he built the first private school in what was then Indian Territory. That school, conducted by him in Oklahoma and later in Texas, carried on as he did work in Texas.

    His life and endeavors in Oklahoma were but an amplification of the work he had done here for the State of people, and in that new commonwealth, as in this one, he builded a reputation second to no man in his time.

    Thus he spent nearly fifty years of his time here on earth in the service of his fellow man. Every minute of it, we who loved him know, was spent in doing good. He was unselfish beyond all measure. He was a man who gave his best at all times, when he was a man of activity. He was busy, just, and cheerful. His life was an endless example of that noble, that inestimable virtue spoken of by old Carlyle, the virtue of work—work done with the whole heart of man.

    You today have dedicated to his memory a beautiful building that will for all time be known as Halsell Memorial Gymnasium. A structure builded by the hands of man to honor his memory will not endure forever; but you have erected a building not made by human hands but eternal and living forever in the hearts of those who knew and talked with him in life, a noble character, a character that endures in the heritage he left his students.

    In behalf of the living members of my father's family, I want to express our deep appreciation for your love and loyalty and the memory of our father, to the citizens of Savoy and to the others who founded Savoy College. We shall never forget your gracious hospitality and the beautiful sacrifices and the great and good work you have done to perpetuate his memory and enliven his ideals.

records.title: Acceptance Address on Behalf of the Schools
records.text:
ACCEPTANCE ADDRESS ON BEHALF OF THE SCHOOLS

By J. Wesley Moulton, Superintendent of Savoy Schools

Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen:

As several speakers have already told you, today is a red-letter day in the history of Savoy, the greatest day, perhaps, in the history of this little town. A day that we have all been looking forward to with eagerness and anticipation for all these months.

Perhaps we Americans people are an impatient people, when everything does not happen just as we think it should, and I am afraid some of us had decided that this building would never be completed; that we had a "white elephant" on our hands, but I am happy to say that we were wrong and here is this magnificent building for your inspection and approval. We do not believe that there is a single man, woman, boy, or girl in Savoy or surrounding communities whose heart is not overflowing with gratitude and pride as they behold this magnificent building. Yes! We are proud of it, and why shouldn't we be? You have just heard Mr. Thomasson tell you that out of about 50 such buildings that have been constructed under his administration that this is one of the very best, if not the best. And you have also heard him present it to us without obligation, but we do feel a great sense of responsibility as a school, as a town, and as citizens, to use this building. Yes, but also to take care of it, and we promise you that as long as it lasts and we are in charge of it, it shall not be neglected, nor allowed to be torn up and run down, but kept in such condition that you will feel just as proud of it ten years from now as you do today.

We are connected with this school in a vital way, and naturally feel some concern about its administration, and so forth, and have given much time to study and meditation about it. We feel that this is a building which has been constructed in the discussion that has been going on these past months as to what kind of a school this is to be, and what attitude the school is to take toward religion, and so forth. And let me say in the beginning, this is not, never has been, and never will be, a Godless school, or a school where religion will be ignored or treated lightly. Far be it from such. We feel keenly our responsibility in the matter of religion, and as far as we are concerned, religion shall always be respected and reverenced here.

Perhaps, who knows, but in some future time that this school, through the aid of some good teacher, and this magnificent building, may develop another Robert Halsell, Sam McSpadden, or some such other character.

records.title: Newspaper Reception of the Reunion
records.text:
Rayburn, or Gus W. Thomasson, and hundreds of other good and useful citizens. When it shall have accomplished that goal, then, perhaps, we shall, in a small way, have paid a part of the obligation we owe to you, Mr. Thomasson, and to our government.

So, stirring toward these goals, in behalf of the Board of Education of Savoy School and the entire citizenship of Savoy and surrounding communities, it affords me great pleasure to accept this magnificent building as a sacred trust to use and to keep.

May this building, dedicated to athletics, be a monument to this man of learning, who helped so many boys and girls to secure that something which lifted them to higher planes than ordinary level, and which planted their feet on the road to fame and usefulness. May this building, in memory, beckoning to unborn generations to seek an education that they may be brighter still and lifted up. May it stand as such a building for many generations yet to come.

The building and grounds were equipped with a loud speaker public address system which accommodated the overflow crowd seated on the temporary bleachers erected in the front of the building.
