records.title: Afterword — 1942
records.text:
AFTERWORD—1942

The Savoy College Ex-Student Association deems it a great privilege to be permitted to sponsor the publication of the History of Savoy Male and Female College and acknowledges a debt of gratitude to its author, Miss Mattie Lee Boyd, for the painstaking care and efficient manner in which she assembled and compiled Part I, which constitutes that portion prepared and used by her as a thesis in obtaining an M.A. Degree from the Texas State University, in 1939.

Although discussion was had by ex-students as to publishing this history, following its completion by Miss Boyd, no definite action was taken to that end until the year 1941. At that time a small sum was pledged as a printing fund. The task of completing the undertaking was assigned to the Board of Managers with full power and authority to act. When it was learned that the cost of printing a first edition in limited quantity would be relatively high to insure a popular sale of the book, an underwriting fund was provided to absorb the excess cost. Former students and friends contributing such fund were: Miss Lou A. Arterberry, Mrs. James D. Brewster (in memory of her husband), Lee A. Clark, Harve L. Davis, John Donaghey, John M. Gist, Charles Halsell (in memory of the founder), Fred J. Harle, Walter S. Jenkins, Mrs. Martha Buford May, Charlton H. McGaughey, Ed A. McMahon, Robert McKee, W. Emmett McMahon, Lewis J. Reynolds, Bernice Roberts, Mrs. Beulah Thomasson Stinnett, Gus W. Thomasson, John Urquhart[?], Guy P. Webb, and Mrs. Lemuel (Olivia) Whedbee (in memory of her husband).

We now send this book on its way to your friends and that it may prove informative and encouraging to all who may read it.

E. A. McMAHON, President,
LEWIS J. REYNOLDS,
BEULAH THOMASSON STINNETT,
GUS W. THOMASSON,
Board of Managers.

Dallas, Texas, April, 1942.

records.title: Mattie Lee Boyd
records.text:
[Photograph: a young woman in a long dress standing outdoors on rocky ground, holding a bow and arrow.]

MATTIE LEE BOYD

The author of Part I of this book refused to permit the use of her photograph therein, and the use of her picture here is unauthorized by her. The publishers believe, however, that those who receive the book will appreciate knowing how she looks; and, again, this is another evidence on their part of their sincere admiration of her work. The bow she is holding was a gift from old Indian students of the school. It is unstrung. That is the Indian's way of denoting peace. The turkey feather on the end of the arrow means friendship, morality and brotherly love. This bow has been placed in the archives of the Association as a sacred relic.

records.title: Chapter I — Off Campus Living: A Famous Debate
records.text:
Chapter I
Off Campus Living

A FAMOUS DEBATE

On April 18, 1890, a debate was held between the Savoy and Whitewright schools on the subject of "Resolved that the negro should be removed to Africa, in peace if we can, by force if we must." Speakers on the affirmative side representing the Savoy school were J. B. Thompson of Marysville, Texas, and James C. Wells of Bells, Texas. On the negative side, representing the Whitewright school, were E. N. Williamson of Shreveport, La., and G. W. Truett of Haynesville, N. C. This G. W. Truett is the present Dr. George W. Truett, pastor of the First Baptist Church at Dallas and world-wide eminent church statesman. When the old program of the debate in question was shown to him he acknowledged same in these words:

"Promptly replying, I beg to thank you most cordially for the distinct courtesy you have done me in sending me a copy of the old program of the debate between the two schools at Savoy and Whitewright, April 18, 1890. The sight of the old program that you sent me awakens the most vivid recollections of that very interesting occasion, when the debate was had. I recall that a big train load of people came over from the Savoy school to Whitewright, where the debate was had. I recall, too, that a member of the faculty was the one who took up the discussion on the other side, and we were all closer friends than ever because of the occasion.

"Yes, I remember quite well the fine and far-reaching influence of the College at Savoy, under the presidency of Robert R. Halsell. There is literally no computation of the far-reaching good done by such schools as the ones at Savoy and Whitewright a generation and more ago. Out land will always be deeply indebted to such teachers as those schools had."

records.title: Squintum Dramatic Club
records.text:
SQUINTUM DRAMATIC CLUB

Following the destruction of the buildings in 1890, funds were raised and new buildings were erected in 1891, at which time the school changed from a privately owned to an Independent School, Professor Halsell and some of his former teachers continuing with the new school for a brief period.

In 1891 a group of students and public spirited citizens formed an amateur organization, named themselves the "Squintum Dramatic Club," and gave a number of plays for the purpose of raising funds for the purchase of a new bell for the school. Harry Naylor (now deceased) and Robert Naylor, brothers, residing at Collinsville, were prime movers in the organization of this club. The bell was purchased and presented to the school that year, and is now given an honored place in the present building, which is a successor to the one built in 1891.

The club was organized at the home of Mr. and Mrs. J. E. Squires on November 13, 1890, with thirteen members. Officers then elected were Eldridge K. Norsworthy, chairman; Pinkney E. Durrett, treasurer; Gus W. Thomasson, secretary. A committee on plays and parts was appointed, consisting of Robert F. Naylor, Claude C. Hodge, Miss Jennie Lacy and Miss Stella Anderson. The object of the club was stated as being "to organize for the purpose of giving an entertainment in the interest of raising funds to purchase a bell for the new college, now in course of construction." The old Savoy Hotel was selected as headquarters of the club. Later, the meeting place was changed to the "new school house." Allie G. Hughes and Gus W. Thomasson were appointed chief janitors.

At a meeting held on November 20 a play was selected titled, "Out in the Streets," and another titled "Joke on Squintum," with a tableau, "Woman's Rights." Thus, began the activities of the club. Early in the program, Mrs. J. E. Squires was delegated the authority to assign play parts. Will H. Davis was selected as curtain manager with Ed A. McMahon as his assistant.

records.title: Squintum Dramatic Club (continued) — The Bell and Membership Roll
records.text:
The first public appearance was on December 22, 1890. Receipts were $7.00. The program was repeated the next night by request. The receipts then were $12.50. The proceeds "so empty lunches"[?] was entered as the official record in the minutes.

On January 15, 1891 an order was placed for a "200 pound bell." This was received on February 10 and presented to the school authorities on February 13, 1891. The presentation was made by Pinkney E. Durrett, treasurer, in the absence of Eldridge K. Norsworthy, manager. The inscription on the bell read:

1891
Presented to Savoy College
By The Squintum Club
E. K. Norsworthy, M'g'r.
Gus W. Thomasson, Sec.
Pinkney E. Durrett, Treas.

While the number of active members was limited to the needs of individual plays, and never exceeded twenty at any one time, the enrollment was much larger, due to the ever changing conditions of a voluntary organization. The following is a transcript of the roll of membership covering the entire period of the life of the club:

Davis, W. F. Dodd, Miss Pinkney E. Durrett[?], Little Miss Susie Durrett, Thomas C. Frank, J. L. Hicks, Claude C. Hodge, Miss Bell Huddleston, Will H. Hughes, Allie G. records.title: APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
topics: S. H. N. & T. Telegraph Company
records.text:
8        APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY

On March 8, 1891, the office of manager having become vacant by the removal from the city of Eldridge K. Norworthy, the club selected Robert F. Naylor as manager, and Henry Naylor as critic.

"East Lynne" was then chosen as a play to be given. Other plays selected were "The Assessor" and "The Sham Doctor". These were given in a public performance on May 14, 1891, with the purpose of "raising funds with which to purchase a bell for Savoy College." Tickets were 35 cents; general admission 25 cents, reserved seats 50 cents. Receipts were $26.75. Some of the plays were repeated the next night, at which time receipts were $18.50.

This appears to have been the last performance of the club and as its objectives—a bell and a belfry—had been achieved, its members met on May 25, 1891, and reluctantly disbanded.

S. H. N. & T. TELEGRAPH COMPANY

While not an activity of Savoy College itself, the formation, in 1888, of a telegraph company, organized by a large group of students of the school, linked its operations closely with the activities of the college. About twenty ambitious young men and women became students of the Morse system and gained proficiency therein, looking to telegraphy as a profession and means of livelihood with marked success. The group constructed a line from Savoy to Potts, meandering en route to touch the stations of its members, and ultimately extended the line an approximate of nine miles. The promoters were W. Tom Sprewls, L. W. (Tobe) Hughes, Eldridge K. Norworthy, Tom Sadusk[?], who was one of the first to drop out of the organization; then his successors were Tom C. Frank, general superintendent; E. K. Norworthy, superintendent division one (Tom); E. K. Rubitski, superintendent division two (Bobs); Miss Ursula Sprewls, commercial department among students of which: Lula Sprewls, William F. Holland, A. P. (Tony) Conway, Charles M. Sadusk, Virgil E. Conway and Miss Bettie Sprewls.

records.title: Chapter II: A Tribute
records.text:
Chapter II

A Tribute

To Robert Rebecca Halsell, President of Savoy College 1880-1888, who never turned away a boy or girl, no matter how poor, who wanted an education.
(Published in the Savoy Rustler, December, 1948.)

As I stood upon the platform at the recent reunion of Ex-Students of Savoy College and gazed upon a sea of faces, my memory slipped back quickly over the years—many, many years—and I saw distinctly in the background another scene, which time has failed to dim for me.

Time—the old bell had just summoned the happy student body for the opening exercises, and a host of young men, young women, boys and girls, with eager eyes and listening ears, were facing the faculty on the platform. A chorus of "Good Morning" was rendered; a scripture reading was offered, after which Robert Rebecca Halsell, president and spark plug of this educational institution, stepped forward and began in his own inimitable way—

"Young ladies and young gentlemen, we are face to face with another week of hard work and progress, and Savoy College expects every one to do his duty."

Our hearts were strangely warmed and our enthusiasm began to bristle. Then he told us in effect, to take a strong rope, tie one end to our wagon, hitch the other to a star, and—

Climb!
Climb!

The occasion was typical. Often at such times he would take up a famous painting or a model, and with a few extra touches, mold it into a model that any boy could admire; he glad to emulate. Sometimes he would take some famous genius of the past and with the deft touch of a master, convert it into rarified[?] spiritual beauty. Then again, with Tennyson, he

records.title: APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
records.text:
10        APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY

"Dip into the future, far as human eye could see,
See the vision of the noonday and the wonders that would be."

His talks, while always impromptu, were not only inspirational and uplifting, but were also models of brevity and gems of diction. He was adept at putting his ideas in a few words of crystal clarity, then driving them home with the warm enthusiasm of a true teacher. He could turn enthusiasm, energy and determination into a bunch of boys and girls and get results that few other men could get; and no man living could so fully reproduce in words, gesture and telling effect, just one of those Halsell gems.

But alas! That master builder is with us no more. He has quit the walks of men. He fought a good fight. He kept the faith; he finished his course, and through the years he helped to shape the lives of hundreds of his pupils for the good of all mankind. Knowing him as I did, and admiring him as only a broadly educated man can admire an intellect and a character like his, the day of his departure came; when his frail body, worn out by ceaseless toil in the cause of humanity, was no longer able to function, his restless spirit, instead of "tying to its star" and climbing to meet the dawn, pulled loose from this side of the river of the Stygian river, stepped unhesitatingly into the waiting boat, and was "ferried across" no screen." And on reaching the far side he turned and stood on shore, and seemed to be gazing toward those whom he was leaving behind—his ex-course, his ex-students.

Listen! Even now I seem to hear him calling to us across the rolling tide: "When I was with you at Savoy I told you to look up and not down—to tie your wagon to a star—and to climb, climb. It is time to lay aside every weight which so easily besets you and press on with boldness. Keep on looking up; but no longer ad astra—let your gaze go beyond the stars—ad lucem, out into the full light; because—for the weary traveler and the

L. J. Reynolds,
Class of '87.

records.title: Chapter III: Reunion Meetings
records.text:
Chapter III

Reunion Meetings

A narrative account of the first (August 6 and 7, 1938) reunion is given in Part I. At that meeting a plan of organization was adopted. Since then, reunions have been held, annually, always at Savoy, the seat of the old school. It is an announced policy of the Association to continue these reunions as long as interest will justify and there is a sufficient number to attend. Some have said that the reunions should be held as long as there remain as many as two of the old students physically and mentally able to attend. This will probably be done.

1939

The second reunion was held at Savoy, Sunday, August 6, 1939, with President Edgar Anderson McMahon presiding, and Mrs. Martha Buford May as secretary.

John Marcus Gist, of Sherman, conducted the opening services, in representation of a typical Monday morning chapel service of old Savoy College; a brief tribute to Harvey Johnson of Breckenridge, and an inspirational talk, of the type customarily given by President Halsell, was given by Bob Martin of Savoy.

Greetings on behalf of Choctaw Indian ex-students were extended by Bill Johnson of Durant, Oklahoma, and again tribute was paid to the memory of Professor Halsell and the old school.

Honorable J. R. May, Mayor of Savoy, delivered an impressive address of welcome on behalf of the citizenship, in which a tribute was again paid the old school and its founders.

Ninety-five members responded to roll call and to each was presented on the program booklet a thumbnail sketch of the history and activities of the old college.

Honorable Sam Rayburn of Bonham, member of Congress and then the Majority Leader of the House of Representa-

[ 11 ]

records.title: APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
records.text:
12        APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY

tives (now, 1942, Speaker of the House), was presented by Gus W. Thomassen and delivered the principal address of the occasion, using as a subject "The Youth of Today."

Bill Gardner presented the symbol of the old, new and eternal law: an olive branch—symbol of peace according to the law, its omission meaning "peace, no war, between you and me"; the turkey feather on the end of the arrow meaning "friendship, morality and brotherly love," he said. The gift was accepted by President McMahon and ordered deposited in a place of safe keeping as a sacred relic.

Martha Buford May read an original poem, titled, "The Second Reunion."

Lee A. Clark submitted a report from the Board of Managers covering draft of a Constitution and By-Laws, based upon a tentative set drafted in 1938, with additional regulations for the guidance of the Association. The report of the Board was adopted.

President McMahon delivered the following address:

"Your president has served for this first year in office. Before the president relates what went on he had the good fortune to be privileged to work with, and to the assistant of a great statesman and patriot. Your association is to be congratulated for having one who has and is yet serving the U. S. Government with skill and faithfulness, as its president.

"The life of this organization began in fact two years ago, and it will be a pleasure to report some of the activities of the first year of our life as it is to be hoped that with the ending of the launching year ends all period of doubt and uncertainty, and the Association swings into its mature stride.

"The provisions of the new Constitution and By-Laws have my hearty approval. They are good; they have been, first, advocated and, afterward, paid by every hours as were destroyed by others—whose constructive work on them justifies their present day drive.

"My official family has by hard work made a success of launching our Association, and I recommend that each of them be returned to office for the ensuing year.

"We are either all nearing the mark of these score

records.title: APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
records.text:
APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY        13

and ten years, or have passed it, and it is necessary to have a yearly turnover in the office of President, that the organization will grace the lives of as many of the faithful as possible.

"The officers presented this booklet to the author with thankful appreciation and humbleness of spirit." A high point of interest was created in a review of the history of Savoy Male and Female College by its author, Miss Mattie Lee Boyd, daughter of a graduate ex-student, Pamelia Paxton (Mrs. P. F.) Boyd, which was compiled, written and submitted as a master's thesis in education to the University of the State of Texas. In recognition of her meritorious services the dedication of honorary membership in the Association was formally bestowed, and she was presented with No. 1 certificate of such membership in the Association.

Officers elected for the ensuing year were as follows: President, John Marcus Gist; vice-president, Edgar Anderson McMahon; secretary-treasurer, Martha Buford May; historian, Miss Mattie Lee Boyd; Board of Managers, Lee A. Clark, Lewis J. Reynolds and Guy P. Webb.

1940

The third reunion was held at Savoy, Sunday, June 16, 1940, with Vice-President Edgar Anderson McMahon presiding at the request of President John Marcus Gist, and Martha Buford May served as secretary.

The opening exercises consisted of "America," led by Mrs. Lewis J. Reynolds, of McKinney, with Mrs. Hugh L. A. Hamilton of Whitewright, as pianist, scripture reading by the Hon. B. Blaine Ragland, and a prayer by H. W. Alcorn of Dallas. An address of welcome was delivered by Honorable H. F. Bell, and a response made by John Marcus Gist of Sherman. A poem by the Association's Historian, Martha Buford May, titled "College Reunion Song" was sung. A roll call was then taken. Greetings were given by Mrs. W. H.1 Davis in her own inimical manner. A trust was given the audience by Bob Martin and Miss Sprewls, by reading a well memorized poem, titled "Briar Rose," which

records.title: APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
people: Eldridge Lee Lindsey (Mrs. S. H.) Montgomery
topics: God Be With You Till We Meet Again
records.text:
14        APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY

had been rendered by her grandmother, Lee Lindsey (Mrs. W. B.) DuJerrett, upon her own graduation many years previous. Happy memories of other days were brought to mind by the singing of "The Old, Old Story" by Mrs. Blanche Ragland, accompanied by her own daughter.

The principal address of the occasion was delivered by Lee A. Clark, in which he praised the students of his day and time in overcoming difficulties in their determination to secure an education. A recess period of two hours followed the morning session, in which lunch was served in picnic style in the Beautiful College Campus.

The afternoon session was opened with a sing-song led by Mrs. Lewis J. Reynolds. Eldridge Lee Lindsey (Mrs. S. H.) Montgomery paid a tribute to old students recently passing on. An amendment to the Association Constitution, offered by Gus W. Thomassen, was adopted, giving the Board of Managers the right to call a spring meeting in place of an annual meeting. President John Marcus Gist extended an invitation to come to Sherman if they failed to meet another year at Milford as his guests. The invitation was acknowledged with expressions of appreciation. It was the last opportunity we ever heard John Marcus Gist give to have at this juncture he was bid farewell by the audience in singing "God Be With You Till We Meet Again."

Lewis J. Reynolds and Edgar Anderson McMahon joined in paying tribute to Martha Buford May for rendering of her services as secretary-treasurer and as a willing and tireless worker in promoting the welfare of the Association. They proposed the creation of a post of honor, to be known as Past Laureate, and recommend Mrs. Buford May for it. A proposal was adopted by unanimous vote.

Telegrams were received from two, notied of their inability to be present from Mrs. Pamela Paxton Boyd and family of, and Mrs. Gus B. and Mrs. Harvey Johnson.

Officers selected for the ensuing year were as follows: President, Lee A. Clark; vice-president, Lee Lindsey (Mrs. Dr. W. B.) DuJerrett; active vice-president, Edgar Anderson McMahon; secretary-treasurer-post laureate, Martha Buford (Mrs. J. B.) May; historian-librarian, Pamelia Pax-

records.title: APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
records.text:
APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY        15

ton (Mrs. P. F.) Boyd; board of managers, Gus W. Thomassen, Guy P. Webb and Kate King (Mrs. S. H.) Montgomery.

1941

The fourth reunion was held at Savoy, Sunday, June 15, 1941. The meeting was called to order by President Lee A. Clark, who then turned the gavel over to Vice-President Edgar Anderson McMahon, with request to preside. Mrs. Martha Buford May served as secretary.

The principal address of the occasion was delivered by Harvey J. Davis of McKinney. There was a prayer for Savoy and the singing of a few songs with Miss Aileen McMahon at the piano. Honorable J. R. May, Jr., Mayor of Savoy, delivered an address of welcome, to which response was made by J. Bettis Brixey of Atoka, Oklahoma.

The principal address of the occasion was delivered by Major M. McMahon of Fort Worth (son of the president), which he closed by saying, "although there is much trouble in the world today, he still maintains his confidence in his country and faith in our fellow man."

The morning session closed with the singing of the College Reunion Song, and an intermission of two hours was had in which lunch and happy memories were shared in the shade of the old walnut trees.

Reports of committees were heard and acted upon in the afternoon session. The report of the Committee on Nominations was adopted without change, in which officers were elected as follows: President, Edgar Anderson McMahon; vice-presidents, John Marcus Gist, Lee A. Clark and Guy P. Webb; secretary-treasurer-post laureate, Mrs. Martha Buford May; historian-librarian, Mrs. Pamela Paxton Boyd; board of managers, J. B. DuJerrett, Gus W. Thomassen and Mrs. Beulah Thomassen Stinnett.

The secretary was instructed to send a message of condolence to Doctor and Mrs. W. B. DuJerrett because of the illness preventing their attendance; an invitation from the Sherman Chamber of Commerce to hold the next reunion in Sherman was received through Barlow Roberts, which was declined with thanks.

records.title: APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
records.text:
16        APPENDIX: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY

On motion of Gus W. Thomassen a fund was started with which to underwrite the cost of printing Miss Mattie Lee Boyd's Supplemental History of Savoy College. The motion prevailed that the book be printed as and when funds were available, and that, in the meantime, the Board of Managers take the matter under advisement, study the needs and take whatever action might be deemed advisable, being thus given full power and authority to act.

By request, Mrs. Guy P. Harris sang, "When You and I Were Young, Maggie." She, then, led the audience in singing, "Auld Lang Syne," whereupon, the meeting adjourned.

AD INTERIM REUNIONS AND BOARD MEETINGS

A number of meetings have been held by the Board of Managers during 1939-1943 inclusive, while in preparation of this book. Each member of the board has assumed a specific task in getting things done. Several joint meetings have been held by the Board with members of an Advisory Committee, a volunteer group of ex-students, living conveniently near each other, who have met on call for the purpose, in connection with plans for the book project. The first meeting was held with Mrs. James A. (Beulah Thomassen) Stinnett at her home in Van Alstyne, on December 28, 1941. Others met there at this first meeting, and several general plans were formulated. The second meeting was also in December (December 29, 1942) at Savoy, at the Edgar and Ed McMahon families acting jointly as hosts, at the former's home, when final plans for the printing of book were completed.

The small group meetings have been held each year since and have come to be called by those in attendance "little reunions," and, as such, have been enormously enjoyed. Ex-students' families and friends occasionally attend and by the former have been dubbed "insiders and outlaws," the former meaning kinship and the latter friendship.

records.title: Chapter IV: In Memoriam
records.text:
Chapter IV

In Memoriam

"Not by lamentations and mournful chants ought we to celebrate the funeral of a good man, but by hymns, for in ceasing to be numbered with mortals he enters upon a heritage of a diviner life."—Plutarch.

We here pay tribute to the memory of all those of whom we have a record, who have ceased their labors upon this earth since the organized activities of this association began and have passed on to their reward in another world.

They were our comrades in days agone when what would now seem minor difficulties in daily routine of life were real and troublesome problems, challenging one's resourcefulness, initiative and determination to succeed. They did not falter, nor admit defeat, nor weaken in the hour of trial, but relentlessly pressed onward, unafraid and unabashed, until, finally they reached their goal. Thus, they inspired and encouraged us. We now revere and honor their memory.

Poems

Post Laureate

—Courtesy The Cardinal, Savoy High School Annual.

MARTHA BUFORD MAY
Post Laureate

A tireless worker in the development of the student association. She has served not only as secretary-treasurer but has filled numerous places of an emergency nature, in making the annual reunions pleasant and successful. She is a gifted product of the old school, as evidenced by her ability to produce from time to time a poem, a song or other literary contribution of high merit. In recognition of this talent she was elected (1940) as poet laureate of the association.

records.title: ADDENDA: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
records.text:
ADDENDA: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY        23

WELCOME HOME
(1939 Reunion)

Welcome back to the old home town,
    Though changed in many ways,
Yet there are still reminders of
    Your young and happy days.
The old school house has long been gone,
    Consumed by roaring flames;
A dwelling on the campus stands
    Where once you played your games.
A more commodious structure built
    Of brick and mortar stands
Within the western boundaries
    Upon much higher lands.
It is there that you are welcome
    To meet your friends so dear,
To walk again down memory's lane
    With pals of yesteryear.
To live again those days of yore,
    When teachers sternly said,
"Those lessons must be well prepared
    Before you go to bed."

—Martha Buford May.

records.title: ADDENDA: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY
records.text:
24        ADDENDA: A SUPPLEMENTAL HISTORY

AMARANTHINE

Did ever an artist, ancient or modern,
    Presume he could blot from the sky
The live, golden tints of an evening sunset?
    Most surely, he never would try.

The firm rock of ages can never be moved
    So long as the earth makes its round,
While deep in the hearts of all music lovers
    Will songs of Stephen Foster be found.

Years have passed swiftly, and removed from our ranks
    Of action, some men great of mind,
Yet, torches they lighted as they passed along,
    Leave a permanent path behind.

We speak of Halsell and Holland and Harshaw,
    And others who added their bit
To the wisdom of these outstanding teachers,
    Whose names in gold letters are writ.

Monuments left to the world at their passing,
    Were not cut from marble, or stone,
But chiseled from minds of brave lads and lassies,
    Through whom their reflection has shone.

The spark of ambition, early ignited
    By masters of wisdom and truth,
Has led ever on to a glad fruition,
    For many a strong-minded youth.

Then, none will presume that the ages of Time
    Can erase from sands on the shore,
The footprints Savoy College students have made—
    They're there, and will be, evermore.

—Martha Buford May.

records.title: The Old Bell (poem)
records.text:
THE OLD BELL

Only a piece of brass, you say,
    A common thing, that's all,
But yet the fondest memories
    Its singing tones recall.

To those whose minds revert again
    To days of long ago,
When some as happy hours were spent
    As they will ever know.

For pleasure they had parties, gay,
    And buggy rides, a few,
All day picnics on river Red,—
    They fought mosquitoes, too.

They didn't have the picture shows,
    Big cars, electric lights,
But youths today cannot eclipse
    Their joys on moonlight nights.

Then, too, the Squintim Dramatic Club
    Was born and did right well,
It raised the money that was used
    To purchase this brass bell.

Some members of the Club are here
    With grandchildren today,
But are they old? No, not in heart,
    They still are young and gay.

—Martha Buford May.

records.title: The Mocking Bird (poem)
records.text:
THE MOCKING BIRD

A fancied conversation between Professor R. R. Halsell and a mockingbird, a poem contributed from the pen of Guy F. Webb, in memory of the old school.

[The poem is set in two columns. It imagines a dialogue between Professor Halsell and a mockingbird recalling the old Savoy College days. Portions are difficult to read at this scan resolution.]

"In what subtle realm, sweet bird,
    Learned thou thy mocking song?
What pranking sprite within thee stirred,
    The neighbors thus to wrong?

"Was there no joy that ought
    For thee less fortunate?
No lesson, good, with kindess fraught,
    To me wouldst[?] thou relate?"

"All other birds, each has one song,
    Which fills his cup to brim,
'Tis thou, of all the merry throng,
    And soul his song from him.

"And, sat content to sing thine own,
    And have to each his gem,
In sweeter notes than they had known,
    Tho' sing their songs to them.

"Can it be true that in the realm
    Where music gave thee voice,
My ear[?] of weak, did overwhelm,
    O'er th' weak, the strong rejoice?

"Or wast thou sent, a master apt,
    To teach the feathered host;
And hadst thy songs from them fore-
    hapt[?],
    Nor one a song could boast?

"And are we wrong when we con-
    demn,
    And call thee, 'Mocking Bird'?
And dost thou teach their songs to
    them,
    Thy songs alone are heard?"

The bird replied: "I am surprised
    That you should so esteem;
And that a voice from out the skies
    Should mean no more to you.

"'Tis with us mocking mind I sing,
    A fashion making host;
I sing thee modestly[?].

"Then, sir, you see, 'tis not with me
    A foolish mocking brawl;
With grief or cheer, I am sincere,
    I sympathize with all."

AN ITINERANT SUBSTITUTE TEACHER

Mr. E. A. DeWitt of Dallas wrote under date of July 22, 1941, interestingly of his recollections of the old school at Savoy and of Mr. Habell, as follows: "Two or three years ago, I noticed the story of a reunion of the ex-students of Savoy College. This called to mind a little incident: on my first trip through Texas, about November, 1885, I stopped at Savoy (you should have been, still, an exuberant, a publisher of text books). The morning I went up to the College building I learned that Mr. Pratchett, Principal, had gone away for the day and that teachers were needed. I told them that I would take the classes, a proposition that the teachers accepted. I taught about ten days, as I remember it. It was this experience which led me to say, jestingly, that I was once a professor in Savoy College. The only person I remember was a teacher named Pritchett. During my first year in Texas, I frequently helped out teachers as I did at Savoy."

records.title: CYCLONE ANNIVERSARY (poem)
records.text:
CYCLONE ANNIVERSARY

Time moves along with rapid pace
    On its incessant way,
Sixty full years have made their score
    Since that sad day in May.

It was the twenty-eighth of May—
    After the sunset's glow
Had faded from the golden west,
    The storm began to blow.

Few realized the danger great,
    Which in those dark clouds lay,
As no roaring, freakish cyclone
    Had ever passed this way.

'Twas only seconds till the town
    A pile of debris made,
Lives were snuffed out, some instantly,
    And houses low were laid.

From neighbor towns and cities
    Came food and clothing, too,
Also many willing workers
    Who knew just what to do.

Soon dead were buried, wounded ones
    Were rescued from its wake
And surrounded with such comforts
    As loving friends could make.

Eye witnesses are growing few,
    Soon they will all be gone,
But never will the memory die,
    It passes on and on.

                        M. May

records.title: Old Savoy College Founded in 1876
records.text:
HERMAN DAILY DEMOCRAT, SHERMAN, TEXAS

Old Savoy College Founded in 1876

Special to The Democrat

SAVOY, Texas. Savoy college was organized in 1876 by Prof. Robert H. Halsell. For four years the institution was conducted by its founder and owner as a local school for the children of families in the small towns and settlements of the region.

Then in 1880, when Prof. Halsell's reputation as a teacher of mathematics and English literature had spread all over North Texas, he decided to enlarge the scope of the bookkeeping and courses more suitable for boys' education were offered.

The institution was granted Jan. 22, 1880, to R. H. Halsell, Lewis Holland, T. J. Chenoweth, James Paxson, and J. L. German. The institution was called Savoy Male and Female college. The purpose for which the charter was founded was "to maintain and support an institution of learning for the education of males and females and to empower the faculty to confer the usual college degrees."

The college prospered and gained renown in North Texas and eventually throughout the South. It had the most exceptional library of any school in Texas at that time, with the exception of the State University at Austin.

LEWIS HOLLAND          ROBERT H. HALSELL

BELL OF OLD COLLEGE IN THIS SCHOOL BUILDING

"Though its glory lives on," one former student has written, "its active days came to a tragic end in the vacation days of 1896, the college building burned and only a heap of ashes and debris was left to greet the eyes of those who loved it so dearly."

After the fire, the college was not rebuilt. Only its influence, as expressed in the lives of its pupils, remains to speak of its service to Texas and the southwest.

Lewis Holland was co-laborer with Prof. Halsell when the college charter was granted. He taught Latin, French and higher mathematics for 10 or 12 years and resigned to enter other activities. He retired from Savoy about 1901 and has lived his life all his life.

After severing his connection with the college, Mr. Holland moved to Whitewright and later to San Antonio and Oklahoma. He inherited some wealth and died in 1914 at the age of 74. One son, Cecil Moore, of Holland, lives in San Antonio and a daughter, Mrs. McKinnon, is a resident of Sherman.

After the college burned, Prof. Halsell taught for a while in the Savoy school district. Then he went to Durant, Okla., where he taught there a few years. He died there in 1924 along with some of his family. Surviving him are two daughters, Mrs. Annie Woodward of Durant, and Mrs. Mollie Durant of Calera, Okla., and one son, Doak Halsell of Durant.

A handsome building was erected on the old site in the southeast part of town but a frame structure was built on the north side of Main Street of the town, which is now highway 69, when the present modern, commodious building (shown above) was erected on the same site.

That frame structure was replaced by a two-story brick, which in a few years was inadequate for the growing needs of the school community and the present modern, commodious building (shown above) was erected on the same site.

It is now being supplemented by a native rock athletic building that has been named Halsell gymnasium. Plans are being made to hold the reunion of ex-students of the old college when the memorial building is dedicated, which will likely be in the early spring.

records.title: Savoy Pioneers Celebrate Sixtieth Anniversary
records.text:
Savoy Pioneers Celebrate Sixtieth Anniversary

MRS. J. A. GLASS
Special to The Democrat

SAVOY, Texas.—Three Savoy pioneers will be at home to their friends June 5 when two of the group, Mr. and Mrs. Tom W. McSpadden, celebrate their sixtieth marriage anniversary. The third is Mrs. J. A. Glass of Savoy whose residence in this section has been as long as that of her brother and sister.

Mr. and Mrs. McSpadden were married June 5, 1872 in Texas. She was Miss Margaret Benton, born Nov. 22, 1850 in McMinn county, Tenn. She was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. F. Benton and was one of 10 children of a second marriage, there being four of the father's first marriage. Only two brothers and Mrs. McSpadden are living of the 14 children now.

TOM W. McSPADDEN

After their marriage, Mr. and Mrs. McSpadden lived on the Captain William Thompson farm a few years and then bought a farm just north of Savoy, which they still own. They saw the wild turkey and deer disappear with the longhorn cattle, and fertile fields develop from prairie. Six children came to their home. Four of them who are living are Sam McSpadden, Dallas, Mrs. Minnie Hodges, Mrs. Mamie Pritchett, Savoy and Will McSpadden, Denison.

The children return home often for a reunion. The home has modern conveniences, with a radio to add to the comfort. Both old people are active, though Mrs. McSpadden is a sufferer from rheumatism. Mr.

MRS. TOM W. McSPADDEN

McSpadden, however, has never in his life had a serious illness, is straight as an arrow and works every day. They are both members of the Methodist church.

Mr. McSpadden has one brother and three sisters living. One of the latter is Mrs. Glass, widow of the late Rev. J. A. Glass, Baptist minister. Mr. McSpadden is a native of Monroe county, Tenn. and was born Sept. 22, 1849, one of a family of eleven children. At the age of 21 he set out in the world for himself, came to Texas and settled where Savoy now is. At that time only three small shacks could be seen on the prairies. He began, like Abraham Lincoln, splitting rails and in a few months started farming, which was his life work.

records.title: Ex-Students Of Erstwhile Savoy College Plan Reunion June 9-10
records.text:
IN MEMORY OF A TEACHER

Ex-Students Of Erstwhile Savoy College Plan Reunion June 9-10

By Elizabeth Large

SAVOY — The 14th annual Savoy College reunion is scheduled for Savoy June 9 and 10 among members of the college, which came to fiery death during the summer of 1890, and still living and no more than 50 of the school's survivors are expected here for the reunion.

The reunion, started in 1937 with Savoy's J. May and Prof. Ed A. McMahon as ringleaders, is the result of the desire of former students to bind a closer relationship with old school ties.

The college was founded in 1876 by Professor Robert R. Halsell. During its first four years it was conducted by Prof. Halsell as a school for the children in Savoy and neighboring settlements.

However, in 1880 Prof. Halsell's reputation as a teacher of English literature and mathematics had spread over all of North Texas and he was able to enlarge his facilities.

As a result, on Jan. 22, 1880, a charter was granted to R. H. Halsell, Lewis Holland, J. T. Chenoweth, James Glasscock and Gus L. German to operate the Savoy Male and Female College.

The charter read that the purpose of the school was "to maintain and support an institution of learning for the education of males and females and to empower the faculty to confer the degrees of bachelor of arts, grant diplomas, certificates of proficiency and awards of merit."

From the first, the college prospered.

EXCELLENT LIBRARY

"Not only the people of Savoy and surrounding country enjoyed the services of its excellent teachers," wrote an early day historian, "but people came from far and wide over Texas and Indian Territory to seek knowledge within its walls. It has the complete first library of any school in Texas except the state university at Austin."

Many of the early day Savoy College students were larger boys and girls. Since there was no dormitories, students—and the Indians included—boarded with farm families in the town.

The private school concept lived prominently between the school's founders themselves usually lacked the foresight in administering schools. Being a new state, many locations were selected unwisely having the institution to a central location and in many cases several schools were located in the same town at the same time. In effect, many of the schools were inadequately endowed and public funds were too meager and in many instances the lack of dormitories was creating overcrowded classrooms and forcing many children back home to help with chores when they were needed.

COULDN'T START ANEW

At the insistence of the citizens of Savoy, in 1892 he returned with L. C. Gee, who later went to Wesley College, in an attempt to reopen the school. For two years classes were held in the schoolhouse manner, but efforts to raise funds to rebuild the college failed.

After the end of that time, Prof. Halsell went to Anson and taught two years and then spent years in Noble, Okla., before going to Durant.

For several years he taught at the public schools in Durant. He served in the state legislature of Oklahoma from 1912 to 1914 and later was appointed by Gov. J. B. A. Robertson as inspector of institutions for a four-year term.

He retired after this because of ill health and died as the result of a heart attack in 1924.

Prof. Halsell left in Savoy a school tie that exists in few schools today. It was memory of the aim as much as of old Savoy College that prompted the organization of the Savoy College Ex-Students in 1937.

Mrs. Jessie Gorrell Young recalled her last talk with the professor. She said he was despondent over the death of the college and it was almost impossible to cheer him up.

"You have had power as a teacher," he shouted, pacing the floor and tossing back his shaggy locks with his hands. "Will you go further with me? I used to be able to put enough thought into my students in 10 minutes to last a month. Now, I can talk my head off and not strike a spark of enthusiasm in the entire school!"

PASSING OF AN ERA

Mrs. Young said she answered him that "you didn't used to talk this way to us. You boosted us and the school went on in high gear; on a forced march, 'there shall be no Alpe'."

"I know," replied the professor, "But I'll tell you what is the matter. It's this confounded sentimentalism in the pupils! Why little 12-year-old girls write love notes to the boys! Their minds are just not on their lessons."

The professors life went on from Savoy to even greater heights in the education field in Oklahoma. And the former students have been closer together by the monthly publication of "Savoy College Ex-Reunion News." This is a small publication financed by contributions from subscribers with Mrs. J. B. Young as editor and Gus Thomasson, Benton Maxey and Fred Reynolds as associate editors.

But like other organizations of a similar nature, where age and

death takes its toll, each year the Savoy College reunion will get smaller and smaller. But out of the 125 living ex-students of the college that burned 61 years ago, at least 50 are expected at Savoy next weekend.

Savoy Dumps Whitewright To Win Red River Valley Basketball Crown

BELLS—You can add the Red River Valley cage title to the growing list of titles won by Coach Weldon Nelson's District 45-B basketball champions from Savoy.

Last night on this neutral court the Cardinals ripped the terrific Tigers of Coach Glenn Howard of Whitewright by 36 to 28 to win the rubber game between the two clubs.

Whitewright had hammered out an eleven point triumph on its home court only to lose by nine points in a return game at Savoy.

The Whitewright Tigers went on to win [?] 27-B district crown and subsequent playoff and will head for Dallas Thursday for the regional tourney. Savoy departs Thursday for Kilgore where the Cards meet Quitman at 3:15 p.m. in the opening game of the regional session.

Savoy jumped to a 17 to 13 half-time lead and then turned on the steam during the third period to pull out in front by 15 points at one time. They wound up coasting home winner by 36 to 28.

Scoring was evenly divided between the Savoy cagers with A. J. Flanagan high with ten points while [?] Lew[?], [?] [?] [?], Denise Beckham each having nine and Pete Newell cashing in with eight.

However, high honors for the evening went to the Tigers' Herman Musser who pitched home 11 points.

records.title: Former Savoy College Students Ready For 14th Annual Reunion
records.text:
Former Savoy College Students Ready For 14th Annual Reunion

(Herald News Service)

SAVOY—Sixty-five of the 131 survivors who attended Savoy College have indicated they plan to attend the 14th annual reunion set for Savoy Sunday, according to Ed A. McMahon of Dallas president of the Savoy College Ex-Student Association.

The vanguard of this group, however, will move into Savoy shortly after lunch Saturday for an informal program that will start at 3 p.m. This is strictly just an old-fashion "chinfest" by former students who have been getting together once a year since 1938 when they organized the association.

Savoy College was chartered in 1880 and had become one of the leading colleges in this area when it burned July 3, 1890. Attempts to revive it failed.

The headquarters for the reunion is the Halsell Memorial Gymnasium, the school building that was named after the founder of the college.

Officers, in addition to President McMahon, include vice presidents John Umphress, H. L. Davis, Benton Maxey, Thomas E. Crabb, and Tom H. Smith; Jessie Gorrell Young, secretary-treasurer; Pamela Paxton Boyd, historian-librarian; and Gus W. Thomasson, Beulah Thomasson Stinnett and Lillian Durrett King, board of managers.

During the past year, seven committees have functioned in keeping the organization intact. Lloyd Hunnicutt, Will H. Davis and O. O. Suddath composed the auditing committee; Mrs. Jessie Young, Gus Thomasson and Mrs. Lillie King put out the monthly news bulletins.

The resolutions committee included J. B. Maxcy, Mrs. W. H. Davis, Mrs. Lee Gregory and Tom Hickman. Mrs. W. F. Dodd, Mrs. L. S. Sivells, Mrs. J. R. Maxwell and John McClure made up the necrology committee.

Benton Roberts, Mrs. Dora Fowler, Mrs. S. H. Reed and Fred Harle operated as the nominations committee and prepared a slate of officers that will be voted on Sunday.

Music for the reunion was arranged by Mrs. Claude Hodge, Mrs. L. J. Reynolds, Mrs. W. P. Carter, Mrs. J. F. Lawrence, Mrs. B. F. Matthews and Fred Hare. The constitution and by-laws committee was made up of Judge J. B. Maxcy, Mrs. W. L. Whedbee, Mrs. V. E. Conway, Mrs. W. F. Blanton, and Mrs. Charlton McCaughey.

records.title: Meeting Set At Savoy Tonight After Blaze Destroys Church
records.text:
FIRE THREATENED TOWN

Meeting Set At Savoy Tonight After Blaze Destroys Church

By ELIZABETH LARGE

SAVOY — A town meeting has been set for the school house at 7:30 p.m. today to start the ball rolling toward getting new fire fighting equipment for Savoy.

Mayor S. A. Bibby called the meeting after discussing the aftermath to the $15,000 fire that destroyed the Savoy Church of Christ Sunday morning.

The blaze, discovered by a passing motorist, at one time threatened the entire town and only the alert work of fire departments from three towns kept at least a half-dozen adjoining dwellings from being destroyed.

Fire trucks from Savoy, Bonham, Trenton, Bells and Sherman answered the alarm.

The fire was discovered about 10 a.m. by an unidentified motorist who went to the church and awakened teacher William Zilliam E. Hallagan, and told him the roof of the building was on fire.

Hallagan quickly passed the word to the Sunday school teacher and of the children's classrooms were speedily evacuated.

The older persons were told of the blaze and they helped get the young ones out, also alerting Hallagan. "There was no panic and no injuries," he stated.

Witnesses said the flames apparently were just waiting for the building to be cleared as the fire fell from the attic into the main auditorium just minutes after it had been emptied.

"It could have been a catastrophe," reported the mayor.

As the fire started spreading to adjoining dwellings the neighboring blocks arrived quickly at the scene. With little chance to save the church, they concentrated on keeping the fire, which was fanned by a stiff breeze, from spreading.

The roofs on the houses of Miss Elizabeth Large, Everett Burris, A. R. Hodges and others had been ignited by the sparks, firemen hosed the roofs and kept a spray of water on them.

Hay in a barn near the church caught on a garage across the street was on fire and minor damages. Dallas man, Mrs. Minnie Hodges, someone reportedly dug the basement with a few shovels at the scene when the fireman [?] arrived at the scene. Mrs. Frances was released with a bruised hand. "The people of Savoy are really aroused this time to the need of adequate fire protection," said S. A. Bibby, mayor, who pointed out to the citizens that it had been as high Sunday as it was a day earlier, out entire town could have been wiped out by the fire."

Some of the many faults that occurred were brought out at the meeting. One was the failure to check fire hydrants at intervals. Two wrenches were broken trying to get one hydrant open and firemen were never able to turn on another.

It was also pointed out that the Savoy water tank was no more than two-thirds full at the time of the fire.

The church building had been constructed in 1913 after a storm had blown the old one off its blocks. The original church had been built "sometime after" the Savoy cyclone in 1880. Before the cyclone the church had held its services just south of town in the old Roberts school house.

New furniture, most of which was installed a year or so ago, was lost. All that was saved from the fire was the communion table and service, two large floor fans, four pews, the pulpit stand and two chairs.

A total of $8,000 insurance was carried on the building and its contents, according to J. B. May, who said it probably would take $15,000 to $20,000 to replace it today.

"We will rebuild," said the minister this morning. "As soon as we can get organized we'll start rebuilding."

But meanwhile, all of Savoy was up in arms about the dire need for fire fighting equipment in town and at the town meeting tonight, it is a good bet that something will be done.

records.title: Aroused Savoy Forms Volunteer Fire Force At Mass Meeting
records.text:
Aroused Savoy Forms Volunteer Fire Force At Mass Meeting

By JOHN CLIFT
(Herald State Editor)

SAVOY, Tex. — Aroused citizens here formed a volunteer fire department in a mass meeting held at the school house Monday night, just a day after fire destroyed the Church of Christ here in a blaze that threatened the entire town.

Joe Houle, a Yankee GI who married a Savoy girl, was named fire chief after it was learned he had been a member of a New York fire department before coming here.

Glenn McKinney was named lieutenant and Holly Doan was appointed secretary.

A 7-man ways and means committee was appointed to come up with a means of financing the purchase of fire fighting equipment. Bibby was named chairman with Alton Winkler, Jim Malone, Thomas DeLerry, Dave Pritchett, Claud Strickland and W. E. Holagan as members. Holigan, incidentally, is pastor of the church that burned.

"The people of Savoy are really aroused this time to the need of adequate fire protection," said S. A. Bibby, mayor, who pointed out to the citizens that it had been as high Sunday as it was a day earlier, out entire town could have been wiped out by the fire.

Some of the many faults that occurred were brought out at the meeting. One was the failure to check fire hydrants at intervals. Two wrenches were broken trying to get one hydrant open and firemen were never able to turn on another.

It was also pointed out that the Savoy water tank was no more than two-thirds full at the time of the fire.

And city officials admitted they "hadn't gotten to it yet" when asked if the town's new 60,000 gallon storage tank had been connected.

Savoy actually has a total of 105,000 gallon storage capacity, al-though probably no more than 20,000 gallons was available Sunday morning. In addition to the 35,000 gallon main tank, it has a 10,000 gallon elevated tank and then the 60,000 gallon new tank.

Mayor Bibby said the 60,000 gallon tank will be used for "emergency storage," since the existing tanks were "adequate" when kept at a maximum level.

"We didn't do a good job Sunday, but if the fire had spread,

records.title: Savoy Church of Christ rebuilding plans; volunteer fire department formation
records.text:
we easily could have," he admitted.

There were 29 men who signed up as charter members of the truckless volunteer fire department. The goal is 50. A $5 membership fee per year was set up. And even as Savoy's citizens were doing something about future fires, the Church of Christ was making plans to rebuild.

The three-man board of elders, J. B. May, C. E. Corry[?] and Malcolm DeBerrry, completed their insurance settlement Monday and were told they would get $8,000 of the $8,000 carried on their building.

"We hope to start rebuilding immediately," said May. "It probably will take at least $18,000 to put up a similar building. However that undoubtedly would mean we would have to go into debt. We never have been in debt and I don't know whether we want to start now," May added.

May said it was possible that the church would see how much it could raise and then make plans to put up a building in that cost range.

With only about 39 families represented in its 100 membership, May said it would take approximately $400 per family to replace the building.

Meanwhile, services will be conducted in the Savoy high school auditorium until a new edifice is erected, the minister said.

"We met there Sunday night after the fire," the minister said, adding "and we have been given permission to hold midweek and Sunday services there."

Holligan[?], a graduate of Abilene Christian College, has been in Savoy for 16 months. He has been in the ministry for about three years. Married, he has three children.

Meanwhile, the ways and means committee had two suggested ways of raising funds for fire fighting equipment for Savoy to start with. A small bond issue was suggested and then the committee was asked to investigate the civil defense program that pays for 50 per cent of the cost so long as certain civil defense obligations are met.

And to get the volunteer firemen training started, the members will stage their first meeting Monday at Bonham when the Bonham volunteers will give them their first drill.

Savoy was supposed to have sent representatives to Monday night's meeting, but a huge blaze on the square kept the Bonham firemen at home.

Mrs. Davis got the tea and coffee going. The drinks and dressings from Kraft, the milk from Borden's and the margarine from Blue Bonnet. Five bread companies—Mrs. Baird's, Pinneys, Holsom, Wonder and Rainbo—contributed the bread. D. Peplar Bargs and Mission orange were furnished free, too.

The Bells Methodist Church and the Marvin Methodists north of Bonham to augment the hundreds of large coffee urns. Dishes came from the Bells school to augment the donation table and service, two large floor fans, four pews, the pulpit stand and two chairs.

Glenn McKinney and Thomas Strickland smoked 800 pounds of boned beef on to barbecue at 7 p.m. Thursday and 22 hours later, cooked it to flavor, not necessarily on wood, the first serving was dished out to Elmore Proctor of Savoy.

A steady stream of people from all neighboring towns poured into Savoy from 3 to 11 p.m. to peer over a wash tub saying "let's do-nate" to the fire truck fund. The sign "buy a fire truck" brought smiles to the faces of well-fed citizens and visitors from their pocketbooks.

General chairman Claude Strickland said the tub added "at least $900" to the total.

There were 600 tickets sold in advance and another 200 bought at the door. That total plus the tub money brought in a little more than $2,700. Total expenses were only $120, with Strickland confident that the "final figure will show a net profit of $2,700."

"That puts about $1,300 into our fire truck fund," he said, since the truck itself would cost $4,000. We're confident of getting the truck—maybe it's fish frys, chili suppers and things of that nature held. We're going to get our fire truck. We'll get it without a bond issue."

Bakers of the Friday night feed had only praise for all who helped. But with $2,700 still needed, they were planning their organizational move next move to congratulate themselves on the success of their initial venture.

records.title: Denison Herald correspondent Miss Elizabeth Large reports on Savoy Church of Christ fire
records.text:
What happens when your house catches on fire? The Denison Herald found out first hand from its Savoy correspondent, Miss Elizabeth Large, last week when blazing embers from the burning Church of Christ showered down on her home. "I might have been less excited if my house hadn't of caught fire," Miss Large told us. "But when the shingles on the roof caught, all I could think of was getting them out." Miss Large said it was one time when she wished ferverently for the old style telephone. "I couldn't dial a number to save my life," she said. Anyway you or Miss Large look at it, it was a hot time in old Savoy last Sunday.

Incidentally, Miss Large's report of the fire Monday morning was a good example of reporting. She had all details wrapped up nicely. She told us later how the Ector fire truck reached Savoy. One of the Witherspoon brothers saw the Bonham fire truck speed west on U. S. 82 and looked in the direction it was taking and saw the smoke and flames from the fire. So, he got into the fire truck, rang the bell and by the time he had the truck backed out, had a pretty sizeable crew of volunteers on hand. We also learned that the alert Ector volunteers saw the smoke and flames from the Bonham fire later in the week and showed up over there to help keep the damage down. That's real fine community work. The Ector volunteers deserve a round of thanks for that kind of cooperation.

records.title: California Gold Rush Nuggets Paid For Town Site Of Savoy
records.text:
BY COLONEL SAVOY, SUH!

California Gold Rush Nuggets Paid For Town Site Of Savoy

(Herald News Service)

SAVOY — There probably were few more early day colorful characters than one Col. William Louis Marshall Savoy, who founded the town of Savoy, paying for it with gold nuggets he dug up during the 1849 California gold rush.

What brought a world traveler, distinguished frontiersman, perhaps one of the finest horsemen or counterspys in American history, has never been recorded. And those who might have had the answer are long since dead.

Col. Savoy was born Aug. 2, 1817 in Mississippi and he died Sept. 1, 1887 in Johnson County, Tex.

He came to Fannin County in 1870 after he had "been everywhere and done everything." He bought the land that ultimately became the site for James William Smith, who according to legend, was about to lose it. He paid for it with gold nuggets he had dug out of the earth in California in 1849.

RAILROAD CONTRACT

In 1872, Col. Savoy made a contract with the Transcontinental Railroad, the forerunner of the Texas & Pacific, to give them 40 acres of land in the center of his holdings, provided they would take the initative in building a town. The deed was formally entered Oct. 29, 1873 in Bonham.

On April 15, 1873 the charter for the town of Savoy was granted and lots sold for from $150 to $500, proving to be another gold mine for the intrepid Col. Savoy.

Where Col. Savoy got his rank isn't known. He enlisted in the Confederate Army in the Civil War, but received a foot injury and never saw active service.

Col. Savoy made the trek to California by water when word of the gold rush swept the nation and he was one of the more fortunate miners. He brought his gold back in heavy cotton bags, twice being robbed en route to his native Mississippi, the first time by Indians and the second time by Mexi-cans. But they missed most of the colonel's "cotton-s a c k gold."

INTERNATIONAL SPY?

After the colonel's civil war injury, he started on his international travels that saw him twice cross the Atlantic and three times the Pacific, doing, according to a daughter of the colonel's much later, secret work for the United States.

On one of his trips a storm hit the ship and damaged the sails to the extent that it drifted three months before it was repaired and the voyage continued. On another of his voyages, all of the crew and passengers were stricken with cholera while in port and he was the lone survivor.

MEET AGAIN

Four years after he came to Fannin County, Col. Savoy, then a widower, married Mrs. Julia Duncan, a widow with three children. Out of five children, only two of the colonel's were alive at the time.

The couple came to Denison on their honeymoon and upon their arrival, were greeted by a brass band and taken to their new home.

In his later years, the colonel traveled extensively by train throughout the same country he pioneered in wagon trains in gold rush days. In 1884 on a train trip through West Texas, a shaggy old Indian across from Col. Savoy, pointed out the window and recalled heading a raiding party that robbed a wagon train there. The colonel looked the old weatherbeaten savage over a long time, then told him "well my friend, we meet again! I am the man you robbed"

records.title: Anxious Moment As Water Falls — Savoy water tower topples
records.text:
Anxious Moment
As Water Falls

3-10-57[?]

SAVOY — A tiny tidal wave hit two Savoy families at dusk Thursday when a 50,000 gallon city water tower toppled. One of the steel legs supporting the tower got a bend in it Sunday when 60-mph winds raked the town, and the weakened support finally collapsed sending tons of water cascading down on the two nearby trailer home residences.

For Raymond Langford it was just another in a series of calamities that have befallen him. A little more than a year ago the service station he owns in Savoy burned to the ground. He had only partial insurance.

Three months ago his house burned and again it was only partially covered by insurance. He bought the trailer house and had it moved behind his rebuilt service station, which sits on the south side of U.S. 82 in the shadow of the water tower.

When the tower toppled, it washed his trailer 10 feet off its concrete block foundation, snapping water, sewer and power lines, ripping down his television antenna and just pulling the bottom out of the trailer. The interior of the trailer house was a shambles.

C. C. Waldrum, who lived just east of the toppled tower, got the brunt of the water.

"It sounded like a bomb explosion," said Waldrum. "The wall of water that gushed out of the huge tank hit my trailer house at window level. It smashed my pickup truck against the chain link fence that surrounded my property.

"One storage house where we kept most of our food and other materials was flattened. My brick walk around the yard was washed out. An air conditioner under the trailer was destroyed and a work shed has more than a foot of silt in it," Waldrum said.

Waldrum admitted he had been uneasy about the tower since the Sunday storm. "We had hail, sleet, rain and wind Sunday, and that old tower almost went then," he declared.

Claud Strickland, Savoy city secretary, said the tank was installed in 1952 and used primarily for storage. He said the city carried a $20,000 insurance policy against wind damage or fire on the tank.

"We put up a 100,000-gallon tank last year and coupled with another 33,000 gallon overhead storage tank, used the 50,000 gallon tower just as an emergency supply," Strickland said.

Strickland said the council meets a week from Tuesday. He said by then insurance adjusters will have had a chance to view the damage and the council will be in a position to know where they stand.

The collapsing tower shook houses all over town and quickly attracted a big crowd of spectators. Strickland said there was no interruption in the town's water service.

records.title: Shelves In Savoy Building Older Than Many Antiques On Sale
records.text:
Shelves In Savoy Building Older Than Many Antiques On Sale

SAVOY — The show cases that display a lot of the wares in Molly and Bridge's antique store here are older than many of the items on the shelves.

"This building was put up about 1900 and the shelves were built in," said E.L. Harden, a retired Amarillo school custodian who holds down the shop for his son, C.R., and J.C. Moore.

The antique store is the offspring of a collection started years ago by Moore. It finally overflowed his yard, located a half block south of the building he and the younger Harden rented, and the two men decided to open a store.

"They've been in business two years now," said the elder Harden. "My son is a truck driver and is on the road about three-four days a week. Moore is a housekeeper at Wilson N. Jones Hospital in Sherman."

"They've given me the authority to buy as well as sell, but I have to be pretty confident I can move an item before I'll buy it," he said.

Harden said the store has "a little of everything. There ought to be something here for everyone who comes in."

Rollop desks are all the rage these days. There's one tucked away in a corner in pretty fair shape. How about a tredle sewing machine? Remember the old GE refrigerators with the motor on top? Or a blacksmith forge and anvil hardly used.

Coke used to be better when it came in metal cases. There is a stack of those oldies handy. How about a 1921 crank model cash register? "Put a roll of tape in it and she's ready to go. That old register is as good as new," Harden said.

Harden reached high up on a shelf and pulled down an old kerosene lamp with a black onyx base.

"This lamp is more than 150 years old," and Harden said if you take the base screws off and you've got the bowl, wick and chimney left.

There was a large box about half full of assorted buttons. "I sell 'em a penny each," said Harden. "In the last two years I've sold more than $60 worth. Yeah," he said, "Some of them might have had a much higher value, but the buyer wasn't about to tell me about it."

Harden said he was glad he wasn't still on the school job. "Kids have changed too much for me," he said. "Their hair style, dress style and even their attitude is different. It isn't like it used to be."

Harden occupies a rocker in the front of one of the two buildings that houses the antiques and junk. He's right in front of the entrance door; The second building's outside door is kept locked and entry is gained through an adjoining door.

"The corner building originally was a drug store and the second building originally was a drug store 75 years ago," he said.

[Photograph caption:] 150-YEAR-OLD LAMP — Savoy Antique Dealer E. L. Harden holds up an old kerosene lamp he says is 150 years old. It has an onyx base that screws off.

records.title: Savoy Approves TP&L Rate Hike; Dr. Shaw Purchases Medical Clinic
records.text:
Savoy Approves TP&L Rate Hike;
Dr. Shaw Purchases Medical Clinic

By EULA PHILLIPS
Savoy Correspondent

SAVOY — A Texas Power and Light Co. rate hike and Dr. John Shaw's agreement to purchase the Savoy Medical Center were top items discussed in a City Council meeting this week.

Councilmen approved a 6.80 percent rate increase for TP&L, as recommended by the Public Utilities Commission in Austin. The increase is effective with the July billing.

H.F. Bomar, trustee for the Savoy Memorial Medical Center Association, appeared before the Council to explain the status of the clinic. Bomar gave the council a copy of the Articles of Association which are now on file at the City Hall.

The Association was founded in November, 1961, a board of trustees consisting of 10 persons were nominated, and only two of those members are still living. They are Harry F. Bomar and Holly Doan.

Bomar, who now lives in McKinney and Doan, who has retired from public work, chose to dissolve the Association as provided for under the Articles of Association.

The By-laws stipulate that after Dr. Shaw has paid a sufficient amount of rent to repay the cost of building the clinic, he was to be given the option to buy the building.

The second alternative in the event Dr. Shaw failed to exercise his option, was to give the building to the city and to divide any funds or monies the Association had on hand with the four churches of Savoy.

Dr. Shaw opened the clinic in July, 1961, and has been the only doctor here for 17 years.

Vernon Mullican, owner of the Mullican Nursing Home, appealed his sewer rates as being too high and asked for relief on his rates. He stated that his water and sewer bill costs $600 per month and he feels entitled to a lower rate. He was advised that the rate has been approved by the State, and the present rate structure is necessary to meet bond requirements, and at this time, no rate reduction can be put into effect.

The Council voted to nullify the action taken by the Board of Equalization which met April 17th, 1978. This action was taken because of the protest of citizens.

Status Of Savoy Medical Clinic Subject Of Study By City Dads

p[?]-7-8[?]

SAVOY — Who really owns the Savoy Medical Clinic?

This is a subject the city fathers pondered at length last night without arriving at any conclusion.

Councilmen Tommy Melugin and Billy Wrenn said they had tried to reach Harry Bomar, who was city bookkeeper at the time the clinic was built.

Melugin said there were no available city council minutes that showed how the clinic was to be operated. He said it was generally understood that Dr. John Shaw had the first chance at buying it.

Melugin said last September the medical board who owns the building, wanted to give the clinic to the city now that it has been paid out. However, it was understood that Dr. Shaw had 90 days to decide whether or not to personally buy it. He is paying $100 monthly rent.

No word has been heard from Dr. Shaw, and the 90 days has long since passed. It was indicated at last night's meeting that Bomar lived in McKinney and he was asked and he wrote and asked him to appear at last night's meeting.

"We wanted him to explain the status of the clinic, but he didn't show," Melugin said.

As a result, Melugin said he would write the secretary of state and try and get the articles of incorporation to find out the clinic's status.

records.title: Savoy Bus Overturns, 11 Students Injured
records.text:
Savoy Bus Overturns, 11 Students Injured

SAVOY — A Savoy school bus loaded with about 25 students overturned on a winding country road Thursday about 3 p.m. injuring 11 students and the driver. None were seriously hurt however, though one remained hospitalized today for observation.

The accident occurred on a loosely graveled road a mile and a half south of the Savoy school. Three or four students had been let off before the accident occurred.

The driver, Jack Morgan, scrambled out the driver's side window aiding students, while students in turn aided each other in getting out of the bus.

Jennifer Francis' hand was pinned between the top of the bus window and the ground. Morgan and a couple of students dug the dirt from around her hand to free it.

About that time Steve Reynolds, Bells, passed by on his motorcycle and drove on to a neighboring home to sound the alarm. Fannin County Deputies and Savoy Policeman Don Freeman hurried to the scene along with a wrecker.

Principal Richard Owmby said seven children were taken to the Fannin County hospital in Bonham, and four children were taken to the Medical Plaza Hospital in Sherman, along with the bus driver.

Owmby said only one student still was hospitalized. He was identified as Carl Bowhay, 16, a junior. He received a bruise above the kidney and is being held in the Fannin County hospital for observation.

Treated and released from Fannin County hospital were the following students:

Theo Dettmer, 6, head injury.
Lisa Harvey, 15, neck injury.
Heidi Bowhay, 12, bruise over jaw.
Jeff Francis, 11, bruises on body.
Sheri Melguin, 8, bump on head.
Gerry Dettmer, 12, bruises.

Treated and released from the Medical Plaza hospital were:

Keith Thomas, 7, bruise on leg.

Donna Francis, 8, broken tooth, one tooth knocked out, cuts.

Jennifer Francis, 9, bruises.

Denise Ballard, wrist and finger injured.

Jack Morgan, 70, driver of the bus, bruises and cuts.

Owmby said Morgan told him that two girls were standing up in the bus. When Morgan spotted them in his rearview mirror, he told them to sit down. In the few seconds it took Morgan to get the girls seated, the front wheels of the bus dipped over the right side of the humpback road.

Morgan told Owmby that as he attempted to make the curve in the narrow road, the rear wheels hit a bump and the next thing he knew the bus was on its side sliding down the hill. It slid about 200 feet before finally coming to a halt.

The mother of the Francis children was first at the scene. She took the four students to Sherman, including two of her own children, but missed her son, Jeff, who wound up at the Bonham hospital.

Morgan has been driving a Savoy school bus for the past 12 years. He is a retired truck driver.

The students not injured were taken home by either the deputies or other residents who came to the scene to give aid and check on the condition of students.

The bus is the newest owned by the system, purchased just six months ago. It was not heavily damaged though the windshield on the passenger side was cracked, along with a dent near the student steps.

As word of the accident spread, dozens of spectators from the area drove to the scene. The country road was covered with automobiles for about an hour.
