records.title: Savoy residents famous as new water system is completed
records.text:
THE BONHAM DAILY FAVORITE — Bonham, Texas — Friday, Feb. 27, 1987 — Page 6

Savoy residents famous as new water system is completed

By EULA PHILLIPS
Savoy Correspondent

SAVOY — The city of Savoy has long suffered the inconvenience of a water system in need of repair, and the lack of funds to conduct exploratory work. Much of the deterioration in the system was attributed to high water consumption that would surely result in a conservation order from the Texas Department of Health, absence of storage facilities and an inadequate water distribution system throughout the city.

In January 1987, the governing body, consisting of Mayor Arlester Jackson, City Secretary Khanell[?], and three council members, Claudia Jones set in motion a plan to secure a new water system for the people of Savoy.

The first requirement was to hire an engineering firm. Assistance in obtaining funding for the project from a community development fund was made available when the Engineering Company of Austin was retained. A resolution was passed to secure a loan from the Texas Water Development Board.

The next requirement was to hire a contractor. Three competitive bids were taken and the Texhoma Contractors of Lubbock was selected.

The report was completed and submitted to the city in August 1985. The next step was for the council to follow a direct program as required to meet the standards. The Texas Water Development Board approved the city's application as a priority project.

The full line was completed in September 1985.

Savoy's officials, including Mayor Jackson and city secretary, attended a public meeting held in May 1985 at the Texas Water Development Board offices in Austin, and were requested to submit a detailed financial needs assessment.

The Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) reduced the cost of the project because of the additional cost of the new meters. The TWDB noted that the total cost of the project was $358,000. The TWDB reduced the loan to allow for the $53,000 TDCA grant of $53,000, to be used for reducing the cost of the project, in September 1985.

The full loan was completed in September 1985.

Savoy's citizens, including 160 those that have bought the water, have also celebrated this with various civic and domestic commitments.

The old threat of the city's water was completely replaced including 16,000 feet of new water lines, and almost all 160 old connections have been replaced — two six-inch lines, one eight-inch line, three two-inch lines, and ten one-inch lines.

Water pressure on the far western end of the system was helped substantially. Well new water transmission lines — as well as new sewer lines — will be added to the water service. Also smaller water mains were replaced with larger ones. Water storage was enhanced. "All the water wasn't reaching the people," said Mayor Jackson. "We didn't have adequate pressure."

The old threat of the city's water system was gradually replaced including new meters.

A new mayor was elected, Brad Jackson, who succeeds Mayor Arlester Jackson, and three new council members were elected replacing Jimmy Deptord and Richell Upshaw. Upshaw had been assigned to water. Upshaw had resigned to run an unannounced race for the mayor's seat.

Mayor Jackson, who continues to serve as city secretary, also said the office staff has been reduced — there is no longer a full-time city secretary. She said the city would consult outside counsel as needed.

Old elected city administrators were being advised that it was a mistake to continue with water, and the board tried to interfere with the new system's plans.

The old council members of this growing community were eager to do the best for the growing needs of the school, and the city administrators, old and new, were doing their best in the early period of the project.

SAVOY — With 177 cheering employees in the background, top officials of Super Sack Inc. broke ground on a bright, sunny Wednesday afternoon for a major addition to the Savoy plant.

Once completed by the summer of 1989, Super Sack will start adding the first of another 100 employees.

"Right now we are one of the top three largest employers in Fa[nnin] County. By the time we co[mplete] this addition and another expansion planned in 1990, we easily should be the biggest single employer in the county," said Ced Derby, vice presi-dent of the firm.

Bob Williamson, president of the parent firm, B.A.G. Corp. of Dallas, said the 12 years Super Sack had been in operation in Savoy had been "good for the area and good for B.A.G."

Williamson said the new additions, to be added in three areas, will cover a total of 26,250 square feet to the Savoy plant. This will bring 74,750 square feet or 1.72 acres under one roof for the fast growing bag company.

In addition, in 1990 Super Sack is looking to an even larger expansion of 43,755 square feet just

See SUPER SACK, Page 2

Super Sack From Page 1

east of the present building that will firmly establish the Savoy industry as the major industrial plant in Fannin County.

Williamson said the enlargement of the test building, which Williamson described as "unique in the bag business," will permit faster, more comprehensive research into how customer products may be more economically handled.

The 6,000 square foot equipment building will free up another 6,000 square feet in the main plant that can be used in fabricating the Super Sack containers, Williamson said. This will give the main plant a total of 68,750 square feet of working space.

Williamson said the biggest of the three additions will be an 18,750 foot addition to the main plant. The north wall will be removed to provide an open space into the new area.

The corporation president said that when B.A.G. opened in 1969 "the bags that we made forever changed the material handling industry. Since then, millions of tons of dry flowable materials have been handled and shipped easily and at a much lower cost in Super Sack containers."

Even though B.A.G. has copyrighted the name "Super Sack" that name has become synonymous with large shipping sacks.

"I have been known to get phone calls from some of our competion complaining that they get calls from people wanting to order some 'super sacks'," Williamson smiled.

Williamson pitched out the first shovel of dirt and later was joined by Derby and Jean Williamson, secretary-treasurer. Other officials on hand included Plant Manager Dave Kellenberger, Super Sack Vice President Webb Cox, Savoy Mayor James Teems, Small Business Administration's Marvin McPherson, Greenville builder Jim Morris, and the 177 plant employees.

Thursday, February 21, 2002

Savoy councilman collapses, dies during Tuesday meeting

ASSOCIATED PRESS

SAVOY — A City Council member in Savoy collapsed and died during a meeting this week.

Councilman Harold Ballard collapsed at a meeting table on Tuesday night and was pronounced dead a short time later at Wilson N. Jones Medical Center, officials said.

A funding cut for the volunteer fire department was being discussed when Ballard slumped down in his chair, said firefighter R. L. Munger.

Another firefighter came forward and administered CPR.

Ballard was elected to the council last May and was a former high school science teacher.

City Hall was closed Wednesday and the flag was flown at half-staff.

Savoy, which has about 1,000 residents, is about 50 miles west of Paris in Fannin County.

records.title: Driver is injured when Savoy grass truck crashes
records.text:
Local News   January 26, 2005
Driver is injured when Savoy grass truck crashes

By Mary Jane Farmer
Herald Democrat

While going to a grass fire Wednesday afternoon, a Savoy grass truck crashed and it's driver was taken to a local hospital after being thrown through the window.

It happened about 4 p.m. on FM 1752, about a mile south of Savoy. Officials at the scene, including Savoy Mayor Clete Stogsdill and Assistant Fire Chief Michael Halford, said Travis Burks was driving the truck when it left the roadway on the left side, then crossed back over to the right.

His father is Savoy Fire Chief Billy Burks, who said he understands that the truck rolled at least three times. It ran through a barbed wire fence and, at some point, threw Burks out. The grass truck was completely destroyed.

Travis Burks went by private car to Texoma Medical Center. Chief Burks said his son is bruised and cut and required several stitches, but is basically all right and was released after being treated in the emergency room.

Chief Burks said that people in the Bells fire district will still be able to expect good service from the Bells FD, in spite of losing one of its two grass trucks.

Bells Fire Chief Tommy Carter stepped forward and said that Bells FD has an out-of-commission engine which Savoy can use until its fleet is again fully equipped and that other departments might step up with help, as they did last year when Van Alstyne FD fire engine was damaged in a wreck. Savoy FD has a mutual aid agreement with Bells FD and also relies on fire departments from other nearby towns, such as Whitewright.

A strap holding the water tank on the flatbed came undone, causing the grass truck to shift its load and become off-balanced.

"Half the load went off the truck," said Chief Burks.

The grass truck was completely destroyed, said Halford.

Savoy's second grass truck and Bells firefighters answered the original grass fire call, said Carter.

[Photograph caption:] Dan Bouge
Herald Democrat

A man photographs what's left of a Savoy Fire Department grass truck Wednesday evening after it rolled one mile south of Savoy on FM 1752.

records.title: Old Savoy church bell to be moved to school
records.text:
The Savoy Methodist Church, above left, now vacant, on Fowler street. Savoy ISD Superintendent Brian Neal, above right, sits on a pew in the old Methodist Church, property of the School District. The 1878 church bell, below left, as it looks today. Nancy Savoy with her late husband, John Savoy, below right, at a Victorian Ball in Phoenix.

Old Savoy church bell to be moved to school

BY VICKI GRAVES
BONHAM DEMOCRAT

SAVOY — The sound of the great, old church bell calling the Methodist congregation to worship won't leave Savoy. But the bell will be moved from the church to the school.

The relocation is being made possible by a heroine from Arizona, Savoy Independent School District Superintendent Brian Neal said Wednesday.

Nancy Savoy, wife of the late John Savoy — the last remaining grandson of Col. William Savoy who founded the town, recently gave $25,000 to Savoy ISD. With the money, Neal will remove and restore the bell and establish a $1,000 annual scholarship. Savoy ISD will sell the church building.

Col. Savoy donated the land for the 1878 church on Fowler Street. Long ago, the congregation blended with another church and the school district came into possession of the building. In the years that followed, the local opry played there, but the building gradually deteriorated, Neal said.

"It's the oldest building in Savoy, to my knowledge, and one of the only buildings that survived the 1878 tornado. It was a new building at the time and the city documents that it was used as a morgue. Over the years, the foundation sunk, and last year we closed it."

Neal said some of the Savoy family members returned and kind of discovered Savoy for themselves a few years ago, renewing ties to the community. At that time, local people made Nancy Savoy aware of the plight of the church. She wanted to buy and restore the whole building, but that was going to be really expensive," said Neal, "and even then, we don't have the money to maintain it. I don't have the money to pay the electric bill."

The school district is never going to be able to restore the church building, but Neal doesn't want to tear it down. He fears, however, that if he doesn't do something soon, he'll have to demolish it in five years. The building is in pretty good shape, but the foundation has rotted, he said, adding, "the Bois d' Arc is still there but the pecan timbers are gone."

The inscription on the bell's side says it was made by Henry McShane, Baltimore, Maryland. Neal thinks it weighs 2,000 pounds and he knows it's five feet tall. He has been in the bell tower.

"I've rung it a time or two, and the manufacturer and the year '1878' is right there on it," he said. "We called and the manufacturer is still in business. They still make bells. They pulled their file and told us when it was ordered and that it cost $40."

records.title: Savoy bell comes down after more than a century
records.text:
Texoma

Savoy bell comes down after more than a century

BY VICKI GRAVES
HERALD DEMOCRAT

SAVOY — Easing the old church bell with pry bars and pulleys, Savoy ISD maintenance personnel slid it over just enough to make a space for the forklift to go under oak timbers that supported it for 128 years.

One of the school parents, Wendell Moore, operated the sky-cab that lifted it down from the Methodist Church bell tower Wednesday morning. "We chained it like you wouldn't believe because the last thing we wanted was to drop that bronze bell and bust it in a million pieces," said Savoy Superintendent Brian Neal.

COURTESY PHOTO
Wendell Moore carefully removes the bronze bell Wednesday morning from the Savoy Methodist Church bell tower on Fowler Street and takes it to the Savoy ISD maintenance shop for restoration.

The school district will get advice from the manufacturer, which is still in business. Henry McShane Bell Foundry of Baltimore, Md. will give instructions on cleaning the timeworn Savoy keepsake, made in 1876.

Col. William Savoy founded the town and Nancy Savoy, wife of the late John Savoy of Arizona, who was the last remaining grandson, donated $25,000 to Savoy ISD last year. With that money, the school district would restore the bell and establish a $1,000 annual scholarships.

Col. Savoy donated the land for the 1878 Methodist church on Fowler Street. That congregation blended long ago with another church and the school district came into possession of the building, which gradually deteriorated over time. It's the oldest building in Savoy and one of the few that survived the 1878 tornado, Neal said.

Savoy ISD moved the bell from the tower without using any of the $25,000. Nancy Savoy envisioned the 1,000-pound bell would be moved to a place where it could be rung on special occasions, perhaps at one of the schools or at the park. A special committee will decide, Neal said.

The preparation to move it took several hours. "We all held our breaths until it actually came on out of there," he said.

While supervising the operation, Neal talked to one retired gentleman as they watched and mentioned that he wondered how they would get it down. They talked about how church builders probably used mules and pulleys to get it up there because there's just no other way they could have done it. "I guess you're right. If they got it up there in 1878, we should be able to get it down in 2006," Neal said he told the other man.

"We still have all the original money Mrs. Savoy gave us and hope to build the bell a new home and have money left for a scholarship that will last a while."

The school board wanted to move the bell before the building lost its integrity and it fell. "That's a very heavy bell and when you got to ringing it, as I have, you felt the place vibrate. I didn't want to come over after some storm and find it broken and neither did Mrs. Savoy. We wanted to act and get it down," Neal said.

Maintenance people moving it noticed the name "Will[?]" carved into one of oak timbers. Neal also said the rope pull had worn a two-inch-deep rut rubbing on the side of the oak timber, over the years.

A church in Wisconsin offered $3,000 for the church bell, Neal said, "But I'm not going to be the guy who lets that bell get out of Savoy. It's been here 128 years. I guess we're going to leave it here."

records.title: Remembering Eula Phillips
records.text:
GOOD MORNING!

Remembering Eula Phillips

BY KATHY WILLIAMS
HERALD DEMOCRAT

Nearly 26 years ago I came into the Sherman Democrat newsroom, pretty old for a cub reporter, but the newby nonetheless. Almost the same day, a tough-as-nails older woman walked in. She was wearing a dusty red felt hat, blue jeans and a work shirt of some sort. I never saw her dressed otherwise, except she got a green felt hat once.

She walked right up to me, held out her hand and said, "Who are you? I'm Eula Phillips and I'm your stringer from Savoy." I thought to myself, "I don't care what you call yourself, I'm pretty sure you're Ma Kettle."

Many of you are too young to remember the countrified film figure, who with Pa Kettle ran a ramshackle little farm and cared for a passle of little kids.

Now Eula had money, so her place outside Savoy wasn't ramshackle. She had rent houses. She was nearly 80 before she stopped doing the roof repairs herself. She had dozens of pecan trees and picked and cracked what must have been a ton of them each year.

A stringer, in newspaper parlance, is a person who gets paid by the paper to write specific stories, like covering city council meetings or football games. Eula was a huge advocate for good government, open government, and fiercely confronted secrecy when she suspected the school district or city had something to hide.

She was a great friend over the years. She always greeted me with, "Hey kiddo, how ya doin'?" She had a broad, infectious smile and keen, often dry, wit. She stuck up for herself and for others. She was honest as any landlady ever and helped out those down on their luck, with the requisite grumbling and curmudgeonliness one would expect.

When I read this week that Eula had died, at 90, I was not surprised to learn that she had served as a drill sergeant in the U.S. Army. My heart grew sad for a moment. Then I could hear her say, "Lighten up kiddo and go pick up all those pecans going to waste in that yard of yours."

Cyclone blew the clothes off boys

Files of Sherman Daily Democrat,
June 1, 1937
(Compiled by Ann Lowry)

SAVOY — Fifty-seven years ago May 28, a cyclone struck Savoy, and moved the town. The freakish wind demolished every house on Main Street and the town was rebuilt on Hayes Street which is now Highway 82.

Not a single resident who witnessed the cyclone remains in Savoy, but several in this area can tell of the storm. H.H. Arterberry, merchant here for 40 years, but now lives southeast of town, recalls a Miss Minnie McMurray who was blown from her home into a pen some distance away.

Dr. S.D. Moore of Van Alstyne and his former roommate, Sam Harle of Durant, Okla., were blown two blocks from their bedroom and every thread of their clothing went with the wind.

Cows were found with their feathers.

Thirteen were killed in the cyclone and the old Halsell College was turned into an emergency hospital.

J.W. BELL & Co.

[N]ext comes this popular firm [that] has been doing business about [several] years. The manager, J. W. [Bell] had many friends and ac[quain]tances before he went into [busi]ness. Having been constable [many] years, his knowledge of the [peop]le in this vicinity is very ex[tensi]ve and has been a great help [in m]aking the business successful. [The] firm also affords a market for [prod]uce, which influences the good [hou]sewives to make this store a [bure]au of exchange and this adds [mate]rially to the funds in the till.

records.title: R. W. Gallaher — drugstore advertisement
records.text:
R. W. GALLAHER.

In the line of Drugs Savoy is very fortunate in having the best. R. W. Gallaher is a registered pharmacist and has been in business a number of years, in fact, prepared himself immediately after leaving college. He has a nice trade that has confidence in him and feel that none but the purest drugs will be used in compounding their prescriptions. His store is always neat and clean and a pleasant greeting awaits every customer. He also carries a nice line of furniture and has built up a good trade with that.

records.title: Edgar A. McMahon — rural mail carrier advice
records.text:
EDGAR A. McMAHON.

When a carrier picks up mail from a box, before accepting it, he is supposed to see that it is properly addressed and stamped. Now there are several boys and girls on Route 3 who, not thinking of this provision, purposely place letters and post cards in the mail box with the back of the first one to me and the next will be facing it but upside down and so on; as a result I am compelled to do a great deal of shuffling to see that each is stamped and properly addressed. Now handlers of mail are not supposed to read cards, but anybody knows that bright colors are easily caught by the eye, especially so when they are moving as being shuffled around to find the address side. records.title: 1907-1908 — New Year editorial, Savoy Star
records.text:
1907-1908

So far as the Star is concerned this issue closes the year of 1907. To many this has been a hard year caused by short crops in this section. To many it has brought sadness. Children have gone from the parental roof to make homes of their own, which, in some instances have not been happy. Sickness and affliction have entered the home, and loved ones been taken from the earth to their home eternal. These things cause sadness, but still, we know this is the common fate of man, and there are other things that should cause us to rejoice as we behold the old year pass out.

We are surrounded by good friends who are ever ready to minister to our needs; and, while we may not have all the money we want, none of us will go hungry or cold because of actual poverty. During the past twelve months, we have had unlimited opportunities for doing good, and it is to be hoped we have improved them.

With these things on our minds, let us take courage and start in the new year with greater expectations, greater determinations, and greater aspirations, and success will be inevitable. We hope to see 1908 bring a good crop and put money in the people's pockets, smiles on their faces, and good cheer in their hearts.

records.title: H. H. ARTERBERRY
records.text:
H. H. ARTERBERRY.

At present, H. H. Arterberry has the oldest dry goods establishment in town. He has lived near here all his life and before going in business for himself, clerked for Russell, Bradford & Co. He has made many friends and established a fine trade by his straightforward business methods. He handles first class goods and sells them reasonably, always allowing his customers all the privileges and time on payments that is consistent with business principles and never crowds them until he is forced to do so. His customers are scattered over all the country intervening between neighboring towns and even across the river Red.

His clerks are courteous and accommodating, which has much to do with holding his trade.

records.title: WOMACK MILLING CO. — business profile
records.text:
WOMACK MILLING CO.

Some seven or eight years ago, a number of our citizens formed a stock company and built a 50bbl. flour mill and equipped it with the most modern machinery. The mill was started and no one ever ate better pancakes and hot biscuit than this flour made. The capital being limited, there was not enough surplus money to supply the grain necessary for the mill to prosper, hence it was sold to the Womack Milling Co., who immediately erected a steel elevator and increased the capacity to 100bbls. With Jno. Parker manager, and T. J. Liggett miller, it has kept up its reputation for fine flour and has made money for the company. Savoy is proud of her mill and many of her citizens would not buy a sack of flour made any whe[re] els[e]

records.title: S. A. Harper — grocer
records.text:
S. A. HARPER.

We would not undertake to say how long the above named gentleman has been in business here. Since the writer has known anything about Savoy, S. A Harper has been weighing sugar and wrapping bacon for his scores of customers. The oldest inhabitants bought their groceries from him and trained their children to do the same thing. From a little wooden building on Water street, his business now fills a nice brick on Hays street.

records.title: Darlene Nolen Becomes Bride Of Robert Blakey
records.text:
Darlene Nolen Becomes Bride Of Robert Blakey

LEONARD — Miss Patresa Darlene Nolen, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. O. H. Nolen Jr. of Leonard, and Robert Derrell Blakey, son of Rev. and Mrs. Robert L. Blakey of Wylie, were united in marriage recently in the Pentecostal Church of Jesus Christ.

Rev. Blakey, father of the bridegroom, performed the double ring ceremony before an altar of candles, flanked by two spiral candelabra and tall white baskets filled with white mums. Gladiolus, pink roses and a kneeling bench completed the altar decor.

Mrs. Charlotte Pitts, organist of Plano, accompanied Miss Bettye Blakey of Wylie, as she sang, "I Love You Because" and "Wedding Prayer."

Mr. Nolen presented his daughter in marriage. She wore a floor length gown styled with winsome Victorian charm. Delicate acetate and nylon lace adorned the empire bodice of nylon sheer over acetate taffeta. The gown featured a graceful A-line skirt. The bodice was fashioned with a demure stand-up collar and Juliet sleeves. Her lace bordered, detachable, chapel length train of nylon sheer, flowed from a ribbon at the waist.

A half halo of acetate and nylon lace petals accented with pearls and crystal held the three tiered bouffant elbow length veil of nylon tulle.

The bride carried a Victorian cluster of white roses and miniature carnations with satin streamers, tied in love knots.

Miss Nolen presented her mother with a long stem pink rose as she walked to the alter and presented the bridegroom's mother a rose as she left, following the ceremony.

Miss Belinda Pitts of Van Alstyne, was maid of honor and Miss Shirley Nolen of Leonard was bridesmaid. They wore pink floral brocade empire style gowns, accented with hot pink velvet ribbon. Their headpieces were of matching ribbon and pink carnations. Each carried a single pink rose with satin streamers. Daretha Nolen, sister of the bride, was flower girl.

James Blakey of Garland served as best man and Larry Ratliff of Bentonville, Ark., was groomsman. Ricky Flanagan of Leonard was ring bearer. Larry Blakey of Marshall and Benny Blakey of Wylie seated the guests. Candlelighters were Dewain and Darvin Nolen, brothers of the bride and Benny Blakey of Wylie.

A reception was held in the fellowship hall of the church, which was decorated in pink and white. White lanterns enhanced the room.

The bride's table was laid with white lace over pink and centered with three candles, surrounded by white carnations. A four tiered cake decorated with pink roses and white swans, topped with three pink satin bells, and punch were served by Mrs. Delores Hutchins and Miss Karolyn McCord, both of Leonard. Crystal appointments completed the table decorations.

Miss Marilyn Johnson served at the bridegroom's table, which was laid with an off-white lace cloth and held a chocolate cake and coffee service.

Miss Roberto Grogan of Leonard registered the guests.

The bride is a graduate of Leonard High School and the bridegroom is a graduate of Wylie High School and attended Texas Bible College, Houston. They will be at home in Plano.

records.title: Native of Savoy Dies at Age 88
records.text:
Native of Savoy
Dies at Age 88

MRS. A. DEATHERAGE.

SAVOY, Texas.—Mrs. Sarah Malissa Deatherage, 88, died at 2 a. m. Friday at her home here following an illness of two months. Funeral services will be held at 2 p. m. Saturday at the residence, with J. B. May, a friend of the family, conducting. Interment will be in Sunnyside cemetery. Talley of Sherman directing.

Born Aug. 8, 1856, in the Nahurin community south of Savoy, she was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. James Ray. She was married to A. Deatherage Aug. 26, 1875. Mr. Deatherage died two years ago at the age of 94. A member of the Church of Christ, Mrs. Deatherage lived in this community all her life and at the present home 50 years.

Survivors include one son, Frank Deatherage of Hugo, Okla.; six daughters, Mrs. B. E. Mathews of Fort Worth, Mrs. W. P. Carter of Dallas, Mrs. J. W. Jenkins of Bells, Mrs. Paul Houston of Lubbock, Mrs. C. D. Hastings of Longview, and Mrs. Ann Tyler, also of Hugo; grandchildren and nine great-grandchildren.

records.title: Savoy Farmer Dies at Age 88
records.text:
J. W. WOODS.

Savoy Farmer Dies at Age 88

SAVOY.—A retired farmer, J. W. Woods, 88, died at 7 a. m. Sunday at his home here. He had been an invalid for 10 years. Funeral services were to be held at 2:30 p. m. Monday at the Baptist church with the Rev. Bob Cates, Methodist pastor, conducting. Interment was to be in Oak Hill cemetery with Glen Earnheart of Whitewright directing.

Pallbearers were to be H. F. Bomar, Earl Blakey, H. T. Blakey, Joe Parkhill, A. R. Deberry and S. R. Large.

Born May 26, 1856, in Tennessee, he was the son of Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Woods. He was married to Miss Jennie Worley of Corsicana, coming to Texas in early manhood. He had lived at Ector and Savoy the past 30 years.

Survivors include his wife and three sons, O. W. Woods and Clyde Woods of Houston, J. D. Woods of Savoy; one daughter, Mrs. A. L. Furr of Houston; 17 grandchildren and 8 great grandchildren.

records.title: Ray Booth — obituary
records.text:
Ray Booth

BELLS—Funeral services were held at 3 p.m. Tuesday in the First Baptist Church, Bells, for Ray Booth, 52, of Bells, Hardwicke-Etter Co. supervisor, who died in a Sherman hospital at 1:45 p.m. Monday, two hours after suffering a heart attack.

The Rev. Robert Baldridge Baptist minister, and the Rev. William Davis, Methodist minister, both of Bells, conducted the services. Burial was in Rose Hill Cemetery, directed by Earnheart Funeral Home, Whitewright.

Mr. Booth was born Aug. 30, 1906 in Savoy, a son of the late V. H. and Sarah Booth. On Oct. 12, 1929, he married Miss Lucille Wilson in Bells. He was a deacon in the Baptist Church, a charter member of the Lions Club, a mason and and a member of the Knights Templar. He was supervisor of the black metal department at Hardwicke-Etter.

Survivors are his wife; one daughter, Sarah Carolyn Booth; and a son, Donald Wilson Booth, all of Bells; a brother, Roy Booth of Waco; two sisters, Mrs. Carl Orndorff of Savoy and Mrs. Roy Stephens of Sherman.

records.title: Mrs. Lucy Durrett
records.text:
Mrs. Lucy Durrett

SAVOY — Funeral services was held Tuesday, at 2:30 p.m. in the First Baptist Church for Mrs. Lucy Durrett, 80, who died Monday 8:30 a.m. in the home of her daughter, Mrs. Maurive Owens in Leonard.

The Rev. C. H. Longino of Omaha and the Rev. W. A. Rudd of Campbell conducted the services. Burial was in Sunnyside Cemetery, directed by Earnheart Funeral Home.

Mrs. Durrett was born July 24, 1879 in Georgia, a daughter of the late Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Dodd. She was a member of the Savoy Baptist Church. She came to Savoy as a child and was married here in 1898 to W. H. Durrett.

Survivors besides her daughter, are one son, Duke Durrett of Savoy; two grandchildren and two great-grandchildren.

records.title: Town Reconstructed / Savoy Mississippian / College Established
records.text:
Town Reconstructed

Reconstruction began at once. The first two blocks, running north and south on Water street, and as many directions now. As the town progressed, and the west block of bricks on the north side of the street were torn away, the buildings were built. One by one the old wood buildings were torn away, and the bricks took their places. Two or three of the old buildings to be torn down are the Drugstore building owned by the late W. L. Teague. After Mr. Teague's death P. O. Teague took over the cleaning. It stood north of the H. H. Arterberry store.

The Gooseberry has served Savoy and the surrounding community in the drug and grocery trade for almost half a century. He established the business in 1892, in what was almost an unpopulated place. After the establishment of the Savoy Tribune, later known as the Savoy Star, H. H. Arterberry was connected with it for a time. After his withdrawal, the newspaper was operated until his son Max was through school, and was made a partner. It now operates under the name Arterberry and Son. Mr. Arterberry was born and raised in Savoy. He has education in the Savoy College.

The Savoy Tribune, later known as the Savoy Star, was first published about 1890, and by 1902, when T. E. Arterberry and L. H. King established the Savoy Star. Mr. King operated the Savoy Star only a short time, then Mr. Arterberry bought out King. Arterberry continued the work together for 23 years when he was claimed by his calling. He left the family alone until her marriage to J. B. May, who is her assistant. The family is dry now and has a Washington hand press of which there is one of the best in the state here today. Besides the local news, advertising, and editorials, Mrs. May has tried to save local history, aided by many who are compiling scrap-books.

Had Flour Mill

In the spring of 1900 there was a flour mill here, located north of the old school building. In 1902 a new elevator was built, known as the Womack Milling Co. It was a place of milling for several years before it was torn down. Until recent years there has been a cotton gin here at one time and at night in the fall. They now have a modern gin up and have not been replaced.

Savoy Mississippian

It has been recalled that in 1884 a man known as "Parson Smith" was minister; there were several before him and quite a few between him and the late Postmaster W. P. Carter. Mr. Carter served a number of years the first appointment, then H. M. Arnon, now of Denton, served eight or nine years. Mr. Carter was reappointed and will serve until December 16, 1941. Claude Strickland recently was appointed postmaster here.

College Established

The Savoy College was established in 1880 when Prof. J. L. Halsell, served as a local school for Savoy and surrounding communities. Through the years Prof. Halsell decided to enlarge the school into a college and applied to the state for a charter, which was granted Jan. 22, 1880, to H. R. Halsell and others; also C. E. Paxton and J. L. German, with the name "Savoy Female College" or "Female College." It is spoken of today as the Savoy College or the Halsell College. The school, much like the school of today, consisted of a grammar school, high school and college all in one system.

The highest degree to be conferred was an A. B. degree. The school did not put much stress on athletics. There were literary and debating societies were more popular. The school had two literary societies, the Platahian, for the older boys, and the Philomathians for the younger ones. The students were made "Keepers of Governmental Laws." Under this system each student was required to write an essay each week. A lady of Spanish descent taught French and Spanish. Among those taught in the school during its 14 years were H. R. Harshaw, R. R. Halsell, Lewis Holman, Watt Pritchard, R. A. Gay and Mr. Henshaw.

College Is Destroyed

The College burned in the fall of 1913, and was never rebuilt. Many of the records, books, and other valuable records were destroyed. Miss Lou Arterberry, an ex-student who had a photograph of part of the school bell that went through the fire and is using it for a door stop.

Prof. Halsell died in Durant, Okla., and is buried in Durant.

The first ex-student reunion was held in August 1937, when the new rock Halsell Memorial Building was finished. The reunion is to be on the same date.

The next school building for Savoy was a two-story wood building, located north of the present building of the school. It was built about 1914. Mr. Hendricks was in charge of the school work for the next five or six years, but an old record that was apparently in the 1920s shows there were four teachers then. The one on the blackboard, W. E. McMahon and Miss Marsha Buford, now Mrs. J. B. May. The routes of Savoy and Mahurin were combined. Owens going to Mahurin and he replaced Miller, Dodson was sent to Bonham, replaced it, this time one story. The school here is provided with modern equipment. There is a modern rock gym on the west, where the F. F. A. class meets, and the bot[?] 13 tennis room is located. There are 13 telephone directors, two recreation directors, six employed in the lunch room. The Randolph Grove school has been consolidated with the Savoy school, the New Warren school, transferred to the Mahurin was also transferred.

Savoy Mississippian

Col. William Louis Marshall Savoy, founder of the town of Savoy, was born Aug. 2, 1817, in Mississippi, died Sept. 1, 1887, in Goshee, Johnson County, Texas.

He came to Texas at an early age, settling first near home, Texas, near the present city of Sherman. The place is known today as the Savoy Prairie.

During the civil war, he enlisted in the Confederate army, but refused active duty while in training and never saw active service. The next few years were spent in travel. He crossed the Atlantic twice and the Pacific three times. It is believed, according to Mrs. Louise Travis, that he was doing secret service work for the government at this time.

Col. Savoy often remarked that he had every kind of contagious disease, except yellow fever, while on an adventure trip in South America. He had secured a large tract of valuable land, but when he fell ill with a tropical disease, without he left very hurriedly, never going back to claim it.

Joined Gold Rush

In 1849 he joined the crowd in the gold rush to California, making a fast trip across country. The gold laden hills he dug with picks and shovels the gold nuggets with his own hands were sent back to Savoy. The gold was carried back to Savoy. It is a story often recalled by Mrs. Travis that her father was robbed twice by bands of Indians, who fought with tomahawks and arrows, once while taking cotton to a San Antonio market from Goshee, Texas.

About 1854, he was making a trip through West Texas by train. An Indian attack or possible one, in front of Col. Savoy, turned and said, "You are the bravest man I've met there," Col. Savoy, remembering the attack replied "Well, my friend you are mistaken."

In 1874 Col. Savoy was married to Mrs. Julia E. Davis, in Savoy. The couple went to Denison to live. When returning from a trip, they were met by the hometown band and escorted to their home. Several churches were located and the Methodist Church building was given to the members of Church of Christ as well as all the other denominations.

The Christian Church was established in the summer of 1838, with a minister by the name of Graves of Sherman. Mr. Graves served as pastor until the fall of [text continues but is cut off]

records.title: William Dault Buried
records.text:
William Dault Buried

SAVOY.—Graveside service was held Tuesday at 2:30 p.m. in Sunnyside Cemetery, near Savoy, for William F. Dault, 93, who died in his home here Monday at 1:40 p.m. after a two-year illness. He was a native of Tennessee.

W. H. Secoy, minister of the Savoy Church of Christ, officiated. Arrangements were in charge of Earnheart Funeral Home.

Survivors are one son, Preston Dault of Fort Worth; two daughters, Mrs. Helen Bennett of St. Louis, Mo., and Mrs. Hazel Miller of Savoy; one sister, Mrs. Maggie Hale of Palacios.

records.title: Savoy Star's 110-Year-Old Press Is Now Museum Piece
records.text:
Savoy Star's 110-Year-Old Press Is Now Museum Piece

The century-old Washington hand press on which the Savoy Star was printed for 41 years until publication was suspended with the June 25 issue, has been purchased from Mrs. J. B. May by the Sherman Democrat. It will be held as a museum piece because it is the same type of press on which the Democrat was printed in its early years, beginning August 14, 1879, and because of the possibility this was the original Democrat press itself.

One of the oldest pieces of printing equipment in the country, the Washington hand press was invented in 1827 by Samuel Rust of New York, but he sold his invention to R. Hoe and Company, who began to manufacture with some improvements. The Savoy Star press bears the legend "IM" in raised letters, a part of the foundry pattern to show it was one of the first thousand presses of its kind made. In depressed figures, the number of the press is 123, showing that it was the 123rd press of its kind made.

An investigation by the Hoe company in the spring of 1939 revealed that the press was made just before 1830 or shortly thereafter and that by 1850 relatively few presses of the type were manufactured.

Another evidence of its early manufacture is the fact that it does not carry the name of the Hoe company, the only legend outside of numbering being the descriptive name Washington Press. It does carry a design of an eagle with extended wings and, on later presses, instead of the name of the press instead of the name of the company, a copy of the American shield. Later presses carried the name of the manufacturer instead of the name of the press, and the faces of the last presses of the late presses were raised figures of the head of George Washington.

A quarter of a century ago the Washington press was beginning to disappear in print shops. A few remain in use now as proof presses. One side of a form can be done at a time, and the service of two persons is required, a operator one to ink the type with a roller and another to pull the lever drawing the weight of the press against the type to form a print.

G. O. Hunter, the North Binkley, one of the founders of the Sherman Democrat who retired in 1932, recalls that a Washington hand press was the principal piece of equipment for The Democrat for some years.

The Democrat's hand press was purchased from Captain Crooke, who was operating the Sherman Courier, a morning newspaper here, later taken to Whitewright by Mr. Hunter and his brother for the Whitewright Democrat, the forerunner of the Sherman Democrat. Some years after the Sherman Daily Democrat was established in 1881, this press was taken to Savoy by Hunter's brother-in-law, Elder Hunter, elder brother of the two founders of the Sherman Democrat, then to Whitewright and later to Caddo, Okla.

The Savoy Star's press was purchased from the late Zeb Spearman, who operated the weekly paper at Whitewright. Attempt has been made to identify the Savoy Democrat as the Savoy Star press but there is no established fact.

[Photo caption:] Mrs. J. B. May is shown here with the George Washington hand press purchased by the Sherman Democrat following the suspension of the Savoy Star after 41 years of publication. The press was made around 1880. Mrs. May operated The Star following the death of her husband, T. E. Arterberry, founder of the paper.

It is considered possible, however, that the press was brought back from Caddo, Okla. to Whitewright and used on the Plow and Hammer or the Whitewright Sun by Spearman.

The Hoe company wrote to The Democrat: "We continue to receive many letters from users of these old presses but to date we can not recall any that has had a machine number that is as low as that on the Star press."

Available history of the Savoy Star press will be preserved along with a copy of the final issue of The Star.

From the time of the Washington press, the Star continued to be printed on several presses, each an improvement over its predecessor. In 1925 the present equipment was installed, a 16-page tubular press capable of printing up to 5,000 copies an hour.

A Washington hand press weighs about 800 pounds and takes floor space about three by six feet while the tubular press now used by The Democrat weighs around [illegible] and occupies a space of 20 by 30 feet. The hand press had only one form, 9 by 12 inches. The larger press has several pieces of equipment for different purposes, occupying altogether a large room [illegible]

records.title: Eight Hurt In Two Fannin Accidents
records.text:
Eight Hurt In Two Fannin Accidents

BONHAM — Eight persons were hospitalized in two separate wrecks in Fannin County over the weekend with five cars involved in the two accidents.

Seven persons were sent to the hospital as the result of a three-car accident on Highway 78 just north of the Bonham city limits and the eighth suffered only minor injuries at Savoy.

In the Savoy accident, C. G. Elliott, Jr. of Windom apparently went to sleep at the wheel of his car and ran off the road and plowed into a parked car belonging to George Feagan of Savoy. Feagan's car was demolished but Elliott escaped with only minor injuries.

The accident happened at 4:30 a.m. Easter Sunday.

Painful but not critically injured in the three-car accident at Bonham were Mrs. Raymond Fitzpatrick of Yuba and Mrs. Sidney Hicks of Bonham. Both suffered cuts about the face, head and body.

Others injured were Raymond Fitzpatrick, Sidney Hicks, Betty Wright and Glen Hamby, all of Yuba, and Tom Vaught, Jr. of Ravenna.

Fitzpatrick was heading south to Bonham from Yuba and Vaught was going north, according to of[ficials].

[Photo caption:] SAVOY PARKED CAR WRECKED—This is all that is left of George Feagan's car after it was rammed by a vehicle driven by C. G. Elliott of Windom. Feagan's car was parked at Savoy and Elliott went to sleep at the wheel of his car. He was only slightly injured. (Photo by Jimmy Reynolds, 13, Herald carrier-agent at Savoy)

records.title: Robert William Denton, Native of Savoy, Dies
records.text:
Robert William Denton,
Native of Savoy, Dies

SAVOY—Funeral service will be held in Savoy Saturday at 2 p.m. for Robert William Denton, 63, a flooring contractor and native of Savoy, who died Wednesday afternoon in the Veterans Hospital in Little Rock, Ark. Burial will be in Sunnyside Cemetery, near here.

Mr. Denton was born Oct. 14, 1893, a son of the late Mr. and Mrs. Joe Denton. For the last three years he had lived in Mena, Ark. In May, 1919, he married Miss Mae Large here. He was a veteran of World War I.

Survivors are his wife; one daughter, Mrs. Francis Horner of Oklahoma; one son, Clarence Denton of Mena, Ark.; a brother, H. A. Denton of Denison; five grandchildren and two great grandchildren.

records.title: Mrs. John Moore, 81, Dies at Savoy Home
records.text:
Mrs. John Moore, 81, Dies at Savoy Home

SAVOY — Funeral services for Mrs. John Moore, 81, who died Thursday morning at her home here, were to be held at 3 p.m. Friday in Savoy Methodist Church. Burial was to be in Rose Hill Cemetery, Bells.

Mrs. Moore had been ill six months. She moved to Savoy from Bells 10 years ago.

A native of Lynville, Tenn., Mrs. Moore was Miss Kate Matthews before her marriage in Bells Dec. 31, 1873. She was a member of Savoy Methodist Church.

Surviving are twin sons, C. H. Moore of Savoy and Clarence Moore of Denison; two daughters, Mrs. Grady Stone of Bells and Mrs. T. L. Beckham of Savoy; a sister, Mrs. Ethel Webber of Austin; 10 grandchildren and seven great grandchildren.

records.title: Savoy Will Observe Its 70th Anniversary Late In October
records.text:
MONDAY, JANUARY 19, 1942

Savoy Will Observe Its 70th Anniversary Late In October

Col. Savoy Gave Railroad Forty Acres For Town

Charter Granted For Town In 1873, One Of Oldest In This Area

By JAMES ELIZABETH LARGE

SAVOY, Jan. 19.—In 1872 Col. Savoy made a contract with the Transcontinental Railway now known as the T. & P. for 40 acres of land on which to build a town if they would build a railroad through the town on land donated. To this they agreed and a deed was given Bonham Oct. 29, 1872. Twenty acres on each side of the track. On Aug. 8, 1873, the charter for the town was granted. Records show that some of the lots sold for as much as $80.

The depot was erected where the present one now stands. Savoy's first business house was erected on Front street and Main street on the south side of the railroad. Hodgson and Beard owned and operated a general merchandise store. The first saloon to be put up was on Front but on the east side of Main street, R. T. Tear opened a saloon. These were Savoy's first merchants.

Until now the only means of obtaining supplies was to haul from Bonham and Denison and sometimes more distant points, this being done with a horse and team, taking several days or weeks to make the round trip. By the time there has now grown to a thriving little village, the census is in a couple of months.

The prosperity continued until May 28, 1880, when the terrible cyclone hit the town. Savoy being the exact date and time by the people was by Johnnie Weir.

'Twas in the spring of '80

Had Flour Mill

In the fall of 1900 there was a flour mill here, located north of the old school building. In 1902 a new elevator was built, known as the Womack Milling Co. It was a place of milling for several years before it was torn down. Until recent years there has been a cotton gin here at one time and at night in the fall. They now have a modern gin up and have not been replaced.

It was replaced by a brick structure. Savoy, unlike so many places its size, still has an Agency and telegraph office, is still served by the Texas & Pacific Railway. Although there are only two passenger trains daily, there were formerly six.

There are six grocery stores, four filling stations, one drug store, two dry goods shops, two blacksmith shops, two produce houses, one cafe, one meat market, one dress and hat shop and some dry goods store.

Had Telephone System

The first telephone switchboard was owned by the late Tom Frank, with Miss Etta King, now Mrs. Etta McMahon, as operator. Mr. Frank sold the board and it was run by Joe Savoy Star office, with Miss Almeda running the board for several years. With the help of her sister, Miss Almeda and Miss Anna. After Miss Almeda married and Miss Anna took a position away from Savoy, Miss Anna Owens, operator. After several years Miss Owens accepted a position in Sherman, Miss Velma Boothe, who is now Mrs. Velma Boothe Woodard[?] was made manager, and still holds the position. The system is owned by the Southwestern Bell Telephone Co.

First Public Water Well

The first public water well was drilled in H. H. Beard's yard in the fall of 1913, and was operated by J. L. Riley. When he sold it and moved to Nevada, there were no other available times, and did not wait for the ones who went to the expense for the larger part of the school bell[?] that went through the fire and is using it for a door stop.

Joe Noah Was Carrier

Joe Noah, it is said, was the first rural mail carrier at Savoy. E. A. Spaddow, now of Dallas; Will McMcSpaddow, carried on the route out of town, and the late R. C. Frank McMaddow[?]. Not long after, until the consolidation of the routes, Jim McMaddow's route was the one to go. Mr. McMaddow's record shows there were four teachers then. The first appointment of Miller of Denison exchanged routes with his death. Miller and Owens both [?], then the routes were combined. Owens going to Mahurin and he replaced Miller. Dodson was sent to Bonham, replaced it, this time one story. The school here is provided with modern equipment. There is a modern rock gym on the west, where the F. F. A. class meets, and the bot[?] 13 tennis room is located. There are 13 telephone directors, two recreation directors, six employed in the lunch room. The Randolph Grove school has been consolidated with the Savoy school, the New Warren school, transferred to the Mahurin was also transferred.

90-Year-Old Citizen

One of Fannie County's oldest citizens resides in Savoy. He is A. Deatherage. He celebrated his ninety-fourth birthday March 22. He was born in Tennessee, came to Texas at the age of 5 with his parents in 1853, has lived within a radius of five miles of Savoy the rest of his life. He was married to Miss Sally Ray Aug. 19, 1875. She died about three years ago. They have eight living children and 15 living grandchildren, several great-grandchildren.

The Savoy Methodist Church was organized in 1873 by the Rev. Graves of Sherman. The building was erected the same year. The lot was given by Col. Savoy and the first load of lumber was hauled from Bells by the late T. W. McSpadden. Most of the members moved away. All denominations except the Seventh Day Adventists used the building for worship.

Baptist Church Founded

The first Baptist Church of the Savoy community was across from Jerdon, located east of town. Many of the older members of the present church united with it in their early childhood. Some time after the original building burned, the church was organized. The Little Church moved back into town and moved to Ector to be rebuilt and before it was completed it was moved back to Savoy. A new church was built. Most of the members moved their membership to the Savoy church. The reorganization of the present church organization took place. Several older members who were interviewed, some time near 1880.

The exact date of the organization of the first Church of Christ in Savoy is not known to any of the older members, but the first organization was before Savoy was a town. It was organized in the Roberts school house south of Savoy. The first officers were Jeff Clevenger, O. H. Clevenger, William Francis and J. J. Jenkins, Sr. At that time there were about 40 members and five of the Jenkins children were members. Also, Mrs. Ada L. Travis of Hondo, Texas and Joseph Savoy of Mission, Texas. Both still living at the time. Mrs. Ada L. Travis was a Spanish war veteran and [rest of column cut off]

Ed McMahon, 79, Dies

W. G. HODGES.

Injuries Fatal To Lifelong Savoy Resident

SAVOY.—Wiley Green Hodges, 85, widely known farmer and landowner and life-long resident of this community, died at 4 a. m. today in a Sherman hospital as the result of injuries he suffered Sunday afternoon when he fell from a horse near his home here. He sustained a broken hip and fractured ribs.

He was the father of Mrs. Roy Johnson and W. D. Hodges, both of Sherman.

Mr. Hodges was born April 8, 1860, on his father's farm southeast of Savoy. He was married in 1884 to Lenora Herndon, who died in 1932.

In addition to the daughter and son of Sherman, other survivors include four other daughters, Mrs. O. N. Saye of Longview, Mrs. Retta Kincaid of Whitewright, Mrs. T. J. Hollis of Waxahachie and Mrs. Ellis Morgan of Savoy; and two other sons, DeWitt Hodges of Artesia, N. M., and Grover Hodges of Savoy.

Funeral arrangements are incomplete, but services will be held in the Savoy Baptist Church and burial in Sunnyside Cemetery, directed by Earnheart-Strickland Funeral Home.

SAVOY, Texas — Corp. T. G. Waldrum, son of the late Tiny Waldrum, was killed in action in Italy June 11, the war department has informed relatives here.

records.title: Old Savoy Home Back In Hands Of First Owners — Page 12, The Denison Herald, Thursday, Oct. 2, 1952
records.text:
Page 12—THE DENISON HERALD—Thursday, Oct. 2, 1952

86-YEAR-OLD SAVOY HOME—This house was originally built in 1866, but recently was moved into Savoy and remodeled. It is now owned by Mrs. W. R. Jones, a great-granddaughter of its original builder. (Staff Photo)

Old Savoy Home Back In Hands Of First Owners

SAVOY— James Wrenn would never recognize the house that his great granddaughter, Mrs. W. R. Jones, is living in today as the same one that he constructed at the end of the Civil War in 1865.

The house recently was remodeled, but the old original beams and sills that were hauled by oxen and wagon from East Texas are still intact.

Since Wrenn built the house, it has been moved to a new site and out of the possession of his family. But today it is back in the same family, albeit with a modern 1952 face.

Mrs. H. A. Ooten, a granddaughter of Wrenn, told how Wrenn had fought his way through the Civil War as a member of the "Confederate Missourians.". The womenfolk in his family came to Texas during the war and he followed later.

They settled in Savoy and hauled the lumber to build the house by oxen and cart from East Texas, a three-week trip with each load.

After his death in 1888, a daughter and son-in-law, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Blakey, moved in. Incidentally, Mrs. Blakey, who was Rebecca Wrenn, lives north of Savoy with a son, Tommy. She is 84.

After the Blakeys moved out, one of their sons, Clyde, moved in and stayed there until he sold the house to Earl Reed. Reed, in turn, had the house brought into Savoy and then sold it to Tommy Hall.

It was Hall who remodeled it and then sold it to Mrs. Jones, a great-granddaughter of its original builder.

records.title: Former Traveling Salesman Recalls Good Old Country Peddling Times
records.text:
Page 6—THE DENISON HERALD—Friday, Sept. 26, 1952

SAVOY'S FORMER TRAVELING SALESMAN, L. A. Brown, eyes a piece of expert needle work done by his wife, who took up that work after suffering a stroke in 1944.

MARRIED FARMER'S DAUGHTER

Former Traveling Salesman Recalls Good Old Country Peddling Times

BY JOHN CLIFT
(Herald State Editor)

SAVOY—One of the last of the old time country peddlers looked back on the "good old days" this week and recollected that the country might be better off if the old peddlers were back in the harness.

L. A. Brown put in some seven years at the turn of the century driving a general merchandise wagon, one of nine such men working for B. C. H. Bradford of Whitewright.

"I put the butter in a large can I carried," he said.

"And it was a long way from being fresh country butter by the time he got back," put in Mrs. Brown.

Forty-five years ago this Feb. 2, will mark the anniversary of the traveling salesman's marriage to the farmer's daughter, in this case the former Miss Weston Jenkins.

Less than a year later he quit the road to become a farmer "something that I've liked better than anything I ever did," he recalled.

SUCCESSFUL FARMER

Brown was a success as a farmer, having his best luck tilling the soil during a 10-year stretch spent in West Texas "where the cotton made two bales to an acre."

However, his love for North Texas plus the fact that his children had grown up and married and lived in the area, brought him back to Savoy and he finished up his career on the farm south of Savoy.

Mrs. Brown suffered a stroke in 1944 and has been confined to a wheel chair ever since. As a result, a daughter-in-law, Mrs. Paul Brown who lives down the street a block or so, comes over at least three times each day. She prepares all of the meals, does all of the housework for the old couple, and, if the occasion warrants, spends the night.

Mrs. Brown has been keeping herself amused since she suffered her stroke by painting and doing needlework.

OWN DESIGNER

She creates her own patterns for her needlework and then puts the patterns on hand towels.

She uses some water color, but mostly crayon or pencil in her drawings. She uses only her imagination and has come up with several lively crayon landscapes.

Too, the portrait of her husband, done from memory, is excellent. When questioned about the amount of hair she put on her husband's head, she replied "that's why I married him in the first place. He had the most beautiful head of hair I ever saw on a man."

Mrs. Brown did one bit of cheating on her art when she peeked into a mirror to complete her self portrait.

"I just couldn't get my chin and mouth right," she defended herself.

Her unusual designs on hand towels has created a waiting list among North Texans who have seen and admired her work. They are especially in demand around the holiday seasons when her handiwork finds its way under many Christmas trees.

WON A SUIT

All of her work has been done since she suffered the stroke, which left her with her left arm paralyzed.

The Browns are looking forward to celebrating their golden wedding anniversary five years hence.

"I might make enough to get my husband a new suit," grinned Mrs. Brown.

"She's kidding me about the suit I won for being the best traveling salesman back before we were married," smiled her husband. "I got a $37.50 suit that was a dandy."

While the Browns rely on their daughter-in-law to keep their house cleaned and to prepare their meals, both still are able to get around very well. Mrs. Brown is 82, her husband 78.

"And I'm feeling so good if I'm not careful I may wind up looking for a job," he concluded.

records.title: 'Uncle Hade' Whitsett's Death Thins Ranks Of Civil War Vets
records.text:
'Uncle Hade' Whitsett's Death Thins Ranks Of Civil War Vets

BONHAM, Aug. 15. (P)—Joseph Haden Whitsett, 103, one of Texas' three surviving Confederate veterans, died today at his home here.

Almost blind and deaf, he had made his home with his niece, Mrs. Zora Arledge.

Even in the past few years he had liked to have visitors and talk about the old days.

He served with Shelby's Escort in the Missouri Cavalry during the Civil War.

His 104th birthday was little more than a month away — Sept. 18.

Whitsett's death leaves only Walter W. (Colonel Will) Williams of Franklin and Thomas Evans Riddle of Austin of Texas' once numerous legions of Confederate veterans.

Whitsett's declining years were sad compared with the happy days of only a few years ago, when he liked nothing better than a noisy, knee-slapping round of checkers.

In recent years he was confined to his bed.

Whitsett was born at Glasgow, Ky., on Sept. 18, 1847. He was the son of Dr. William and Elizabeth Edmund Whitsett. He came with his parents to Texas in 1853. They settled in the English community southeast of Bonham.

It was on May 6, 1864, that he enlisted in the Confederate Army. He returned home a year and a month later. Then he attended Carlton College here. He got permission to carry a gun to classes.

Before the Texas and Pacific Railway came into Bonham, Whitsett hauled freight by wagon. After marrying Miss Betty Stone, March 18, 1873, he went into the mercantile business at Dodd City. About 1900 he returned to Bonham.

He had made his home with Mrs. Arledge since his wife died in 1931.

Whitsett never fired a shot in the Civil War.

"The only thing that bothered me during the war," he told reporters in 1948, "was the itch. The itch and creepers. Did you ever see a body louse? Well, in those days we called them creepers."

He broke his hip shortly before his 98th birthday — an accident usually fatal to a man of that advanced age. But Uncle Hade recovered from that.

He was a 50-year Mason, an Odd Fellow, and a lifetime member of the Bonham Volunteer Fire Department.

He had no children. Several nieces live in the Bonham area.

records.title: Double Ring Ceremony Unites Savoy Couple
records.text:
MRS. H. F. BOMAR, JR.

Double Ring Ceremony Unites Savoy Couple

SAVOY.—Miss Cecil Inez Bibby and H. F. Bomar, Jr., were married Sunday afternoon at 4 o'clock at the home of Mr. and Mrs. Otis Baker. The Rev. Evert Springfield, pastor of the Baptist Church, read the double ring ceremony.

The bride is the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. B. P. Bibby, of Savoy and the groom is the son of Mr. and Mrs. H. F. Bomar, also of Savoy.

The pre-nuptial music was by Mrs. G. N. Morgan and Mrs. Gene Hardy of Bonham sang "I Love You Truly."

The vows were exchanged before an altar of palms, white gladioli and magnolia blossoms, with white candles in candelabra on each side. Miss Carolyn Brown lighted the candles.

The bride wore a pink eyelet dress and her only jewelry was a lavalier belonging to her mother.

A reception at the Baker home followed the ceremony.

Mrs. Bomar is a 1946 graduate of Savoy High School, where she was valedictorian of her class and voted sweetheart of the football team.

Mr. Bomar also graduated from Savoy High School. He received his Army discharge last April, following four years' service, 18 months of which were spent overseas. The couple will make their home in Savoy.

records.title: A. Deatherage To Observe 94th Birthday On March 22 / Savoy Couple Soon Will Observe 67th Wedding Anniversary
records.text:
SAVOY PIONEERS—Mr. and Mrs. A. Deatherage of Savoy are among the oldest married couples in North Texas. They will observe their 67th wedding anniversary next August. Mr. Deatherage will be 94 years old March 22. Mrs. Deatherage will observe her 86th birthday Aug. 8.

A. Deatherage To Observe 94th Birthday On March 22

Savoy Couple Soon Will Observe 67th Wedding Anniversary

By MISS ELIZABETH LARGE
Herald Correspondent

SAVOY, March 7—A. Deatherage, who will observe his ninety-fourth birthday March 22, is a Savoy pioneer in the truest sense of the word. He has lived in this community 89 years and has seen progress made over that span of years.

A retired farmer and painter, Mr. Deatherage was born near Sweetwater, Tenn., March 22, 1848. He came to Texas with his parents, Mr. and Mrs. John E. Deatherage, when he was 5 years old. The family settled five miles west of here and he has not lived further away from Savoy during the 89 years.

Freighted Supplies

As a young man he freighted supplies from Jefferson and other distant points with an ox team. The round trips often required weeks and often disaster marred the trip before reaching home. He recalls an accident once when crossing a river which almost cost him his life. One ox drowned and a wagon load of supplies was lost.

His hobby is music. He was leader of the "Sacred Harp Leaders" and it is believed he is the only member of that group now living. He still walks to town almost every day in pretty weather.

Have Seen Savoy Grow

He was married to Miss Sally Ray, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Ray, Aug. 19, 1875, at Savoy. She was born Aug. 8, 1856, and is Savoy's oldest woman. Her hobby is flowers and quilting. Her sweetpeas are the most beautiful in the community and each year are shared by her friends. They have spent their entire married life in Savoy, the last 50 years at their present home.

They have seen Savoy grow from open country to a little town. A modern concrete highway today marks the trails when he came here. They have used candles for lighting in their early married life but their home is equipped with electric lights today. In earlier days they waited weeks for mail, but it is delivered to their front door daily now.

They began life at the peak of the horse and buggy days, but today modern automobiles whiz by their home all hours of the day and night.

Eight of their 10 children are living. They are Mrs. Rose Mathis of Texarkane, Mrs. Laura Carter of Dallas, Frank Deatherage and Fred Deatherage of Hugo, Okl., Mrs. Alfa Jenkins of Savoy, Mrs. Montia Houston, of Slaton, Mrs. Bernidene Hastings of Longview and Mrs. Annie Tyer of Hugo. They have 15 grandchildren and 10 great-grandchildren. Mr. Deatherage has a brother, Dr. William Deatherage, at Dallas.

Both are members of the Primitive Baptist Church, both their fathers having served as ministers of that church.

In Memory of

Mrs. Aditha Woods

records.text:

THOMAS M. GARRETT

Thomas M. Garrett, 86, passed away Tuesday at 11 a.m. at a Sherman hospital, just 26 hours after he was struck by a car as he crossed the street in Savoy. Funeral services were not complete but will probably be held at the Savoy Methodist church Wednesday.

Mr. Garrett was born March 4, 1858, in Tennessee. He was married to Miss Florence Killman Jan. 28, 1889. His wife died March 23, 1912. He came to Texas in 1882 and to Savoy in 1912, where he has since resided. He was a retired farmer and served as city marshal for 10 years.
