records.text:
L. A. Brown, Retired Farmer, Dies in Sherman

SAVOY — Funeral services will be held Thursday in the Savoy Church of Christ at a time to be announced for L. A. Brown, 81, a retired Savoy farmer who died in the home of a son, Paul Brown, 811 S. Walnut St., Sherman, Wednesday at 9:15 a.m.

Burial will be in Sunnyside Cemetery, near Savoy, directed by Earnheart Funeral Home of Whitewright.

Survivors are his wife; two other sons, Berry Brown of Wichita Falls and Jack Brown of Savoy; two sisters, Mrs. Lula Mitchell of Dallas and Mrs. Frank Ponder of Arkansas.

records.title: Savoy Funeral Held Today For Mrs. Wrenn
records.text:
Savoy Funeral Held Today For Mrs. Wrenn

SAVOY. — Funeral services for Mrs. R. W. Wrenn, 62, who died at her home in Savoy Thursday, were conducted in the Savoy Baptist Church today at 3 p.m. with the Rev. Claude Johnston of Sherman, the Rev. J. D. Flemings of Whitewright and the Rev. Everett Springfield of Savoy officiating.

Mrs. Wrenn, a life-long resident of Savoy, was ill for two years preceding her death. She was born in Savoy in 1885, and was married to Mr. Wrenn in 1907. She was a Sunday School teacher for several years in the Baptist Church of which she was a member.

She is survived by her husband, two brothers, Allen T. Short of Whitewright; G. M. Short of Savoy; two nieces and a nephew.

Burial, directed by Earnheart Funeral Home of Whitewright and Strickland Funeral Home of Savoy, was in Sunside Cemetery, Savoy.

Active pallbearers were members of her Sunday School class, Jack Morgan, Pierce Bibby, Joe Lynn Dodson, Newt Morgan, A. C. Lyles, and Frank Morgan. Honorary pallbearers were other members of the class.

records.title: Savoy Newspaper Publisher Many Years Dies At 72
records.text:
MRS. J. B. MAY

Savoy Newspaper Publisher Many Years Dies At 72

SAVOY—Mrs. J. B. May, 72, former correspondent for the Sherman Democrat and publisher of the Savoy Star for 41 years, died at the family home at Savoy Saturday at 9:25 a. m. She was a native of Van Alstyne. She had been ill for two years.

Funeral arrangements are incomplete, but will probably be held Tuesday, pending the arrival of a sister, Mrs. M. Henry Gant of Miami, Fla.

The service is scheduled for the Savoy Church of Christ with Robert D. Bankes, Church of Christ minister of Sherman, conducting the service. Burial will be in Sunnyside Cemetery, Savoy, directed by Earnheart-Strickland Funeral Home.

Mrs. May was born May 4, 1878, a daughter of the late Mr. and Mrs. T. P. Buford. She was married to T. E. Arterberry. He died in 1925. On May 31, 1932, she was married to J. B. May. She attended Haskell College at Savoy and published the Savoy Star from April 1902 until June, 1943.

She had a dress, hat and gift shop at Savoy. At one time, Mrs. May taught in the Savoy schools. She was a past secretary of the Savoy College Ex-Students Association, and officer and leader in the Civil League and was a member of the Church of Christ.

Survivors include her husband, J. B. May of Savoy; one sister, Mrs. Gant; two nieces, Mrs. Roy Booth of Waco, Mrs. Cy Kaulback of San Antonio; a great-niece, Miss Martha Frances Booth of Waco, one nephew, Buford Penlace of Dallas; one step-daughter, Mrs. O. L. Jones of Whitewright and three grandchildren.

records.title: Leslie Reece Swinney obituary
records.text:
Leslie Reece Swinney

SAVOY — Funeral servie will be held at 10 a.m. Wednesday in Savoy Church of Christ for Leslie Reece Swinney, 52, a native of Savoy and former resident of Denison, who died June 9 in Chicago, Ill.

C. D. Price, Church of Christ minister, will conduct the service. Burial will be in Sunnyside Cemetery, near Savoy, directed by Johnson-Moore Funeral Home, Denison.

Born May 5, 1905, Mr. Swinney was a son of the late Mr. and Mrs. John Swinney. In May 1925 he married Miss Lorene Paige in Denison. He was an automobile mechanic and had worked in Chicago for the last year.

Survivors are three daughters, Miss Beverly Swinney, Mrs. N. C. Spradlin and Mrs. O. C. Spradlin, all of Denison; two sisters, Mrs. M. E. Baldwin of Fulton, Ill., and Mrs. W. L. Wright of Savoy, and four grandchildren.

records.title: Short Illness Fatal To Mrs. W. T. Bibby
records.text:
Short Illness Fatal To Mrs. W. T. Bibby

SAVOY — Funeral services for Mrs. W. T. Bibby, 86, who died Tuesday in the home of her son, Pierce Bibby, after a week's illness, were to be held Wednesday at 2:30 p. m. in the Savoy Baptist Church, with burial in Sunnyside Cemetery.

Mrs. Bibby had lived in Savoy all her life, having been born here in 1867. She is survived by her husband, W. T. Bibby, three sons, S. A. Bibby, Kenneth Bibby and Pierce Bibby, all of Savoy; one daughter, Mrs. Laylah Baker of Savoy; one brother, C. C. Pierce of Lawrenceburg, Tenn., five grandchildren and two great grandchildren.

Pallbearers will be Earl Blakey, R. W. Wrenn, Doyle Withrow, Frank Baker, Ernest McCollum and Max Arterberry.

records.title: Willie Campbell Dies
records.text:
Willie Campbell Dies

SAVOY.—Funeral service will be held Thursday at 3 p.m. in the Savoy Church of Christ for Willie James Campbell, 68, Negro of Savoy. He died Monday in his home in Savoy after an illness of one year.

O. A. Ross, minister of the Church of Christ, will officiate. Burial will be in Savoy Cemetery, directed by Grayson Funeral Home.

Survivors are two daughters, one son and two grandchildren.

records.title: W. C. McLemore — business profile
records.text:
W. C. McLEMORE.

A few years ago W. C. McLemore went into the hardware business with only a small stock of goods. He soon built up a nice trade and in a short time he built a handsome brick with nearly three hundred feet of floor space. This building he filled from top to bottom with implements and vehicles, having sold in a job lot his shelf hardware. He has put out farming tools and buggies all over this country. So great has been his business during good crop years that many times buggies were never rolled into his house, but sold as soon as they were set up. This year has been more or less trying on all business, but Mr. McLemore has fared as well as anyone for he handles none but the best goods.

records.title: Savoy City Marshal Dies
records.text:
Savoy City Marshal Dies

SAVOY—William Hollingsworth, 59, Savoy city marshal and a native of Whitewright, died suddenly of a heart attack at 4:30 a. m. today at his home.

Funeral services will be held at 2 p. m. Thursday at the local Baptist Church with the Rev. Evert Springfield, pastor, officiating. Burial will be in Sunnyside Cemetery, directed by Strickland and Earnheart Funeral Home. Pallbearers will be K. J. Bibby, W. C. Beckham, M. O. Brooks, Earl Blakey, Duke Durrett and A. C. Lyles.

Mr. Hollingsworth was born at Whitewright Feb. 2, 1886. He and Miss Ivy Johnson were married at Savoy. He had been a member of the Baptist Church 41 years.

Surviving are his wife; a son, Leon Hollingsworth of Savoy; a sister, Mrs. J. W. Smith of Denison; his stepmother, Mrs. A. J. Hollingsworth of Denison and four stepbrothers.

records.title: Savoy Children Claim Record With 11 Living Grandparents / In Memory of Mrs. Lucy Durre
records.text:
ELEVEN LIVING GRANDPARENTS—When Jackie and Jean Moore, shown sitting in their parents' laps, call for "grandfather" or "grandmother," they never know who or how many will answer. They are shown here with their 11 living grandparents, 10 of whom reside in Savoy. They are shown with (front row) Mrs. C. H. Moore, paternal grandmother; J. C. Moore, father; Mrs. J. C. Moore; Jean Moore; Evert Burris; maternal grandmother; (middle row) Mrs. Joe Burris, great-grandmother; Mrs. Mollye Burt, great-grandmother; Mrs. John Moore, great-grandmother; Mrs. E. T. Lawrence, great-grandmother; E. T. Lawrence, great-grandfather; (back row) Evert Burris, grandfather; C. H. Moore, grandfather; Joe Burris, great-grandfather; and John Moore, great-grandfather.

Savoy Children Claim Record
With 11 Living Grandparents

By ELIZABETH LARGE

SAVOY.—Jackie and Jean Moore, son and daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Moore, believe they have more grandparents than any other children in this area. They top the list with five grandfathers and six grandmothers, with a total of 11 in Savoy.

Jackie will be four years old and Jean will have her second birthday July 15. Recently they had them all together for the first time in the home of Mr. and Mrs. E. T. Lawrence, great-grandparents.

Their mother is the former Miss Mildred Burris, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Evert Burris of Savoy. Before her marriage to J. C. Moore on Dec. 27, 1914, in Randolph. She was born in Huntsville, Tenn. Her mother, Mrs. Mollye Burt of Randolph, who was Miss Mollye Price before her marriage to W. M. Burt on Oct. 15, 1891, in Tennessee. She was born in Hillboro, Tenn. on July 22, 1865, and moved to Randolph 45 years ago. Mr. Burris is the son of Mr. and

Mrs. Joe Burris of Savoy. He was born in Hidalgo, Ky., and has a twin brother, Aaron, of Savoy.

Mr. and Mrs. Joe Burris are the oldest of the group and have been married a few months longer than any of the other couples. Mr. Burris was born on Oct. 15, 1870, in Gray Creek, Ky. He was a railroad employee for 22 years, then retired and engaged in farming several years before moving to Savoy 11 years ago.

Mrs. Joe Burris was Miss Florence B. Murphy before her marriage to Mr. Burris on Nov. 17, 1891, in Hidalgo, Ky. She was born July 10, 1873, in Humble, Ky.

The children's father, J. C. Moore, is the oldest son of Mr. and Mrs. C. H. Moore. He is employed as storekeeper at Perrin Field. He came to Savoy 21 years ago with his parents. His mother is the former Lula Williams. C. H. Moore was married to Mr. Moore on Nov. 23, 1920, in Bells. Mrs. Moore's mother, Mrs. E. T. Lawrence, was Miss Lula Williams before her marriage to Mr. Lawrence on March 3, 1895, at Tom Bean. She was born June 6, 1875, in Farmington, Tenn. Mr. Lawrence

was born May 4, 1874, in Okaloosa, Ky. He is a retired farmer. The couple moved to Savoy one year ago.

C. H. Moore is the son of Mr. and Mrs. John A. Moore of Savoy. He was born in Bells. He is employed as a barber in Bells. Like Mr. Burris, he also has a twin brother, Clarence, of Denison. His mother was Miss Jessye Kate Mathews before her marriage to Mr. Moore on Dec. 31, 1893, in Bells. She was born March 15, 1874, in Lynnville, Tenn.

Mr. Moore was born May 18, 1873, in Culleoka, Tenn. He was engaged in stock raising before selling his farm north of Bells and moving to Savoy.

In Memory of
Mrs. Lucy Durre

Born July 24, 1877
Died August 22, 1957

Officiating Ministers
Rev. Clifford Longino
Rev. W. A. Rudd

Interment, Sunnyside Cemetery
August 23, 1957

records.title: John Durretts Are Oldest Couple Residing At Savoy
records.text:
PIONEERS AT SAVOY—First couple at Savoy from the Standpoint of age and length of married life are Mr. and Mrs. John Durrett, who have been married 62 years and have resided in Savoy since 1889. (Herald photo.)

John Durretts Are Oldest Couple Residing At Savoy

Herald News Service)

SAVOY.—Mr. and Mrs. John Durrett have the honor of holding the first place in Savoy as to their age and the length of marriage.

Mrs. Durrett celebrated her 86th birthday April 3, and her 62nd wedding anniversay last Dec. 18. She is a native of Kentucky, and was born near Greensburg on April 3, 1861. The couple resided in Kentucky about five years before coming to Savoy to make their home. She was Miss Fannie Robinson before her marriage. She had two sisters, but no brothers. Her mother was Mrs. Mary Teresa Robinson, and made her home with the Durett family. She died in 1925 in Savoy at the age of 87.

Mr. Durrett will celebate 87th birthday Sept. 7. He als a native of Kentucky. He was born in 1860, near Campbellesville, Taylor[?] County, Kentucky. He came to Texas the first time with his brother, the late Jim Durrett, in 1881, making the trip in a wagon. The trip took 36 days. They encountered all the hardships of the pioneer travel.

His parents, the late Dr. and Mrs. Joel Durrett, joined them in Savoy later, bringing with them the family of two other brothers, the late Bill and the late Ed[?] Durrett, and five sisters, Mrs. Lily King of Dallas, Mrs. Sue Pedigo of Dallas, and Mrs. Pink Davis of Wichita Falls, and the late Mrs. Hattie Simmons and the late Mrs. Sally McQueen.

Dr. Durrett practiced medicine in Savoy and the surrounding communities until a short time before his death at the age of [illegible]. Mrs. Durrett died at the age of [illegible]. The couple lived to see all their children past middle-nine were living at the [illegible] their mother's death.

Mr. and Mrs. Durrett have their home in Savoy since[?] with the exception of two[?] they resided in Gunter. M[?] rett owned and operated [illegible] ton gin for several years [illegible] engaged in farming before [illegible]

The couple have two so[?] mie Durrett of Post, Te[?] Herbert Durrett of Sherm[?] two daughters, Mrs. Ella Hood of Fort Worth, and [illegible] esa Morgan of Savoy, th[?] daughters, Miss Maxine [illegible] of Post, Miss George An[?] of Savoy, and Mrs. Mar[?] Hood Berry of Fort W[?] one grandson, Thomas Mu[?] of Grand Prarie and t[?] grand children.

records.title: Clyde Blakey — obituary
records.text:
Clyde Blakey

SAVOY — Funeral will be held at 2 p.m. Thursday at the First Methodist Church here for Clyde Blakey, 67, who died at his home here early today. Interment will be in the Sunnywide Cemetery under the direction of Earnheart Funeral Home of Whitewright.

Blakey was born Nov. 5, 1898 in Fannin County and married Lera Nix Nov. 23, 1937 at Ector. He was a retired farmer and a Methodist.

Surviving is his wife; a brother, James of Savoy; and a sister, Mrs. Ina Elk of Savoy.

records.title: James Blakey Dies Saturday
records.text:
James Blakey Dies Saturday

SAVOY (Spl.) — James T. Blakey, 72, of Savoy, died Saturday morning, Feb. 26, 1966, at 11:10 o'clock in a Bonham hospital.

Funeral services will be held Sunday afternoon in the Pentacostal Faith church in Savoy at 2:30 o'clock. The pastor, the Rev. Cecil Watson, assisted by the Rev. J. D. Flanagan of Sherman, will officiate. Earnheart Funeral home of Whitewright will direct interment in Sunnyside cemetery at Savoy.

A retired farmer and member of the Pentacostal church, Mr. Blakey was born Jan. 3, 1894, at Whitewright, and was the son of the late Robert and Rebecca Blakey. He married Miss Lizzey Burris Nov. 12, 1916 at Savoy.

Survivors include his widow of the home in Savoy; two sons, Robert Blakey of Wylie and Joe Lee Blakey of Maysville, Okla.; a daughter, Mrs. D. B. Withrow of Garland; a sister, Mrs. Ina Elk of Savoy; 15 grandchildren and nine great grandchildren.

records.title: Savoy Woman Passes 81st Anniversary
records.text:
Savoy Woman
Passes 81st
Anniversary

SAVOY—The 81st birthday of Mrs. L. A. Brown was celebrated at her Savoy home Tuesday. Mrs. Brown, who was very active until stricken with paralysis in June of 1945, was born in Alabama in 1870 and married Mr. Brown in 1908 at Ector.

Before the stroke, Mrs. Brown had been very active, looking after all the household duties as well as raising turkeys and chickens and tending her garden.

Being a wheelchair patient for a number of years has not kept Mrs. Brown from pursuing a natural talent for painting. In earlier years she worked with oils, but at present has been using crayons. Mrs. Brown is also known for her beautiful needlework, at present being occupied with difficult designs on guest towels that prove a tedious procedure for a person using two hands and looking almost impossible for one with the use of only one hand.

Mr. and Mrs. Brown live alone. He handles most of the house work and cares for her with the aid of a daughter-in-law, Mrs. Paul Brown.

records.title: Savoy Man Dies Three Days After His Wife
records.text:
Savoy Man Dies Three Days After His Wife

(Herald News Service)

SAVOY—Funeral services for C. H. Booth, 79, were held at 3:30 p.m. today just two days after the burial of his wife on Tuesday. He died Wednesday at 9:15 p.m. at his home in Savoy from a heart ailment. Interment was at Sunnyside Cemetery with Earnheart-Strickland in charge.

Robert D. Bankes, minister of a Sherman Church of Christ, Ralph Edmonson, minister of the Savoy Church of Christ, and the Rev. Baxter Bryant, pastor of the Bells Methodist Church, officiated. Pallbearers were E. L. McCollum, R. W. Wrenn, Earl Blakey, Ralph Duncan, O. L. Baker and W. H. Blount.

Booth was born Nov. 26. 1870, in Virginia. On Oct. 21, 1894, he married Miss Sarah Jane Hanna in Denison. He was a farmer and had been in the trucking business. He was a member of the Savoy Church of Christ.

Mrs. Booth had been in ill health for some time and died at 6:30 a.m. Monday.

Survivors include three sons, Roy Booth of Waco, Ray Booth of Bells and E. H. Booth, Jr., of Savoy; three daughters Mrs. Carl Orndorff of Savoy, Mrs. Dan Sweeney of Savoy and Mrs. Roy Stephens of Sherman; two brothers, W. F. Booth and Jim Booth, both of Virginia; six grandchildren, and three great-grandchildren.

records.title: Tiny Savoy Doing He Man's Job In Giving Men For Uncle Sam
records.text:
Tiny Savoy Doing He Man's Job In Giving Men For Uncle Sam

BY JOHN CLIFT
(Herald State Editor)

SAVOY— One of the smallest towns in North Texas is supplying one of the largest amounts of manpower for the armed forces in the nation. On a percentage basis, that is.

The latest head count in Savoy listed the population at 312. As of next week when Lewis Beckham reports to the air force at Lackland in San Antonio, some 33 Savoy residents will be currently in service.

"Somebody ought to give us an 'E' for excellence in supplying men for the armed forces," said Postmaster Claud Strickland, who, as postmaster, keeps probably as close a watch as anyone on men's immediate families.

Of Savoy men in service, two have been killed, both in the early days in service in Africa. They were Peter Farr, Pan Seals, and Wirt Terry.

However, another died overseas in World War I. He was Isaac Le Large, who succumbed to pneumonia.

SON-IN-LAWS, TOO

Several families have two or more sons in service and two families with one have additional male members 1-A.

Mrs. Fae Miller has two sons and a son-in-law in uniform. Sgt. Bill is in the air force at Laredo and Capt. Sam is now on his third overseas hitch, this time in Japan. The son-in-law is Joe Bailey Springfield, who also is in Japan.

The two Hensley boys, Eugene, who is in Germany and Henry, now stationed at Camp Dafter[?], are also in service. They are sons of Mr. and Mrs. Lester Hensley.

A son-in-law, Maj. Foy L. Shoemate, is serving in Japan.

Another brother combine is Harry and Jimmy Arterbery, both serving in Japan. They are the sons of Bob Elk.

One of the questions asked most frequently in Savoy is "when is the Korean war going to end?" It is asked not only by parents, but by everyone. When you take 33 servicemen out of a town of 312, you know that most families in the town are directly affected.

The Savoy boys have seen the world. Postmaster Strickland handles letters from all over the globe. "They've been in Greenland and Alaska," he said. "They have sent silk from China, cameos from Italy, and perfume from France, India, Germany, England, any place that America has sent troops a Savoy boy has been there," Strickland added.

Airman Max E. Arterbery's last letter to his parents, Mr. and Mrs. Max Arterbey, came from Matador Island in the Pacific. Earl Blakey, son of Earl Blakey. Is in the air force and is making some of the training flight over Korea.

Bascom Blount, son of Mr. and Mrs. Willie Blount, isn't far from home at Caswell AFB, N. C. Often, however, he frequently hops "almost around the world" as a B-36 crewman.

Naturally, a lot of the Savoy men are still getting stateside duty

[Photo caption 1:] ANOTHER TRIO IN UNIFORM—Mr. and Mrs. Lester Henry, and their son-in-law, Maj. Foy L. Shoemate, Henry, an dtheir son-in-law, Maj. Foy L. Shoemate.

[Photo caption 2:] THREE IN SERVICE—Mrs. Fae Miller straightens the photos on top of the piano of her two sons, Sam and Bill and her son-in-law, Joe Bailey Springfield.

records.title: Third Place Winners in Southwest AAU Tourney
records.text:
Third Place Winners in Southwest AAU Tourney

Shown above is the Savoy girls' basketball team, which was eliminated in the semi-finals of the Southwestern AAU cage tournament at Celeste. Prior to their entry in the AAU tournament they were undefeated in 34 games this year, and lost only one contest last season by a one-point margin. Shown in the picture, from left to right, standing: Johnnie B. Wood, Ola Lea Hutchins, Billy Brown, Tiny Bibby, Joyce Sharp, Mary Lou Carruth, Tommie Smith and Irva Fae Miller. Front row, kneeling: Lena Fay Winkler, Coach Joe Lynn Dodson and Peggy O'Neal.

records.title: Top Student — Tiny Bibby, valedictorian of Savoy High School
records.text:
Top Student
Tiny Bibby, 17, has been named valedictorian of the Savoy High School senior class with a four-year average of 96.28. She is the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. B. P. Bibby. Runnerup in scholastic average is Helen Horn, the salutatorian and daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Lee Horn. Third high was Tommy Smith with 91.9. She is the daughter of Mrs. Emma Smith of Savoy.

records.title: C. C. GLASS
records.text:
C. C. GLASS.

Savoy has an up-to-date confectionery and cold drink stand owned and operated by C. C. Glass. He carries a nice line of fresh confections and drinks and through the summer he has a cream parlor[.]

records.title: Everybody In Savoy — basketball district title
records.text: EVERYBODY IN SAVOY went to Bonham to see the boys basketball team win the district 45-B title for the first time in history, said Postmaster Claud Strickland. And Strickland, a boys fan of 25 years standing, says that the fans will go to Kilgore if Savoy can get past Quitman. "There will be some present anyway, but not the mob that will show if they win," he said.

records.title: R. S. Blakey — obituary
records.text:
R. S. Blakey

Funeral services for Robert S. Blakey, 71, who died at his home three miles north of Savoy Sunday following several weeks illness, were held at the Methodist church at Savoy Monday at 2 p. m., the Rev. E. J. Holifield officiating. Burial was in Sunnyside cemetery. Nephews were pallbearers.

Mr. Blakey was born in Grayson county February 2, 1870, son of Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Blakey. He was married March 2, 1890 to Rebecca Wrenn. He had lived near Savoy for many years.

Surviving are his widow; two daughters, Mrs. George Short and Mrs. R. C. Elk of Savoy; two sons, J. T. and C. A. Blakey of Savoy; a sister, Mrs. Fannie Badgett of Whitewright; a brother, T. E. Blakey of Savoy; 14 grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.

records.title: Blakey Rites Are Held At Savoy Church Monday
records.text:
Blakey Rites Are Held At Savoy Church Monday

[The Herald News Service.]

SAVOY, July 22.—S. R. Blakey, 71, died Sunday after an extended illness at his home in the Elizabeth Grove community. Funeral services were held Monday afternoon at the Methodist Church here with the Rev. E. J. Holifield officiating. Burial was in Sunnyside Cemetery here.

He was born March 12, 1870, in Grayson county, son of Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Blakey. He was married March 2, 1890, to Rebecca Wrenn. He had lived near Savoy for many years.

Surviving are his widow; two daughters, Mrs. George Short and Mrs. R. C. Elk of Savoy; two sons, J. T. and C. A. Blakey of Savoy; a sister, Mrs. Fannie Badgett of Whitewright; a brother, T. E. Blakey of Savoy; 14 grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.

records.title: Dr. W. S. Wrenn Dies at Home in Margaret
records.text:
DR. W. S. WRENN
DIES AT HOME
IN MARGARET

Funeral Services Held
At Margaret Monday
Afternoon

records.title: Clarence Melugin Jr. and Clarence Rino — military service
people: Mr. and Mrs. S. R. Melugin
Mr. and Mrs. C. R. Melugin
Mr. and Mrs. S. E. Rino
records.text:
CLARENCE MELUGIN JR. (left) and CLARENCE RINO are cousins and were born in Savoy, grandsons of Mr. and Mrs. S. R. Melugin of Port Arthur.

Clarence Melugin Jr., son of Mr. and Mrs. C. R. Melugin of Dallas, is an instructor at Jones field, Bonham. He is a graduate of a Dallas high school, attended Southern Methodist university and completed his flying course at Randolph field.

Clarence Rino, petty officer first class, son of Mr. and Mrs. S. E. Rino of Savoy, recently spent a short furlough with his parents and his grandmother came from Port Arthur to visit him. He is a 1938 graduate of Savoy high school and immediately enlisted in the navy. He served three years in China, returned home and entered training at San Diego, Calif., and has been on a submarine destroyer in the Pacific for 19 months. This was his first visit home.

records.title: Pvt. Joe Lee Blakey Stationed At Howze
records.text:
Pvt. Joe Lee Blakey Stationed At Howze

Camp Howze is the army home of Pvt. Joe Lee Blakey, son of Mr. and Mrs. Tom Blakey of Savoy. Young Blakey, who was 20 years old July 28, was inducted Jan. 26 of this year at Camp Wolters and later was assigned to Camp Howze. He was a student at Savoy High School at the time of his induction.

His brother and sister, Robert and Mabelle Blakey, live at the family home in Savoy.

records.title: Savoy Farmer Dies at 82
records.text:
Savoy Farmer Dies at 82

S. S. BAKER.

SAVOY, Texas.—Sam S. Baker, 82, died suddenly of a heart attack at his home here Saturday evening. He had been in ill health about three years, but was feeling better than usual the past few days. Funeral services were held Monday afternoon at the Methodist church, conducted by the Rev. W. H. Vail of Van Alstyne and the Rev. Roy Bagley, local pastor.

Interment was in Sunnyside, directed by Earnheart-Strickland. Pallbearers were nephews of the by, Otis Baker, Bob Baker and Ray Lewis.

Born in Marshfield, Mo., March 1, 1861, he was a son of John and Mary Baker. He was married to Miss Jessie Brake on Nov. 9, 1887, and the couple came to Texas in a covered wagon in 1888, settling at Weston. They moved to Savoy in 1904 and have resided here since that time. He was engaged in farming until his retirement about three years ago, at which time he purchased a house in Savoy and moved into it.

Survivors are his wife; a son, Elmer Baker of El Segundo, Calif.; two daughters, Mrs. Ed Reed of Savoy and Mrs. Alta Bell of Ector; seven grandchildren and three great grandchildren; a brother, A. M. Baker of Marshfield, and a sister, Mrs. Martha Hargess of Waurika, Okla.

Out-of-town relatives attending the funeral were Mrs. E. T. Williams and Miss Alice Brake of Springfield, Mo., Mrs. Hargess of Waurika and Sgt. and Mrs. G. L. Reed of Camp Hearne.

records.title: Roy Gist obituary
records.text:
Roy Gist.

SAVOY, Texas.—Funeral services were held Tuesday afternoon in Paris for Roy Gist, 55, native of Savoy, who was killed early Monday in an automobile accident in Pittsburg. The body was returned to Savoy for burial in Sunnyside cemetery.

Mr. Gist, who owned a feed store in Paris, had gone to Pittsburg for a load of hay and had stopped at a store for a drink when his truck was struck from the rear by an automobile. Having just stepped from the truck he was knocked to the ground by a part of the hay rack and was run over by the automobile. He died instantly.

Son of Mr. and Mrs. G. N. Gist, pioneers of this county, he was born and reared in Savoy. He was married to Miss Ethel Alston of Ector and for the past 12 years the family has resided in Paris.

Survivors are his wife; four children, Oleah Gist of Talco, Mrs. Leslie Counts and G. A. Gist of Tyler and Morrell Gist of the home address; two sisters, Mrs. Sam Martin of Shawnee, Okla., and Mrs. Essie Woodward of Wolfe City; and a brother, E. N. Gist of Bonham.

T. P. BUFORD.

About fifteen years ago, T. P. Buford opened up a little stock of groceries and confectioneries in a frame building on Water street. D. T. McMAHON.

Our little write-up would not be complete without including D. McMahon, grain and coal deale[r]. records.title: W. H. DAVIS
records.text:
W. H. DAVIS.

It has been said that there is a grocery store for every family in town. While that is an exaggeration, the town has a goodly number of first class groceries. Among this number is W. H. Davis. He has been here only a few years and his stock is new and clean, hence, he holds his customers by giving them pure goods and the newest things on the market. Mr. Davis is also the city tinner and hardware dealer, and the same straightforward methods p[rev]ail in these departments, and his attentive clerk assists him greatly in keeping up his trade. Mr. Davis is an old [t]ime Savoy boy and has such a [ple]asant disposition that he wins [cus]tomers and holds them.

records.title: Mrs. Jacky Wrenn — pioneer history
records.text:
MRS. JACKY WRENN.

Away back in the long ago, there lived a family of Smiths. There are many Smiths, but this particular Thomas Smith and wife lived in Pennsylvania and on Jan. 19, 1832, a bright little daughter was born to them. It is to this daughter, Jacky Smith, that we want to direct your attention for a while. This girl grew to womanhood and married James M. Wrenn in Stockton, Missouri. To this union were born two boys and three girls, and all went well with this happy family until the cruel hand of war in[vaded—] the ho[me and] led the father to the fro[nt to fi]ght for the cause he believ[ed] to be right. This left Mrs. Wrenn with a battle to fight also[,] that of rearing her little childre[n] and providing them with the necessaries of life. This was no easy matter and many times while brooding over her cares and thinking of her companion, not knowing whether he were dead or alive, she could not keep the tears from coursing down her cheeks. A few months before the war closed, she, with about a dozen other women decided that by coming to Texas they might be nearer their loved ones and, perhaps, see or hear from them often[er]. So they loaded their families and provisions in their ox wagons, and started on their long journey, without a man in the crowd.

After about [two] months out, they landed in F[annin] county and Mrs. Wrenn stopped on the old Mallory farm—known in later years as the Jo[e] Pritchett farm.

In about six months the war closed, her hus[band] came home and they mo[ved to] their farm just south of Savoy there Mr. Wrenn died in 1888.

records.title: Bank — Farmers Deposit Bank / First National Bank
records.text:
BANK.

A few years ago the citizens of Savoy and community put their surplus capital together and organized the Farmers Deposit Bank. It was a paying business from the start and a few years ago the capital was increased to $25,000 and a charter secured for the First National Bank. The deposits were reasonably good and business increased under the management of E. T. Cook and each year the stockholders have realized a divi dend on their investment. Last year Mr. Cook was promoted to the president's chair and J. B. King elected cashier. The bank has been a great help to the town and in fact few small towns can boast of a bank so good. It stood firmly through the money panic and the last statement showed it to be in good shape.

records.title: Savoy Cyclone — 1879/1880, from Fannin County Folk and Fact, 1977, Page 43
records.text:
that our men had and told them to go home and 'me ketch you again me shoot you.' Our men said they were very glad to get off that easy. They thought the Indians would kill them. Most of them had to walk home. After that our men never went to the Plains any more. They stayed in camp here until the government sent some troops to Texas and they built a fort where Fort Worth now is. After that we were not bothered much with the wild Indians.

"I will now give you the names of men that settled here in 1836: Judge Inglish, John Hart, Gavelin, Merfill, Cliff, Logan, Heath, Quillen, Joe Swagaty, Joe Sowell, Thomas Journey, Westbrook, Willis Boon, Damron and Carr."

"Thus, I have given you some of the worst troubles we had in the early days."   BY ANDERSON ROWLETT

SAVOY CYCLONE — 1879 / 1880

"After a residence of five years in Denison, I moved to Savoy, a station on the Transcontinental line, 11 miles from Bonham, and I was in the mercantile business there when the cyclone struck in 1879 or 1800. I retired early on the night of the cyclone which came at about 10 o'clock. Before I dosed off to sleep I cautioned my wife, who was in the room with a glass oil lamp in her hand. I told her she was liable to set the house on fire. The next thing I knew I went out of bed as if by a force not my own and fell sprawling on the floor. What appeared to be a terrific hailstorm was raging. Hailstones weighing ten pounds each were bombarding the house. I opened the door and at once realized that tremendous mischief was afoot. By the incessant flashes of lightning which made a continuous light, I saw the railroad station vantish, perceived that the business district of the town was bare of houses and realized that what I took to be hailstones striking the house were the flying shreds and fragments of demolished buildings. The wind was so strong that I could not shut the door. I called Harry Naylor my nephew to assist me. The blow was all over in a minute or two. Then came a veritable deluge of rain, a regular waterspout. We could hear on all sides cries of men, women and children in distress.

"Going to the rescue Harry and I found the cyclone had made a path about 250 yards in width through the town, carrying away every business house and every dwelling in its path except mine. We began to pick up the injured and to carry them into my house. Before long people of the town living outside the path of the storm came to our assistance. We worked all night, but were unable to afford much relief. There were two physicians in the town and one of them was so old and feeble he was of little use. It was not until the next day that relief trains came from Sherman, Denison and Bonham bringing surgeons and supplies. Men, women and children with fractured limbs and other injuries went all that time without surgical attention.

"Eleven persons were killed by the cyclone and five others died later of injuries, making a total of 16. I do not remember how many were injured. The population was about 300. Of the dead and injured, not one had a stitch of clothing on and many who escaped injury found themselves naked in the street. The rescuers wrapped the injured in bed sheets or quilts as they picked them up. Strange as it may seem, I have no recollection of the funeral services that must have been held during the two or three days following the calamity. A situation such as we had that night is calculated to open new founts of emotion in a man. If you ever go through a cyclone, the fear of another one goes ghosting through your head every time the wind begins to blow hard."   BY W. S. ADAIR AND J. M. NAYLOR

MORGAN FARM

I first heard of the Morgan Farm from my father. Dad helped G. W. "Will" Morgan make a two-team crop on the farm at Riverby on the Red River in the late 1800's. Morgan had just given up a law practice in Honey Grove to settle on 200 acres of land he inherited. Within his lifetime he would accumulate 10,000 acres in the Riverby area and employ hundreds of people, but for that first crop, Morgan and Dad each worked a team of ponies to work the ground that was cleared for cropping. Part of the 200 acres was in heavy timber.

records.title: Fannin County Folk and Fact, Page 60 — Education / Fannin County Schools 1838-1900
records.text:
EDUCATION

While there was no organized system of education in Texas when the first settlers came to Fannin County, all the families knew the value of education and worked to provide some sort of academic training for their children. The first schools were neighborhood schools, established by churches or people in the communities and parents usually paid a great deal of the credit must go to local men who located school, sometimes several families joined together to hire a teacher to educate their children. Many times the teacher boarded with the families and received their pay in farm produce.

In many villages school buildings were simple log cabins usually with split-log seats, slab tables and dirt floors. Even the larger and better schools had poor equipment and the length of school days and school terms varied depending on weather, the threat of Indian attack, or the planting and harvesting when the children were needed at home.

A typical school day was spent learning the bedrock three R's — reading, 'riting, 'rithmetic — with an occasional subject as history, geography, and such subjects as art. Great importance was placed on repetition and memory work. Students recited their lessons aloud in unison. The rod was a widely accepted educational practice by educational axiom practiced by every teacher of the day, and the importance placed by every child switch was very much a part of the normal day as were the grueling spelling bees and debates during school hours.

"It is to their undying credit," the early historian continued, "that the Indians gathered no scalps, at least while Savoy College students were around and at least while Savoy College graduates went out into the world and became doctors, lawyers, judges, preachers, teachers and businessmen. Several even became missionaries and taught in the Orient."

A state school system was tried in 1876 when counties were expected to provide facilities and assume local control and even to sell them. With localized control of schools

the community system came into existence and Texas at last provided a free public school system. No sooner had the system been put into effect than it was found to be faulty. By 1882 the average school term for most East Texas counties was 3-8 months and few school districts had been able to comply. Despite these shortcomings in 1882 every county in Texas used this community school system for the public schools.

It was not until the reconstruction era that the community school of Texas lost its status as being the best method of reaching children and getting money for taxes ... may be used for ... buying school sites, buying, constructing and equipping school buildings, controls and clearly defined legislation which supported the laws operating only for rapid development of the public school system in Texas.

The strong determination and unselfish dedication of many Fannin County residents provided the children of the area with a community school system during Texas' early growing period. Without the advantages of organized public or private education, the people of Fannin County could not have progressed as did the rest of the county. Few counties could boast of the same number of educators and the same diversity of instruction as was offered or the quality of education as could Fannin County.

FANNIN COUNTY SCHOOLS 1838-1900

The first school in Fannin County was in a stable at Warpen, one of the first settlements in the county near Red River. The teacher, whose name is not known, looked around for a school and obtained permission from the owner of the stable to use it. The stable became a school building by moving the horses and cattle to the open air. The students sat on wooden legs in holes drilled in the rough side of the logs to form the seats. The seats had no backs, but pupils managed to stay on them. The teacher had twenty pupils from nine to fifteen with ten pupils. There is no record of how long it continued or if anyone ever learned anything of value from that school. The information about the first school was taken from a reminiscent article that appeared in the Paris, Texas, papers of the 1880s and 1890s.

Education for children and youth was carried on in numerous small schools from 1838 to 1876, generally with one teacher, until the late 1860's when several in different parts of the county were growing and were established.

A state school system was tried in 1876 when counties were expected to provide facilities and assume local control and even to sell them. With localized control of schools, communities in Fannin County became centers for private accommodation for the more advanced subjects such as Latin, Greek, philosophy and geography were taught compulsory were strictly enforced. Carlton College in Bonham and the Savoy Male College were the best of the district's two leading colleges in the area.

FANNIN COUNTY SCHOOLS

The first school in Fannin was in a stable at Warpen, one of the first settlements in the county near Red River. Carlton College in Bonham, established in 1867 in Bonham by Charles Carlton. During its operation, Carlton and one or two of his daughters made up the complete faculty with civic minded faculty with civic minded teachers at different times from year to year. As president of the college and for Pastor of the First Methodist Church, Carlton taught Latin, Biblical Literature, Mathematics, Moral Philosophy, Latin, Biblical Literature, Mathematics, Moral Philosophy, and also taught drawing and painting. His daughter, Sallie Joe, taught music and a variety of other subjects.

The influence of this college was profound. The girls were to wear a uniform of simple navy blue material and at Commencement they were to wear white muslin dresses. The influence of this college which operated until about 1891 educated and influenced and talented women in the county for two generations.

records.title: Fannin County Folk and Fact, Page 61 — Savoy College and private schools
records.text:
In 1881 the Masonic Female Institute was established in Bonham. The Masonic Lodge had sponsored schools during the years since it had begun in the 1840's, both in Bonham and Honey Grove. The Institute was a school whose students not only from Bonham and the surrounding area, but the Carlton College of Honey Grove students attended as well as West Texas. Both of the girls' schools stressed classical education, emphasizing the academic and musical subjects.

The third private school in Bonham during this period was Fannin College, incorporated in 1883 for boys only. On the same campus was the Lyceum, which was the boys' auditorium, which was attended by boys and girls together until they reached a certain age. Boys who completed their studies at Lyceum were expected to continue at Fannin College or the neighboring Carlton College. The boys were expected to continue at Carlton College or similar institution.

One who attended the Lyceum School in the 1880's remembered about having a cistern on the yard of the junior who was in it. It was equipped with a large stove with pot-bellied stone burning coal. Sometimes the stove would smoke and the children would sleep or stay over it until the janitor could fix it. Lyceum was a two-story frame building with the recitation rooms downstairs and the ninth and tenth grades upstairs." This information is from an interview in the Bonham paper, November 17, 1952.

The purpose for which these schools were functioning is also an example of differentiation and integration of formal schooling in the region. In Ladonia there were three schools: Featherstone School of Dallas — an academic institution — which was boarding school. It made Ladonia a desirable place for settlers coming with their families. And after the Civil War, in 1909 Ladonia had a school called Farmers Improvement Society, which was an organization for the Black community.

During the 1850's the Masonic Lodge in Honey Grove opened convenient schools in an old Masonic Lodge building. They rented or owned a two-story building of the Methodist Church built the Paris District Honey Grove school and by 1885 had 8,000 books. Honey Grove continued to be used as a school even after lack of funds caused the closing of the Masonic Lodge facility. The Old Masonic Hall School was operated mainly as a boys' school. The school was a large private school for business, this building became part of the public schools. An Old Masonic Hall school was a large private school for accounting, bookkeeping, language and literature, civic selections, mathematical studies, shorthand and penmanship — "taking ad-vantages" of instrumental and vocal music.

This advertisement from the Dodd City High School:

"The course of study is thoroughly classical and practical. All pupils who desire to comply with state regulations must regularly attend. Pupils who have been irregular are not wanted at any terms."

1. From High School catalog of 1895-96 stated the regulations governing the pupils in the school: '1) There shall be no association of males and females. If the teachers see fit to suspend the rules. 2) Students are required to attend all exercises. No use of obscene language is forbidden. 4) Any student wilfully associated in the breaking of any rule or the school regulations shall be accounted accessory to the offender and shall be dealt with in the same as the offender. 5) There shall be no secret societies. 6) Students in the third year and above for any reason shall have their conditions will be dropped to the next lower grade.' "The grades in the English course were to be English in two classes — differential and integral calculus and mathematical astronomy. Four years of English were required of all students taking English courses. Texas and U.S. history, government and economics were required of all students along with a wide range of academic curriculum.

A boarding school, as well as a day school was Savoy Male and Female College, which came from the various parts of the county and from out of state. Medals were awarded for various accomplishments. A medal was awarded for spelling excellence during the session.

The Savoy Male and Female College influenced the lives and hundreds of young men and women during the years before. As required by the Lyceum School and the other private schools, it had periods of financial uncertainty. The years 1876-1895 saw the school in its greatest era of growth. From 1884-1895 Professor Halsell, the president, encouraged a closer relationship between the school and Indian Territory provided a means for the education of Choctaw and Chickasaw students enrolled in the school. In other boarding schools, Liberal subsidies of $20 per month were granted by the two main Indian nations — the Choctaw and Chickasaw tribes who were settled in southern Oklahoma. These subsidies made the school prosperous and self-supporting. The charter was obtained in 1880.

Private schools were conducted in numerous rural communities in the county, including Dodd City, Ladonia, Ravenna, Bells and Dial. Such schools were designed to give more advanced instruction at the rural level. Many had probably been established in the 1880's. Children in the rural communities were under the shared administration of the county judge, acting as the county superintendent of schools. A judge would be responsible for inspecting and certifying the credentials of the teachers and registering pupils. For the year 1885 a $5.30 per child apportionment was given to the total enrollment in county schools for six months. At one time there was a total of 172 rural schools in Fannin County and an additional 40 schools for the colored children. Many of these rural schools had one teacher with an average of about twenty children per pupil.

Many of the rural private schools in Fannin County during this period had full academic programs. The Savoy Male and Female College during its most prosperous years brought many young men and women to the West to obtain an education not available locally. It was one of the finest private schools for any capable, talented, well-educated persons in the late nineteenth century in Texas. Those who played piano or stringed instruments had full classes. Drawing, china painting, weaving and water colors were also offered.

for the school but with the death of the great man whom an institution had been built around, it was practically impossible to maintain the forward progress of the founder. In 1913 the school joined with Carr-Burdette College in Sherman, but this effort was abandoned in 1916 and the graduates of Carlton College were adopted into the alumni fellowship of Texas Christian University.   BY BARBARA C. JONES

SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE

Savoy Male and Female College was probably the first collegiate coeducational school in Texas to admit men and women to the same classes on the same academic standards. Founded in 1876 at Savoy, the college was chartered in 1880 by Robert R. Halsell, president, Lewis Holland, vice president and James L. German, Thomas Chenoweth and James Paxton, trustees. By 1885 the college was conferring B. S. and A. B. degrees. The A. B. degree required four years each of Latin, Greek and mathematics with courses in physiology, physics, chemistry, rhetoric and elocution. By 1887, 1888 enrollment was 66 with 102 and 133 pupils in the primary and preparatory departments. During the same years 44 Indian students, one of course came from across the Red River with federal funds for tuition.

Academic and social standards were strict with social contact between men and women students rigidly forbidden except on carefully chaperoned occasions. Extracurricular interests produced a dramatic club, debates and three literary societies, of which one published monthly "The Platonian Messenger", a combination literary magazine-newspaper.

The college building burned in 1890 and the school was not rebuilt until 1892. The founder is commemorated in the Halsell Memorial Gymnasium built for the Savoy public school through the Works Progress Administration funds in 1937. The Savoy Alumni Association, organized in 1937 with 128 members, has held annual reunions.

LADONIA MALE AND FEMALE INSTITUTE

Founded in 1860 by the Sister Grove Baptist Association comprised of 23 churches in seven counties, the Ladonia Male and Female Institute was organized in Ladonia instead of Bonham at the last minute because it offered a two-story building and more than $2,600 in donations. It then conducted a private school in the building and became the first principal with J. C. Averett becoming principal in 1861.

The school was moved in 1863 to a similar facility but soon closed because of inadequate enrollment. It was reopened by W. B. Featherstone in 1867 and returned to Ladonia in 1868. The school was finally closed in 1875 because of insufficient funding.

MASONIC FEMALE INSTITUTE

The Masonic Female Institute was the only institute or college in Fannin County devoted solely to the education of females. Operating during the late 1800's and located a half mile north of the courthouse in Bonham, the Institute was leased by the Constantine Lodge #13 to Professor E. H. Adams who was judged well qualified to educate, to discipline and to refine young women for the duties of home and society. S. D. Nunnelee, R. B. Scarborough, R. C. Thompson and J. A. Duncan were Masons serving on the committee which selected Adams. W. D. Allen presented J. A. Duncan as secretary; and J. W. Newman as treasurer. Primary courses included such subjects as reading, spelling, penmanship, primary arithmetic and geography. A preparatory course consisted of reading, spelling, penmanship, geography, English grammar and practical arithmetic. The collegiate course was divided into two departments: classical study and classical study. Collegiate departments cost $166 for boarding students and $41 for local students.

STEPHENSON SCHOOL

Among the many things connected with early history of Bonham is Stephenson school.

In the beginning it was organized as a private school and taught by Mrs. S. J. Stephenson in her home. The Stephensons had come to Bonham about 1884 from Lone Ridge, Arkansas and soon after their arrival Mr. Stephenson died leaving a widow and 6 children. About 1887 the widow erected a one room building on the front of her lot on south Main Street. The building is still standing at the south end of Main Street, having been remodeled and used as a residence. Inside the building the homemade desks seated two pupils, one large homemade blackboard was nailed across the east end of the building, which was heated by a woodburning stove in the center of the room. McGluffy's reader, Blue Back or Ray's arithmetic, Harvey's grammar and Rand McNally geography were the subjects taught.

About 1890 the school was incorporated into the public school system of Bonham and for awhile Vertus was the first superintendent. Classes from first through seventh grades were taught, but that soon changed as grades above third grade were transferred to a building called the college which was later named Duncan school. The older pupils who were transferred and later graduated with the 2nd graduating class of Bonham Public school in 1897 were Sophronia Bali, Clara Crittenden and Charlie Swope.

records.title: Upholstering, Scouting, Hobbies Of Space Scientist's Family
records.text:
Upholstering, Scouting, Hobbies Of Space Scientist's Family

By Audrey McAlister

Their dad's three weeks vacation is not a time for "all play" for the children of Mr. and Mrs. Jim Ralph Elk of Friendswood, near the NASA Space Center in Houston.

While visiting their grandparents, Mr. and Mrs. Jack Harden in Bonham, and their father's mother, Mrs. R. C. Elk in Savoy, they are helping their parents upholster their grandmother's overstuffed furniture. And they love every minute of it.

Elk, who is head of the Lu[nar Trajectories Studies at the Space Center], took up the hobby of upholstering as a family project, as he and his wife believe in children learning to work and he busy part of the time, and they also believe in their earning some of their spending money.

In "the hobby house" which they built on the back of their property in Friendswood, they have turned in many professional jobs and also used it to aid their neighbors in re-doing their furniture when their house flooded. A wedding present sofa which the family built from the oak frame to the complete cut velvet upholstery, was admired by a neighbor who offered them $1,000 for it—but it wasn't for sale.

Completing his eighth year with the Space Flight Center, Elk is a little at a disadvantage talking to a layman about his responsibilities as head of the Lunar Trajectories studies. Most of it is over their heads. He and his crew of 30 designed and mapped the mathematical procedures for certain very complicated trajectory developments for the lunar landings. They were completed and computer programmed months ahead of the launches. You can bet they were right there watching the launchings, orbits and landings in case they were needed and just wouldn't miss it for the world, as they are a part of "the team."

While growing up, he admits he never dreamed of an opportunity to be a part of the team at NASA. And he insists that it is really "a team effort." The past successes and those of the future depend upon the team of men collected from science, flight, engineering and ever[y] contractors, he says.

Elk also believes that some practical advantages will come to the United States. Some advantages have already shown the way to more explorations and benefits. He and the other key men involved in the program believe that, like all new ventures undertaken by man in exploration and discovery, time, effort, and enterprise will prove their worth in effort and expense in first hand knowledge of outer space for the future.

But when this physicist begins to talk about Scouting, he is almost as enthusiastic as he is about outer space!

He is a graduate of East Texas State University, where he earned both his B. S. and Masters in Physics. His wife is the former Anita Harden, daughter of the Jack Hardens and a 1953 graduate of Bonham high school. Before going with the [Space Center, he was involved in the development of cyrogenic aeronautical rocket engines for Lewis Research Institute in Cleveland, O.]

But, Scouting, now, that is another matter! As a Scout leader he speaks of taking the eldest son, James, canoeing down the Rio Grande river, he talks of camping trips, and all that Scouting involves. He points out with pride that James, 15, is an Eagle Scout, Lee, who is 12, is a First Class Scout, Leslie, 11, is in the Webelos, and Bruce, 8, is in the Cub Scouts. Denita, the only girl in the family, is six, and planning to be a Camp Fire Girl or Girl Scout.

James makes wooden antique purses and the whole family is also involved in making vinyl and other handbags. They have sold over 100 of the handbags already. Even the youngest child, Gary, almost 4, can pull pass tools and earns part of his allowance.

Living in the Houston, Galveston area, they also enjoy beach parties and are involved in the work of United Methodist church, and enjoy many other activities. This family practices and resists the "togetherness." They always visit in Bonham and Savoy during the Christmas and summer holidays.

records.title: Savoy Tornado of 1880
records.text:
Savoy tornado of 1880

By Allen Rich, with excerpts from the Bonham News and Holton Recorder-Tribute. May 29, 2026.

Savoy, Texas — In Savoy, they have a saying: "Twas in the year of 1880 on the 28th of May, that a tornado hit Savoy and blowed it all away."

At first, it sounded as though a train was approaching Savoy, Texas from the west; then it was the sheer bedlam of complete destruction as buildings were ripped apart and trees came crashing down.

It was 10 minutes past 10:00 p.m. on Friday, May 28, 1880 when a tornado brought death and devastation to Savoy, Texas.

It happened so quickly that the hotel keeper in Savoy said he reached for his pantaloons when he heard the cyclone approaching, but in what he described as five seconds of terror, the town was almost completely destroyed before he could even get them on.

Telegraph lines were down in Savoy. Word of the disaster reached Bonham three hours later when a train that passed through Savoy shortly after the tornado pulled into the Bonham depot at 1:00 a.m. Saturday; by daylight, the livery stables in Bonham were empty as people rushed to aid their neighbors in Savoy.

The Bonham News had this description:

"Savoy, a beautiful little town of about three or four hundred inhabitants, eleven miles west of this place on the Transcontinental Railroad, was literally swept from the earth by a cyclone at 10 minutes past 10 o'clock last Friday night. The cyclone was about 178 yards wide, striking the town a short distance southwest of where the post office used to be and passing centrally through the place, demolishing 40 houses, including every business house except one, killing nine persons and wounding 50 or 60 more."

In today's digitally connected world, it is hard to comprehend just how important trains and telegraph lines were for transportation and communication in 1880. The Bonham News article goes on to say:

"The first news of the catastrophe was brought by Maj. Hays and Charlie Blaire, passengers on the eastbound train that came through Savoy a few minutes after the cyclone was over. This train reached Bonham at about 1 o'clock, in a blinding rain, and, after getting telegraphic orders from Marshall, went on to Dodd City, 9 miles east, for an extra engine to go to the relief of Savoy. This engine, belonging to the dirt train, under Geo. B. Lee, waited some time at Dodd for orders, but getting none, pulled out anyhow. [A heroic action on the part of the conductor and deserving all praise, when we consider that it might have lost him his situation.]

Physicians, nurses, etc., from Bonham were waiting at the depot for the extra, the rain being too heavy for them to get through by other conveyance.

Finally, about 4 o'clock, the first extra carried the following physicians and nurses from this place to the relief of Savoy: Doctors Dabney, Martin, and Bacon Saunders, Mayor Lyday, J.P. Holmes, Emmett Peeler, John Agnew, B.S. Burton, W.G. Pierce, W.T. Hightower, White Ragsdale, F. Heunsch, Wirt Saunders, Ben Dyer, Jim Noble, Will Martin, Tom Kennedy, Everett Duncan, G.L. Anthony; also Dr. Wells and F. Caldwell of Dodd City.

This party reached Savoy about 5 o'clock. They were preceded possibly 15 minutes by Dr. Briggs and Dr. Foute of Bells.

By this time, doctors King, Steagall and Matthews, resident physicians of Savoy, with the assistance of the uninjured inhabitants, had found and extracated all the wounded except little Rilla Kerns, whom the wind had dropped 40 or 50 yards from any debris, so that she was not found till after daylight that morning. She was taken to the schoolhouse, with the other wounded, where she was attended to by doctors Bacon Saunders and J.S. Dorset.

The engine was sent back to Bonham at once for ice, medicines, provisions, clothing, etc., and had made two trips before anybody arrived from Sherman or Denison. We give these two cities credit for acting as promptly as possible but by the time their trains got in, there was little left to be done in the way of immediate relief — Bonham already having sent a sufficient number of nurses and physicians, and a carload of supplies."

The seminary was quickly transformed into a hospital with makeshift beds. Guards were placed at the doors and a rope barrier encircled the building to keep the crowd of sightseers — estimated at 2,000 — at bay. Inside, as life slipped away, little Rilla Kerns lay silent.

According to the Bonham News article, Dr. Stell, of Paris, Texas, sat beside Rilla all Saturday night. The little girl was covered with wounds and bruises. When she drew her last breath, Dr. Stell cried as if he had lost his own child. The newspaper article said Sam Gill's head was split open and his brains were scattered out on the ground until a freedman scooped them up and placed them in Gill's coffin.

The Bonham News reported how witnesses described the moments before the tornado approached Savoy.

"From all accounts, the cyclone at Savoy was not immediately accompanied by a drop of rain. It had been raining shortly before, but as the destroying whirl approached, with a roar like a railroad train, all else was still. When it struck the town, the roar was a thousand times intensified, and mingling with the crash of falling houses and the noise of timbers snapping and breaking into kindling wood, produced a chaos of deafening sounds. In a second or two the cyclone was gone, the air clear of flying timbers, and the ruins of McKnight's Drugstore had taken fire — threatening a most horrible death to a number of wounded imprisoned under that and adjoining wrecks. Fortunately at this juncture the rain poured down in torrents, aiding materially to put out the fire, and filling the streets so full of water that it could be dipped up by the bucketful anywhere. A number of buckets were soon obtained and the fire extinguished. But for the very heavy rain immediately following the cyclone we have no doubt the wreck would have taken fire in various places, burned several of the wounded, and presented a calamity even more heart-rendering and appalling than the one it has been our painful duty to record.

Dr. Sam McKee says that when he came to himself after the cyclone, it was pitch dark and perfectly still — no rain falling. Almost immediately he heard his little girl cry — not as if she was hurt, but as if she was under something. Feeling around in the darkness for his child, he found Mrs. McKee, with the child under her. Asking his wife if she was hurt, she replied that her arm was broken. The doctor felt and found this to be the case — also that she was bleeding profusely. Taking the little girl across the street to the nearest remaining house, he returned for his wife, about which time the rain commenced pouring down in torrents. Help now arrived to get out the balance of the family, and they were all soon rescued and carried under shelter."

Word got around that the Savoy blacksmith, Mr. Brooks, had acted on a premonition of an approaching disaster, and removed his family from their residence. The house was destroyed by the cyclone.

Josie Kerns had a piece of white pine, two inches long and half an inch thick, removed from her back. Eva Horne was found in shock with a piece of pine driven through her forearm. Mrs. Finnis Horne's fractured femur was stabilized by plaster of Paris applied by Drs. Saunders, Hoy, Dorset, Wells and others.

Newspapers across the nation reported on the disaster at Savoy. Here is the June 10, 1888 edition of the Holton Recorder-Tribune newspaper published in Holton, Kansas.

"The tiny village of Savoy, Fannin Co. Texas, on the Transcontinental Railroad was almost literally wiped away by a tornado on the night of the 28th of May, 1880. Nine persons were killed and over sixty were injured, some ten or twelve of the latter having died within a few hours afterward. The village contained a population of about 400. The only buildings of any account left standing are the Houston Methodist Church and the Academy, the latter of which was transformed into a hospital for the wounded. Some nineteen business buildings, including the Railroad Depot was almost totally demolished.

The list of the killed is as follows: Dr. Joseph Kearns, William Sudduth, E. L. Andrews and child, Sam Gill, Ellie Gallagher, T. J. Cox, Miss Mattie Best, Miss Pantha Johnson. The more seriously wounded are Mrs. McKee, Edna, Robert and Sam McKee, Ema John, Ollord Horn, Mrs. Dr. Kearns, F. W. Foster, Prof. Holland's daughter, Hattie Johnson, Robert Johnson, Robert Gallagher and wife, Mrs. William Sudduth, Mrs. Dennis Horn, Mrs. M. I. Taylor. A number of these have since died."

Mr. and Mrs. William Sudduth are both buried at Sunnyside Cemetery in Savoy.

And now you know why, about this time of the year, the folks around Savoy remember an old saying:

Twas in the year of 1880 on the 28th of May, that a tornado hit Savoy and blowed it all away.
